title: Packers Bye-Week Rookie Report Card: It’s Been a Snap for Draft Picks
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers general manager Brian Gutekunst faced a draft with great challenges but great importance.
The challenge? The Packers didn’t have a first-round pick because of the Micah Parsons trade and had only one compensatory pick. The importance? Gutekunst had built a top-heavy roster, so there was a need for young, low-cost talent to come in and fill holes.
The Packers wound up with only six draft picks. Three of them have played well in considerable playing time. Here’s a look at the draft class at the bye, with grades done on a curve relative to their draft positioning.
Even while missing most of Sunday’s loss to the Vikings with a rib injury, Brandon Cisse leads all rookie cornerbacks with 573 snaps. He hadn’t given up a touchdown since Week 2 until bouncing off Minnesota’s Myles Price on the play in which he was injured.
“He’s a smart player,” position coach Daniel Bullocks said on Tuesday. “Doesn’t make the same mistake twice. As a defensive back, you got to have a short memory because, JG’s right, you play this game long enough, you going to get beat. He has the resilience to not get beat twice by the same play and that goes with his preparation. That’s a credit to him getting better, working the technique each and every week.”
The JG from that quote is, obviously, defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon. Gannon was bullish on Cisse’s potential from the jump, which is why he worked with the No. 1 defense throughout training camp.
What Gannon needed to see was how Cisse would respond to adversity. That first taste came when he gave up a touchdown pass to Justin Jefferson in the opener.
“Remember you guys asked me where can he go, and I said I’ll tell you when I see some balls get caught on him,” Gannon said last week. “Week 1, he got a bomb caught on him and he responded the right way. So, that was huge to me. That was kind of the first measuring stick of when we get into the season how is this guy going to be? He’s got quite a bit of resilience about his game.”
Gannon said resiliency is the key for any cornerback. There is no such thing as a “shutdown cornerback.” Just go back to how the Packers beat up on Christian Gonzalez a couple weeks ago against New England. Even the best corners in the league get beat. Only seven are giving up a catch rate of less than 50 percent.
“You are going to get beat,” Gannon said. “They are going to make plays and they’re going to catch the ball on you. It doesn’t matter how talented, how good you are. I think there’s a mindset and a resiliency, there’s a focus, all that psych, that goes into being a good player, especially with that position.
“When you get back in the huddle, are you saying, you want the ball to come to you again or do you get back in the huddle and you say, ‘Man, I hope the ball doesn’t get thrown at me?’ The great ones I’ve been around want the ball thrown right to them again. So, I think that’s a huge thing.”
Chris McClellan leads all rookie defensive tackles with 315 snaps. He has not made a huge statistical impact with 19 tackles, zero sacks and zero tackles for losses in 10 games, but the Packers aren’t asking their defensive tackles to be game-wreckers.
Position coach Vince Oghobaase said McClellan has done well in playing multiple positions up front while helping the team overcome injuries that sent Javon Hargrave, Jonathan Ford and Warren Brinson to injured reserve.
“One of the hardest things is consistency as a defensive lineman,” Oghobaase said, “especially early on in a young guy’s career like that – taking on the double-teams, preparing a certain way every single week, making sure everything from a scouting standpoint, a rep standpoint, a practice standpoint, that he’s doing the same things over and over again. That way he can perform consistently on Sunday.
“That’s my biggest deal for him is just being consistent because he makes some plays when he’s out there. But sometimes he has those bad plays that kind of stand out and how do we get back from those.”
Dennis-Sutton ranks fourth among rookie edge players with 314 snaps even while being the 120th pick. He has three sacks, four tackles for losses and two passes defensed. According to PFF, he’s third among rookies with 23 pressures; only No. 2 overall pick David Bailey and second-round pick Gabe Jacas have more.
His strong play against the run should keep him on the field once Micah Parsons returns.
“I think his attention to detail in the classroom carries over to the practice field,” position coach DeMarcus Covington said. “His effort makes up for a lot of things where he can just win with effort and not giving up on plays. You see him on special teams running down, you see him trying to block a freakin’ punt. He’s doing whatever we ask him to do at a high level and with no hesitation. And he’s able to line up in different spots.
“So, of course, you’re going to have some rookie mistakes here and there, but he does a really good job playing with high effort, getting out the stack, rushing the passer, setting the edge and all the above. So, I’m excited about his development and where he’s going, trending upwards and as long as we continue to do that, I think he’ll be a find for the Green Bay Packers.”
He already has been a find.
Jager Burton made his first career start against Atlanta in Week 3. His struggles in that game led to the Packers signing Laken Tomlinson, Kevin Zeitler and Mekhi Becton in the following days.
“For me, it’s like how can you find a way to turn stuff into positive things, and now I have guys that have been doing it at a really high level for 10 years,” Burton said at the time. “It feels like, if you’re in the business world and you go to a conference and see all these other people and pick their brains. Now we’ve got all these guys here who have been everywhere and so it’s just awesome to get to talk to them.”
Domani Jackson is the only one of Green Bay’s six draft picks who did not make the 53-man roster. He’s spent the season on the practice squad and not gotten into a game.
His development this season will be important with Keisean Nixon and Carrington Valentine set to be free agents.
Trey Smack missed a 53-yarder against Minnesota on Sunday. Out of 30 kickers who have attempted more than 10 field goals, Smack is 28th in field-goal percentage (71.4) and 27th in extra-point percentage (87.5). He’s missed a league-high nine total kicks.
Special teams coordinator Cam Achord chalked some of it up to “rookie growing pains” on Tuesday. Among the three rookies with more than 10 field-goal attempts, Smack is last in field-goal accuracy and second in extra-point percentage.
“You look at the league right now, I think there’s a couple other rookies that may not be doing great, too,” Achord said. “Some of that is the rookie stuff, and some of it is the consistency of the contact, which I think we can improve. You hope the more you get through the season, like that continues to get better and improve, and you hope you’re on the trend of the upward part of it towards the end, that you’re playing your best football here, December, moving forward.”
Smack was the first kicker drafted this year. Over the last 20 drafts, 13 kickers were drafted in the sixth round and attempted at least one field goal as a rookie. Smack’s 71.4 percent ranks last.
Typically, I'm a glass-half-empty kind of person. Today, let me bring some sunshine to a cloudy day. Yeah, the Packers got trounced on Sunday, but I've got six reasons why they can (and will) rebound. ⬇️ https://t.co/YPVQLYyTHn

title: With Sky Falling, Here Are Six Reasons Why Packers Can (And Will) Rebound
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers were beaten to a pulp by the Minnesota Vikings in every way imaginable on Sunday.
A high-powered passing game that dropped a series of bombs on the Patriots last week bombed against the elite Vikings defense. Green Bay’s defense couldn’t get off the field against a Vikings passing attack that played without three top performers. Green Bay’s special teams were outplayed.
It’s easy to be consumed by the doom and gloom, especially given how coach Matt LaFleur’s team seemed completely unprepared for the challenge. However, the Packers are 6-4 and, in a lot of ways, the arrow is pointed up.
Here are six reasons for optimism heading into the home stretch.
Lost in the shuffle of Green Bay’s inept offensive performance is Kaleb Johnson carried the ball five times for 35 yards in the second half. It wasn’t a case of one 20-yard run, one 12-yard run and three carries for 1 yard apiece. Instead, it was 6, 8, 9, 4 and 8.
“Yeah, I thought he did a nice job” coach Matt LaFleur said on Monday. “I thought he was hitting the hole, running with good pad level, pressing the line of scrimmage, and you can kind of feel him a little bit. I thought that was a positive performance.”
He played one pass-protection snap and “showed the urgency” necessary to stuff Eric Wilson.
With Josh Jacobs coming back – perhaps against the Rams next week – the Packers might finally have a one-two punch with Jacobs and Johnson carrying the load and Chris Brooks getting the third-down snaps.
“I’m excited about that,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said on Tuesday. “Josh’s situation is kind of fluid – hopefully, we can get him back soon – but I think that would be good for our offense, for sure.”
The Packers don’t need to run the ball great. They just need to be able to run the ball so the play-action game has some teeth and provide advantageous down-and-distance situations.
The Packers aren’t going to find a combination on par with Washington’s famous Hogs or the bullying Eagles line that won the Super Bowl a couple years ago. All they need is a line physically able to not get destroyed in one-on-one situations and mentally capable of diagnosing blitzes.
Maybe the Packers will roll out that line against the Rams. Center Sean Rhyan might be back after missing most of the last four games with an ankle injury and Kevin Zeitler was set to get his crack at right guard before he was injured at practice last week. The mini-bye leading up to the Rams game could get him healthy.
An interior of Laken Tomlinson (or Aaron Banks), Rhyan and Zeitler might be good enough to open holes in the running game, protect Jordan Love and overcome the coaching.
“I think probably half the teams in the NFL are kind of dealing with what we’re dealing with, you know what I mean?” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said. “Just injuries, all the things that come with playing a season. You get to Week 10, Week 11, that’s just kind of what comes with it. Certain position groups, whether it’s the receivers, the o-line, the running backs, any position group in the NFL, you deal with this stuff.
“Is it ideal? Absolutely not. But that’s the situation, and we’ve got to embrace it and got to make the most of it. So that’s what we’re going to do.”
Micah Parsons had 12.5 sacks in the first 13 games of last season before he suffered a season-ending knee injury at Denver. Now, after a long comeback, he might make his debut against the Rams.
“Well, that’s my plan. I think my plan’s been different than everyone else’s this whole time,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “We’ll see. Obviously, having been in practice and banking some reps, there’s still a couple more hurdles for him to clear before we can definitely say that he’s a go. But he’s been showing progress and we’ll see where he’s at by the end of the week.”
Here are a few Micah Parsons clips from today pic.twitter.com/PdywEhndBD
Parsons is a Hall of Fame-level player. Along with all the sacks, he was fourth in pass-rush win rate. He was capable of making a game-changing play at any moment.
“I'm expecting him just to go out there and perform and help our football team win and execute at a high level,” edge coach and assistant head coach DeMarcus Covington said on Tuesday. “That's really what I'm managing those expectations on whatever. I do know he's Micah Parsons and he can do what he needs to do to help us win.”
There has to be reasonable expectations, though. Tucker Kraft hasn’t been the same dominant player since last year’s torn ACL. Parsons will be a game-changer – at times.
“I think it’s realistic and I think I’m going to have terrible plays,” Parsons said when he returned to practice. “I didn’t go through training camp. So, am I going to be the All-Pro Micah, the person I once was this year? Probably not until later, after I go through all my phases and things like that. …
“I think you’ll see flashes of All-Pro Micah when I get to pass rush, and there’s going to be times when you’re going to be like, ‘Dang, what was Micah doing?’ There’s going to be times when I question myself, too. Like, ‘What was I doing right there?’ I’m not ashamed of that. I’m not afraid of seeing the failure because I just came back from an 11-month injury. So, I’m not shying away from the possibility of my bad plays but I will look forward to is things that I do do good.”
The Packers enter their bye ranked second in the league with 20 takeaways – one behind Tampa Bay, three more than Minnesota and at least six more than 27 teams. Their streak of six consecutive games with at least two was snapped vs. the Vikings, when Xavier McKinney intercepted one pass and Karl Brooks had to settle for a sack after forcing an interception.
That’s a sustained run at taking away the ball, leading to belief that there’s some staying power that the Packers can force turnovers as the calendar turns to December and runs into January.
Moreover, of the final seven games, the Bears and Saints have the fifth-most giveaways, the Seahawks have the seventh-most, the Rams are tied for the ninth-most and the Bills are tied for the 11th-most.
There’s a reason why Jordan Love had moved into the top five of the MVP race after his bombs-away masterpiece against the Patriots. The production dropped off the cliff against the Vikings for a myriad of reasons, but he is a top-tier quarterback – and any team with a top-tier quarterback has a chance to win any game.
Love is a modest 12th with a 96.9 passer rating. Importantly, he’s a solid ninth in passer rating, seventh in completion percentage and fifth in yards per attempt when pressured. Not surprisingly given the number of pressures he’s faced, he’s first by a wide margin in yards when under duress.
If the Packers can keep Love on his feet, he along with his dynamic duo of receivers can carry the team into February.
No, the remaining schedule absolutely is not easy. Green Bay’s final seven opponents have a combined .547 winning percentage, which is tied for the sixth-toughest remaining slate of games. They will play four games against teams that have a winning record, along with a home game against the Texans, who have rallied a bit with three wins after a 0-4 start.
Instead, the highlight of the schedule for Green Bay is it won’t have to play the Vikings again until either the playoffs or next season. The Packers are 6-2 against teams not from Minnesota and might have been 7-1 if not for some dubious calls at Detroit.

title: Week 11 Consensus NFL Power Rankings: How Badly Were Packers Punished?
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers might have been blown out of the NFC North championship race on Sunday, but they weren’t blown out of our Week 11 Consensus NFL Power Rankings.
Our Consensus Power Rankings take eight sets of national power rankings and turn them into one superior power ranking. The first-place team gets one point, the second-place team gets two points and so on.
After the Packers pummeled the Patriots for their fifth win in six games last week, they surged to 10th . After the Packers were pummeled by the Vikings on Sunday, they slid back only two spots to 12th.
The Bills are No. 1. The Packers’ NFC North rivals dominate the top 10, with Chicago fourth, Minnesota eighth and Detroit ninth. After the bye, the Packers will play at the Los Angeles Rams, who are 11th.
Here’s where you’ll find the Packers in each of the individual rankings, with more extensive analysis at the links.
Nick Shook is the only writer who has the Packers as a top-10 team . Barely, obviously, after he dropped them two spots and said the Packers are on the “edge of the quagmire” after their reliance on their big-play passing game was crushed by the Vikings.
“One might simply say the Vikings have the Packers' number; I tend to think Minnesota merely exposed a weakness that might hold back Green Bay as it fights to remain in the playoff hunt in the toughest division in football. That’s not enough to knock the Pack out of the top 10, but it does shake my confidence in them.”
The Packers inched back only two spots in Ralph Vacchiano’s rankings. The Packers were rolling until they were “completely bullied” by the Vikings’ defense.
“Sure, it’s just one game against a really good team, but the Packers are now two games back in the loss column of the three other NFC North teams. Green Bay has the bye week to think about that before trying to get back on its feet in two weeks in Los Angeles against the Rams.”
The Packers plummeted seven spots from No. 5 in Conor Orr’s rankings.
“At the end of the day, after several beautiful and frantic Jordan Love games, the truth is this: The Packers’ offensive line cannot handle a defensive front like Minnesota’s. Period. Love had one of the fastest snap to throw times in the NFL this past weekend. It. Did. Not. Matter.”
The Packers were pummeled but only fell one spot in ESPN’s rankings , which are selected by its team beat writers.
This week’s theme is non-quarterback midseason MVP, with Rob Demovsky picking receiver Christian Watson, who referenced his contract extension that seemed questionable because of his limited production and injury issues.
“Now that Watson is third in the league in receiving yards (916) and tied for third in touchdown catches (seven), a deal that doesn't even rank him among the top 20 highest-paid receivers in terms of average per year looks pretty good.”
The Packers fell three spots in the rankings selected by Chad Graff and Josh Kendall. Their breakout player is Christian Watson.
“The ambulance clip alone gives Watson the nod here, but the fifth-year wide receiver is having a career year on top of that. Watson is third in the league in receiving yards (916) and tied for third in receiving touchdowns (seven). Watson had not topped 620 receiving yards in any of his previous four seasons.”
The Packers tumbled four spots in Frank Schwab’s rankings. There are “concerns” after getting smashed by the Vikings, namely on the offensive line and a limited running game. However, the “bye comes at a good time,” he said.
“They were playing very well before Sunday, when they were crushed at home by the Vikings. The break gives the Packers a chance to regroup, and also perhaps get Micah Parsons back for a game against the Rams the day before Thanksgiving. The Packers should rightly believe that Parsons will transform their team upon his return.”
The Packers tumbled three spots in Pete Prisco’s rankings.
“The offensive line was a disaster against the Vikings,” he wrote. “That led to quarterback Jordan Love being abused all day, which can't happen if they are to be a playoff team.”
The Packers dipped two spots in Mike Florio’s rankings. He said the Packers “desperately” need a running game.
The Packers will (sort of) have their bye this week. It won’t be a full week off, though, with the Packers playing at the Rams on Wednesday. That means they’ll be on the practice field on Saturday, Sunday and Monday, on a plane on Tuesday and on the field on Wednesday.
The Rams are at No. 11 in the Consensus Power Rankings. They are No. 12 in Ralph Vacchiano’s rankings at Fox Sports, one spot behind the Packers. As part of a longer summary, he wrote:
“Don’t look now, but the supposed Dream Team has won four straight to salvage some respectability out of their season and maybe, just maybe, turn them into a threat again. The way the Rams are hemorrhaging players, it might be too little, too late. They will be without their two best wideouts, Davante Adams and Puka Nacua, for a while, and they’ve got the Packers, Chiefs, 49ers, Cowboys and Seahawks lined up when they come out of their bye week.”
Sportsbook odds are not used in our rankings, but they do provide an additional insight on how the teams are viewed. In Packers-related odds at FanDuel Sportsbook :
The Packers were +2000 to win the Super Bowl at the start of the season, crashed to +6000 after their slow start and finally rebounded to status quo after beating New England. However, they’re back to +3000 after losing to Minnesota. That’s 12th on the board and behind all the NFC North teams, with Chicago at +800, Minnesota at +1400 and Detroit at +2000.
Green Bay opened the season ranked seventh in the NFC playoff odds, fell to as low as +250 but were -230 after beating New England. Now, they are +128, which ranks eighth in the NFC.
Quarterback Jordan Love’s express train to NFL MVP was derailed. At FanDuel , Love opened at +2200, crashed to as long as +10000 but was fifth on the board at +700 after dropping a series of bombs on the Patriots. Now, he’s +5000, which ranks seventh.
The Packers are viewed as completely out of the NFC North race . The Vikings with Kirk Cousins are +145, the Bears are +175 and the Lions without Aidan Hutchinson are +250. The Packers are the caboose at a distant +2700.

title: Latest NFC Standings, Projections Show Packers Might Have Dug Playoff Grave
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Had the Green Bay Packers beaten the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, they would have taken a big step out of the seventh-seed pit they’ve been stuck in the last three years.
Now, it might be seventh seed or bust.
Here’s a look at the NFC playoff standings at the end of Week 10.
1. San Francisco 49ers, 8-1.
3. New York Giants, 5-3-1.
4. Carolina Panthers, 4-5.
The Three Wild-Card Front-Runners
5. Minnesota Vikings, 7-2.
7. Green Bay Packers, 6-4.
In the Hunt Because of Lousy Divisions
11. Washington Commanders, 3-5-1.
12. Tampa Bay Buccaneers, 3-6.
13. New Orleans Saints, 3-6.
15. Arizona Cardinals, 3-7.
16. Philadelphia Eagles, 2-7.
Had the Packers beaten the Vikings, they would have been in the No. 6 spot in the NFC and just a half-game behind the Lions, who they’ll host in Week 18, and the Bears, who they beat earlier this season. That would have placed the NFC North championship and a move up to the No. 2 seed – meaning a home game in the wild-card round with the potential of another in the divisional round – within their grasp.
Instead, the Packers are clinging to the No. 7 spot because of a flimsy tiebreaker. Seattle is No. 8 and Los Angeles is No. 9 because Seattle has the better NFC West record. Thus, the Seahawks rank ahead of the Rams, but the Packers are ahead of the Seahawks because of a better record in conference games.
With eight weeks left in the season, the tiebreakers are subject to change.
In this case, the tiebreakers are irrelevant.
After this week’s phony-baloney bye, the Packers will visit the Rams on Thanksgiving Eve. The winner, obviously, will be 7-4 and own the head-to-head tiebreaker. The loser, obviously, will be 6-5, so one game behind officially but really two games behind because of the tiebreaker.
So, it won’t be a must-win game for the Packers but it’s not too far off.
“Oh, for sure,” quarterback Jordan Love said after the game about being behind the 8-ball in the playoff race. “We’ve talked about [how] these are the games you’ve got to win – NFC North games, and we’re 1-3 in the North. So, yeah, we’ve got to obviously just keep rolling, take it one week at a time, like we’ve talked about.
“But we’ve dropped the ball in three of these games, obviously – two against the Vikings, one against the Lions – that you’ve got to win these games to have a chance in this division. Obviously, we talk about, ‘Everybody’s good, everybody’s winning.’ So, it starts with the division games. You’ve got to handle business, and we didn’t do that today.”
The No. 7 seed is a bad spot to be in because it means a wild-card game at the No. 2 seed and a potential divisional-round game at the No. 1 seed. But, at this point, the No. 7 speed would be better than nothing.
According to Tankathon , the Bears have the toughest remaining strength of schedule, with their eight opponents having a combined .630 winning percentage. The Rams are next at .597, with the Packers fifth at .547, the Seahawks seventh at .538, the Lions eighth at .534 and the Vikings 10th at .527.
So, once again, the Packers blew a huge opportunity against the Vikings. They would have been hot on the heels of the NFC North front-runners, all of whom have difficult closing schedules.
Remaining Strength of Schedule pic.twitter.com/gpSDHvHqyH
In the seventh-or-bust race, the Packers’ remaining schedule includes games against the Rams, Bills, Lions and Bears. The Rams have two games left against the Seahawks along with the Packers, 49ers and Chiefs. The Seahawks have the two games against the Rams along with the 49ers and Giants.
The Packers and Rams will have the equivalent of a mini-bye to get ready for their Thanksgiving Eve showdown.
“Certainly, we’re all disappointed by the product we put out there yesterday,” coach Matt LaFleur said on Monday. “When you’re playing a good football team, you can’t lose the turnover battle like that. We knew that was a critical element going into the game. They were 6-0 when they won the ball; now, they’re 7-0.
“It’ll give our guys a chance to reset, gives us a chance as a coaching staff to try to put together the best plan possible, because we know we got a really good football team in the Rams. I know they’re beat up in some spots, but I think there’s no disputing they’re one of the best teams in the National Football League.”
Here’s what the computers say about the Packers’ playoff chances.
According to The Athletic’s Playoff Predictor before last week’s games, the Packers had a 64 percent chance of qualifying for the playoffs, with a 13 percent chance of winning the division. At the time, a win would have moved the Packers’ playoff chances to 76 percent and loss would have sent them down to 46 percent.
Instead, the Packers have a 35 percent chance.
If the Packers can beat the Rams, that would rebound to 58 percent. With a loss, it would fall even further to 23 percent.
At ESPN , the Packers had a 62 percent chance of reaching the playoffs. With a win, that would have improved to 75 percent; with a loss, that would have fallen to 45 percent. Instead, it plunged to 33 percent.
At NFL.com , the Packers had a 62 percent chance of reaching the playoffs. Instead of 74 percent with a win and 45 percent with a loss, their playoff probability is down to 34 percent.
At Playoff Status , the Packers had a 66 percent chance of reaching the playoffs. Instead of 87 percent with a win and 56 percent with a loss, their playoff chances fell to 47 percent.
Using Stick to the Model ’s Playoff Machine, the Packers had a 62 percent chance of reaching the playoffs, with a swing of 72 percent with a win over Minnesota but 40 percent with a loss. Instead, their playoff probability tumbled to 35 percent.
“I think you’ve got to take it one week at a time,” Love said. “We’re 6-4, so it’s not like we have a losing record. We got to obviously just overcome, take it one week at a time, and win games. But it’s a disappointing loss, and like I said, you just got to get back to work.”
The LaFleur-Love teams have been good during their three-plus years together. They’ve never been great. The Packers' loss to the Vikings was the latest example, writes @JacobWestendorf . ⬇️ https://t.co/uBFicTGOLQ

title: Packers Rule Out One Big Change on Offensive Line But Not Another
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – In light of the Green Bay Packers’ offensive line crumbling like a house of cards against the Vikings on Sunday, coach Matt LaFleur said he will not be firing position coach Luke Butkus.
“First of all, it all starts with me,” LaFleur said on Monday, one day after a 30-10 loss to Minnesota. “I’ve got to be better and then Steno’s [offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich] got to be better, Butkus has got to be better and then our players got to go out there and execute and play with great technique and fundamentals and do their job.”
To be sure, nobody was good enough against the Vikings. Jordan Love was sacked eight times, tied for the most allowed in the league this season and three more than the team’s previous worst during LaFleur’s tenure. While there will not be a change on the coaching staff, there could be – another – change to the lineup.
The Packers lined up against the Vikings with Laken Tomlinson at left guard and Travis Glover at right guard, part of their sixth starting combination of the season. Kevin Zeitler, who was signed following the Week 3 debacle against Atlanta, would have started at right guard if not for what LaFleur called a “freak” triceps injury sustained at practice.
“That happens when you play football and you practice the way we practice. Things can happen,” LaFleur said. “You never want that to happen, especially in a practice, but you have to prepare and put these guys in as many game-like situations for them to go out there and compete to the best of their ability. Unfortunately, those injuries happen.”
LaFleur said Zeitler was “fighting” to play against the Vikings, anyway. If Zeitler was in line to start against Minnesota and thought he could play through the injury, it stands to reason he could be in the starting lineup against the Rams on Thanksgiving Eve.
The Packers have given up 25 sacks this season. A dozen came in the two games against Minnesota with the other 13 divided over the other eight games.
So, maybe the Packers’ pass protection is just fine so long as they’re not facing Brian Flores. Minnesota has won six of the eight matchups since Flores was hired in 2023, including five of the last six.
“I hope it’s just a Vikings thing, but you’re as good as your last game and, unfortunately, it wasn’t good enough,” LaFleur said.
They’ll need to be better – much better – against the Rams. In what could be a make-or-break game for both teams’ playoff hopes, the Packers must contend with two of the all-time greats with edge rusher Myles Garrett and defensive tackle Aaron Donald.
“This next D-line we’re going against is the real deal,” LaFleur said. “There’s some things I know we absolutely can be better at, and that gives me a little bit of confidence that we should’ve been able to pick up and then there was holes over the middle of the defense, which we were trying to exploit and, unfortunately, there were too many times where we just had too many free runners.”
It all took a toll on Love. Love was one of the worst-under pressure quarterbacks last season but had been much better in that regard this season. Meanwhile, Love has been a clean-pocket monster.
Against the Vikings, Love was 11-of-14 passing when pressured but that was offset by the eight sacks. When given time, he was just 6-of-13, including a bad red-zone interception.
“I think it speeds up the quarterback,” LaFleur said. “The more he’s getting hit, the more it speeds him up. You saw that late in the game when it’s 20-7 and we had a choice route called and Tuck did a good job of sitting down vs. zone coverage and the corner clamped down on it, and you had Christian Watson going over the top.
“But I think the culmination of hits affects the quarterback in such a way that he’s just trying to get the ball out of his hands, and I can’t blame him.”
With confidence, whether it’s warranted or not, LaFleur will go forward with Butkus coaching the offensive line and Stenavich coordinating the offense. It’s no surprise he’s going in that direction. Other than replacing coaches who left for other jobs, he’s made very few changes to his staff over the years – and certainly never in-season.
“Because he was the same guy when we were rolling,” LaFleur said of Butkus. “I think it’s easy to pinpoint and point the finger and everybody wants to pinpoint blame, but the blame can go to everybody. It’s all of us in this together. Certainly, again, it starts with myself and then it goes to everybody else. It’s coaches and players collectively.”
It starts with the coaching. LaFleur called the protection “pretty bad” and incorrectly believed his aggressive, downfield passing game would work against Minnesota’s aggressive, downhill defense.
“It’s hard to throw downfield when you’re on your back,” LaFleur said.
The game plan was a problem but so was the execution, with the protection unit losing physically, mentally or both on any given snap. Whatever is being taught on the practice field isn’t showing up with great enough frequency on Sundays.
He believes Butkus is the right man for the job, a belief that could determine the fate of the season.
“We lost some one-on-ones and we got to be better in those situations,” LaFleur said. “We’ve got to figure out a way with everything that they do to try to put our guys in the most advantageous position, and that can be tough when you’re playing against a defense of that style. I’d love to full churn all the protections, but even when we had more than they were bringing, we were still struggling.”

title: Loss to Vikings Followed Familiar, Predictable Script for Packers
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Never has a shrug of the shoulders said so much while saying so little.
Jordan Love was asked two ways why the 2026 Green Bay Packers were going to be any different than the last two iterations that were one-and-done after finishing with the NFC’s seventh seed in the playoffs.
The first time, he shrugged his shoulders before giving an answer that was straight out of the coachspeak handbook.
“I think you’ve got to take it one week at a time,” Love said moments after a 30-10 loss to the Vikings. “We’re 6-4, so it’s not like we have a losing record. We got to, obviously, just overcome, take it one week at a time and win games. But it’s a disappointing loss and, like I said, you just got to get back to work.”
When he was asked later about why he thinks this version of the Packers would finish any differently than the last two, Love punted again.
“You’ve got to take that one week at a time. I’m very confident this team still. It’s a frustrating loss. We’ve talked about it. We’ve been here before this season,” Love said.
“We’ve had some frustrating losses. We’ve had some good wins. So, it’s all about getting back to work, cleaning it up. Still a lot of season out in front of us. We get a little bit of a break to be able to get some guys back, get some bodies back. But, yeah, we’ve just got to find ways to overcome and be better.”
Love, to a certain extent, is right about taking things one week at a time. The Packers were on top of the world after blowing out the Patriots last week in Foxborough. This week, they’re back in the basement after getting blown away by the Vikings.
The problem for the Packers since Love took over as the starting quarterback is they have not won nearly enough games that have given them a chance to catapult to the top of the division, the conference or the league.
The big-game disappointments come every year. They are hyped coming into the week, but they make silly mistakes, turn over the ball and lose by looking largely outclassed by those top-tier teams are on the other side of the line of scrimmage.
The 2023 season, for all intents and purposes, was a gap year for the franchise. Aaron Rodgers had moved on, and the Super Bowl expectations that accompanied having him under center every year went with him.
Whatever happened that year to the Packers was fine as long as they got a definitive answer on if they had their next star quarterback in Love.
They did. Love and Matt LaFleur helped the Packers dig out of a 3-6 hole by winning six of their final eight games. They won a playoff game in Dallas and were a play or two away from knocking off the 49ers in their building for a chance to go to the NFC Championship Game.
To date, that was the peak of the LaFleur and Love era. The Packers have not won a playoff game since.
They’ve been considered Super Bowl contenders each of the last two years. They made big moves in free agency and on the trade market to try and shove them over the top of the mountain and into the winner’s circle.
Instead, the last two seasons have largely looked the same as the one the Packers are wrapped up in now.
There are moments of brilliance. The Packers were 9-3-1 last season in early December in 2025. The 2024 team had some high moments to put themselves in position to get back in a divisional race against Minnesota and Detroit.
The 2026 team has followed a similar path. They blew away New England last week to get to 6-3 and put themselves in position to tie Minnesota in the standings after being run out of U.S. Bank Stadium in the first game of the year.
If you watched either of the last two seasons, you should have known exactly how Sunday’s game was going to play out.
The Packers were outcoached, outplayed and outclassed en route to a 30-10 destruction at the hands of a team who has owned them since Kevin O’Connell took over as Minnesota’s coach. LaFleur is 3-7 against O’Connell since 2022. He is 2-6 since Flores was hired as defensive coordinator in 2024.
Losing in the division has become the norm since LaFleur and Love were aligned at the hip. The Packers have seen Detroit, Chicago and Minnesota all win the NFC North since they last claimed the division in 2021. The loss to Minnesota all but ended any hopes the Packers had of ending their drought this season.
Perhaps Xavier McKinney, one of the leaders of the team, said it best.
“We got too many ups and downs. We got our moments where we’re really good, we got some moments when we’re not,” McKinney said.
He’s right. The problem is the moments when they’re not really good always seem to be in the biggest games of the year.
That’s not going to cut it in a city named Titletown. Seventh seeds and playoff appearances are not supposed to be the standard. Greatness, is.
Even when the Packers do score a big win, there is often one big caveat to it. Their biggest win in 2024 came against the perennial thorn in their side, the 49ers. They were playing with a backup quarterback.
Their biggest win this year came against the Bears. Caleb Williams was on the shelf.
To be clear, the Packers have had injuries, as well, but Love has been available more than he has not.
The LaFleur-Love teams have been good during their three-plus years together. They’ve never been great.
After Sunday’s beatdown against Minnesota, it’s not hard to connect the dots to figure out this year’s team is not great, either.

title: Packers Overreactions: Enough Is Enough After Embarrassing Loss to Vikings
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers were crushed by the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday. Their offense was overwhelmed at the line of scrimmage. Their defense gave up too many third-down conversions. The special teams missed a field goal and fumbled.
The Packers had a chance to play their way out of the dreaded seventh seed. Now, they’ll be fortunate to sneak into the playoffs as the No. 7 seed.
That’s the lead-off to our weekly Packers Overreactions.
The Packers haven’t reached the Super Bowl since 2010. It’s an insanely long drought given the team’s uninterrupted run at quarterback.
Had the Packers beaten the Vikings, they would have had a chance to make a run at the NFC North championship. That would have meant a first-round home game (at least) to greatly improve their odds of postseason success. If nothing else, they would have gotten out of the No. 7 seed, which will be vital this year.
Now, they are clinging to the seventh seed like it’s a life raft. We’ve said it before and we’ll say it again. The No. 7 seed is a playoff death sentence if the ultimate goal is to win the Super Bowl. The wild-card game would be at the No. 2 seed. Win that game, and the divisional-round game would be at the No. 1 seed.
The Packers know that fate too well. In 2023 as the No. 7 seed, they upset the Cowboys before losing at the 49ers. In 2024 as the No. 7 seed, they were squashed by the Eagles. In 2025 as the No. 7 seed, they imploded at the Bears.
Avoiding No. 7 is especially important this year. As it stands, the No. 6 team will get to play the NFC East champions (the Giants) and the No. 5 seed will get to play the NFC North champions (the Panthers). The No. 7? Either the NFC North champions or the 49ers.
The Packers traded for Micah Parsons and signed him to a four-year contract with an eye on finally getting back to the Super Bowl. Now, two years are on the verge of going down the drain with the Packers no closer to the Lombardi Trophy than they have been the last few years. This coming offseason, the Packers will have to deal with a challenging salary cap and no first-round pick.
Beating the Vikings, obviously, would not have put the Packers on the fast track to the Super Bowl. But losing to them probably has put them on the fast track to another long offseason, an unacceptable reality in Titletown.
Offensive line coach Luke Butkus has been with the Packers since Matt LaFleur became coach in 2019. In 2022, LaFleur promoted Adam Stenavich to offensive coordinator and Butkus to offensive line coach.
Butkus’ group was overrun by the Vikings on Sunday. Again. Given all offseason to prepare for the Vikings, his group was trounced in Week 1. Given a chance to make amends on Sunday with the homefield advantage, film study and veteran reinforcements, his group was trounced again.
To be sure, the personnel is an issue , and that problem is way above his pay grade. However, the draft-and-develop Packers have drafted nine offensive linemen during Butkus’ tenure. Where has there been development?
On Sunday, the Packers rolled out a line that included a first-round pick at left tackle (Jordan Morgan), a second-round pick at right tackle (Anthony Belton), a sixth-round pick at right guard (Travis Glover) and a seventh-round pick at center (John Williams). The group has been fortified by a bunch of veterans, ranging from Aaron Banks and his colossal contract to Laken Tomlinson from the Cowboys’ practice squad.
None of them are good enough. None.
The Packers rolled out their sixth starting offensive line combination on Sunday. They had the entire offseason, training camp and preseason to figure out their so-called best five. Sure, Zach Bako-Bewele’s season-ending injury complicated matters, but that has nothing to do with what’s gone on at guard, where there have been four starters at left guard and three at right guard. Through 10 games, it’s anyone’s guess who will be in the lineup when the Packers return from their make-believe bye week for a showdown against the Rams.
It’s been a game of musical chairs, and they’ve all ended with the infamous sound played for the losers on the Price Is Right .
Against the Vikings, there were missed assignments.
Which of the safety blitzers should be picked up? How about neither. pic.twitter.com/reFvQUdXQH
When the assignments were handled correctly, the fundamentals were botched.
Geez. pic.twitter.com/0OAW1qD6oY
It’s only pregame warmups, but this was their first snap on Sunday. It meant nothing, obviously, in the grand scheme of things but was the perfect encapsulation of everything.
Tomlinson and Glover are the guards. pic.twitter.com/UWepTE60tM
Over the last seven drafts, the Packers have drafted 15 linemen and signed Banks to a $77 million contract. And yet, they still had to go to the scrap heap to find Laken Tomlinson, Kevin Zeitler and Mekhi Becton.
Player procurement is the obvious starting point, but shouldn’t the Packers have found a couple of solid starters through dumb luck? It’s fair to say that what Butkus is teaching on the practice field on Wednesdays, Thursdays and Fridays is not translating to Sundays.
Green Bay’s playoff hopes might rest on the outcome of next week’s game at the Rams, who feature Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald. If the Packers couldn’t block the Vikings’ Dallas Turner and Levi Drake Rodriguez on Sunday, how on earth are they going to stop a pair of Hall of Famers?
LaFleur preaches accountability, but it’s been absent with his coaching staff. To be clear, firing a coach is the easy part. Replacing him is more difficult – especially in the middle of the season. But given what happened on Sunday, there is absolutely no reason to believe Butkus can find a winning solution on the line. It’s time to give someone else a shot.
If there was one positive development on Sunday, it was the second-half running of Kaleb Johnson.
After getting stuffed in the first half alongside the rest of Green Bay’s offense, he carried the ball five times for 35 yards during the second half. Sure, the Vikings might not have cared about Green Bay’s rushing attack due to the score and, to their credit, the offensive linemen opened some holes. But Johnson ran hard and decisively.
All you can ask of a running back is to gain the yards provided by the linemen and then a little more. Johnson did that. When there was nothing, he found something. When there was something, he stepped on the gas, fought hard and fell forward.
There at least were some positive running plays with Kaleb Johnson getting some blocking. pic.twitter.com/BmJ7eits4T
It’s easy to see why he was an All-American at Iowa and a third-round pick by the Steelers last year.
More promising run game with Kaleb Johnson getting an opening. pic.twitter.com/E84dDROCzz
A total of 51 running backs have had at least 50 carries. Johnson ranks eighth with 3.62 yards after contact per carry. Johnson has 188 yards after contract on his 52 rushes. In a combined 97 rushes by Josh Jacobs and MarShawn Lloyd, they have 191.
Kaleb Johnson with some burst to beat the defender and then gains some yards after contact. pic.twitter.com/vcO4zNLOHB
There’s a chance Jacobs will be back to face the Rams. If not, he’ll be back in the lineup for the stretch run. A running back tandem of Jacobs and Johnson could be pretty good and deliver the offensive balance needed to take some of the pressure off the linemen to protect Jordan Love for 40 dropbacks a game.
The Packers' offensive line was ransacked by the Vikings today. You can blame the players. You can blame the coaching. You can blame the game plan. Really, it was an organizational failure, which obviously starts at the top. ⬇️ https://t.co/d7U3hc78tL

title: Snaps, Studs, Duds and Defining Stats From Packers’ Horrific Loss to Vikings
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers were exposed as paper tigers by the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday. Again.
Two months after the Packers were buried under a fourth-quarter avalanche against the Vikings, they were buried under a first-half avalanche in the rematch. Five minutes into the third quarter, the score was 20-0.
Game over. Drive home safely.
Here’s our weekly look at the snaps, some important stats and some studs and duds from a pivotal loss.
The Packers played 55 snaps on offense.
Quarterbacks: Jordan Love played 52 snaps before being saved from a further beating for the final three snaps, which went to Tyrod Taylor.
Love was 17-of-27 passing for 220 yards. He would have fallen short of 200 passing yards if not for a ball that went through the hands of tight end Tucker Kraft and safety Harrison Smith and into the hands of Savion Williams. Another 59 yards were lost on sacks.
The Vikings had Love seeing blitzes and pressures when there were neither. From a clean pocket, he was a woeful 6-of-13, including a red-zone interception in the direction of Kraft.
Running backs: As expected given the pressure-packed nature of the Vikings’ defense, Chris Brooks went from injured reserve to playing a unit-high 26 snaps. He was about the only player who performed well in protection. Kaleb Johnson and MarShawn Lloyd got 14 snaps apiece.
Kaleb Johnson with some burst to beat the defender and then gains some yards after contact. pic.twitter.com/vcO4zNLOHB
When Johnson was in the game, he got the rock. He was effective, too, with 10 carries for 42 yards. In the first half, he made something out of nothing. In the second half, there was some actual running room and his no-nonsense approach took advantage. By our count, 40 yards came after contact.
If you’re looking for some optimism, a one-two punch of Josh Jacobs and Johnson could be effective.
Receivers: Christian Watson (47) and Matthew Golden (46), as usual, led the way, with Savion Williams (20) retaining his role as the No. 3 receiver.
Watson has been on a heater for most of the season but the Vikings threw him on ice. He caught three passes for 37 yards. Golden was shut out until late in the first half and led the way with five catches for 70 yards; PFF charged him with two drops and he was 0-for-2 in contested-catch situations.
Returner/receiver Skyy Moore returned after missing five games with an ankle injury, only to suffer another ankle injury. So, he was limited to three-kick return snaps and zero on offense. Bo Melton also exited with an injury after zero snaps on offense and 10 on special teams. So, J. Michael Sturdivant played nine snaps as the default No. 4. He scored a 32-yard touchdown but fumbled on a kickoff return.
Tight ends: Tucker Kraft played all but three snaps. With Josh Whyle sent to injured reserve, Mark Redman played 21 snaps, Jonnu Smith played three and Drake Dabney played three.
For the second consecutive game, Kraft caught one pass. Redman was strong in the run game but his fumble handed the Vikings a quick 3-0 lead. Added together, the Vikings’ tight ends without T.J. Hockenson dominated the positional matchup.
Offensive line: The No. 1 line went the distance. The grouping of left tackle Jordan Morgan, left guard Laken Tomlinson, center John Williams, right guard Travis Glover and right tackle Anthony Belton was the team’s sixth starting unit. The team’s highest-paid blocker, Aaron Banks, played just three snaps on special teams.
Which of the safety blitzers should be picked up? How about neither. pic.twitter.com/reFvQUdXQH
It was a ghastly performance. Williams gave up two sacks; Sean Rhyan might return for the Rams game. Tomlinson, who was shifted back to his “natural position” of left guard, had his worst game since joining the team. Morgan played better after giving up a sack early in the game; Myles Garrett is next.
Mekhi Becton played three snaps as an extra tight end. He gave up one sack and one pressure.
The Packers played 69 snaps on defense.
Defensive tackles: Karl Brooks and Devonte Wyatt played 42 snaps apiece. They were followed by Chris McClellan with 32, Jordon Riley with 28 and Anthony Campbell with 25.
Brooks had one sack; the pressure almost created an interception. Wyatt had just one assisted tackle and one pressure. The Packers aren’t getting nearly enough bang for their buck with him.
Edges: Lukas Van Ness, who was questionable with a back injury, played a unit-high 37 snaps as part of a typically balanced approach. Brenton Cox played 35, followed by Barryn Sorrell and Dani Dennis-Sutton with 34 apiece. Sorrell’s workload was bolstered by another 19 on special teams.
Van Ness was probably the Packers’ best player in the game. He had 1.5 sacks; the half-sack was shared with Sorrell.
Linebackers: With Zaire Franklin missing another game with a shin injury, so it was up to Isaiah McDuffie (every snap) and Ty’Ron Hopper (all but one snap) to hold down the fort.
Franklin did some work pregame, which would signal that he’s on track to return next week against the Rams. Getting Franklin back on defense will allow McDuffie and Hopper to play more on special teams. McDuffie, a special-teams captain, played only three snaps in the kicking game. Speaking of special teams, Nick Niemann played a team-high 23 snaps and Kristian Welch played 20.
McDuffie led the team with nine tackles and Hopper had seven and one pass deflection. They tackled physically but didn’t make any plays.
Cornerbacks: Brandon Cisse suffered an injured rib when he bounced off Myles Price on his third-and-23 touchdown catch, so his day was limited to just 14 snaps. Keisean Nixon went the distance and Carrington Valentine replaced Cisse and played 55 snaps.
Kamal Hadden played two snaps on defense and gave up a long third-down completion on third-and-15 that the Vikings turned into a touchdown to lead 17-0. Benjamin St-Juste is a total afterthought on defense, though he did play 12 snaps on special teams.
Nixon was excellent. He gave up three completions for 20 yards and broke up two passes. Valentine gave up four completions for 33 yards. His physicality really stood out.
Safeties: Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams played every snap. Javon Bullard, who didn’t practice on Wednesday and Thursday and was questionable, played 36 snaps in the slot. Kitan Oladapo didn’t play on defense but logged 17 on special teams.
McKinney grabbed his NFL-leading sixth interception. Williams has been a stud for most of the season but not so much against Minnesota. He wasn’t bad – he’s a menace as a blitzer – but missed a tackle on the Vikings’ clinching touchdown.
RB Kaleb Johnson: Johnson carried the ball five times for 35 yards in the second half. Sure, the Vikings probably didn’t care about the run game at that point, but he ran hard and with a purpose. He had to play one snap of pass protection and stopped the Vikings’ blitzer in his tracks.
S Javon Bullard: The Vikings put Justin Jefferson in the slot at times, and he beat Javon Bullard for a pair of first downs, but Bullard also destroyed a couple receiver screens and pressured the passer with his blitzes.
Edge Lukas Van Ness: Van Ness, as mentioned above, was probably the Packers’ best player. PFF credited him with a team-high four pressures, giving him a dozen over the last three games. He’s had to lead the group without Micah Parsons. With Parsons coming back, Van Ness might get better chances to get after the passer. With six sacks in 10 games, he’s got a chance to get to 10.
CB Keisean Nixon: Justin Jefferson finally had some production, catching nine passes for 74 yards following his reunion with Kirk Cousins. However, according to PFF, Nixon allowed 1-of-3 passing for 8 yards, including a second-and-goal breakup that helped hold the Vikings to a field goal.

title: Packers Report Card: Grades From Another Beatdown Against Vikings
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The grades are in and, as you’d suspect, they resemble my marks in high school geometry. OK, jokes aside, even I was not as bad as the Packers were in Sunday’s game against the Minnesota Vikings.
In what was billed as a showdown between two of the top teams in the NFC, the Vikings dismantled the Packers in every perceivable fashion.
Arguably the best play of the game for Green Bay’s offense was one that probably should never have happened. Jordan Love threw a ball down the middle of the field for Tucker Kraft in the third quarter that bounced off his hands, off a defender’s hands, and into the arms of Savion Williams. The play was good for 25 yards, and could only be chalked up to sheer dumb luck.
That’s basically all the Packers had on Sunday. Here are our grades from a dreadful performance.
The success of this game was going to be on the shoulders of Green Bay’s offensive line. If the Packers could protect Jordan Love, the offense would have an opportunity against Minnesota’s secondary to put up some points.
If they couldn’t, it was going to be a long day for the offense. The score was 20-0 in favor of the Vikings in the middle of the third quarter. Jordan Love was sacked eight times in the first two-and-a-half quarters as the Vikings built an insurmountable lead.
When Love was pressured, he was snowed under. When he wasn’t, it was almost as if he was anticipating pressure. He sailed the ball over Tucker Kraft’s head on an interception that came as he was fading away from the throw. Even if Kraft is at fault for cutting off his route, Love’s process was bad on the play.
Love was actually better under pressure (11-of-14) than from a clean pocket (6-of-13 with his one touchdown and one interception). It’s just that the frequency of the pressure – 62.9 percent, according to Pro Football Focus – either led to sacks or simply made him uneasy on most dropbacks.
The Vikings defense pressured Jordan Love on 21 of 35 dropbacks (60.0%) and sacked him 8 times. Love faced a career-high pressure rate despite averaging 2.33 seconds to throw, his second-quickest time in a game. @MINvsGB | #Skol
“I think to your point, you take some hits in the game, things like that. As a quarterback, that’s the job,” Love said of the interception, when he acted as if pressure was coming when he actually had a strong pocket.
“You’ve got to be able to stay in there and trust the guys are going to get the job done around you and still be able to deliver. So, I’ll never make an excuse for that. You’ve got to be able to sit in the pocket and just trust what’s going on around you. And we didn’t do that on that play.”
Tyrod Taylor entered the game because of the lopsided nature of the score.
Love and Co. had very few answers for Brian Flores. They showed little interest in a quick passing game that likely needs to be employed against a defense like Minnesota’s. Instead, they tried their bombs-away offense but never had time to find any shots down the field.
They did find a little success in the second half when they switched to a no-huddle offense, but it was too late by then.
Christian Watson and Matthew Golden, who caught 17-of-18 targets for 335 yards last week, caught 8-of-13 for 107 yards vs. Minnesota. PFF charged Golden with two drops. Kraft had one catch for a second consecutive week.
Green Bay’s offense goes by Jordan Love and their passing game. They went nowhere on Sunday.
Perhaps the Packers have found something with Kaleb Johnson leading the way in their backfield? Green Bay’s bar to clear in the run game is incredibly low, but Johnson looked decisive on his runs and was averaging 4.2 yards per carry before the game got out of hand.
Of course, part of the reason the game got out of hand was the Packers’ need to be one-dimensional because of the scoreboard and their inability to consistently rely on their run game.
Josh Jacobs will likely take his role as starting running back when he returns from his finger injury, perhaps as soon as next week against the Rams or perhaps the following week. In the meantime, Johnson needs to be the one who is the bell cow, if such a thing exists for the 2026 Packers.
The good was that the Packers sacked Kirk Cousins three times and picked him off once. They held him to 207 yards on 21 completions. The bad? They gave up three huge third-down conversions that were at least 12 yards in length.
One was a 38-yard touchdown to Myles Price to give the Vikings a 10-0 lead in the first quarter.
The final one was a third-and-12 in which Minnesota was set up in a formation that made a receiver screen feel inevitable. Cousins got the ball to Justin Jefferson quickly and Jefferson did the rest, picking up a back-breaking first down. The Vikings would score a touchdown four plays later to put the game on ice.
Those plays were the difference between a competitive fourth quarter and a blowout.
Aaron Jones found his way into the end zone and did a Lambeau leap, which gave the Vikings a 27-10 lead against his former team in the fourth quarter.
Jones and Jordan Mason were solid if unspectacular for most of the game. Green Bay’s defense was good enough but did not make any significant plays against the run, either.
The final numbers were fine. The Packers gave up 106 yards on 27 carries to Minnesota’s running back tandem. They gave up 129 rushing yards total. That was not awful, but certainly not good enough.
Trey Smack missed another field goal. This one was from 53 yards and never had much of a chance. He’s missed nine kicks this year, which leads the league. The Packers are going to continue to ride the wave of a rookie kicker, but should they?
Ultimately, the loss of points did not matter on Sunday because the Packers’ offense could not do anything against Minnesota’s stingy defense, but it could matter in other games that play out this season.
The return game did little after Skyy Moore dropped out of the game with an ankle injury. J. Michael Sturdivant gave the ball away on a kick return in the fourth quarter. Meanwhile, Minnesota’s coverage was excellent and their kicker was automatic.
The third phase of the game was a decisive victory in Minnesota’s favor.
A lot of discussion is going to surround Matt LaFleur’s decision to give the Vikings an extra down in the first quarter. Minnesota was facing a third-and-8 when it was flagged for a facemask penalty. LaFleur’s options were to back the Vikings up 15 yards or allow them to kick a field goal from Green Bay’s 23.
LaFleur opted for a third-and-23 that put the Vikings back at the 38. Minnesota scored a touchdown on the next play.
From here, LaFleur made the right decision. Points are going to be at a premium against Minnesota’s defense, and Green Bay’s defense had played well up to that point. A sack would knock Minnesota out of field-goal range. An incompletion would have made the field goal harder to make.
Yes, the result was bad. The process, however, was good. A criticism of LaFleur is that he’s often too conservative. In that case, he’s coaching aggressively. Green Bay failing to execute in that situation falls on the players, not the coach.
“You got to roll the dice there and, certainly, that was a pivotal play in the game,” LaFleur said. “We can’t get beat in third-and-23. The odds of that are very, very low and they made us pay.”
The rest of the game? That’s fair to question. LaFleur did not seem interested in getting the ball out of his quarterback’s hands quickly as he was snowed under by Minnesota’s pressure packages.
“We’ve got to have better concepts to be able to get those balls out quicker,” Love said as part of a long answer about the pressure.
LaFleur and his offense found a little bit of rhythm in the second half by using some no huddle, but it was far too late by the time they made that adjustment.
Defensively, Jonathan Gannon’s defense did well to limit the damage from four takeaways to just three field goals but also didn’t take advantage of the Vikings playing…

title: Blame the Organization for Butt Whoopin’ Packers Were Handed by Vikings
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – It takes every player on the field for a play to succeed.
It takes every player on the 53-man roster – heck, it takes all 70 on the team – to win a game.
It takes an entire organization to win a championship. Or not having a chance to win a championship.
The Green Bay Packers got sacked by the rival Minnesota Vikings on Sunday. All week, the players and coaches talked about how playing at Lambeau Field would help with the communication necessary to deal with the Vikings’ pressure packages. The Packers had a veteran offensive line, unlike the first game, and should have been prepared after getting blown out in the opener.
All of that was nonsense. Complete and utter garbage.
“That was a butt-whoppin’,” coach Matt LaFleur said to kick off his introductory remarks.
Yeah, it would be easy to blame the offensive line for missing blocks. It would be easy to blame LaFleur for expecting that game plan to win against that defense. It would be easy to blame quarterback Jordan Love for being skittish in the pocket.
And all those things would be true.
The reason for the loss, however, starts at the top with general manager Brian Gutekunst.
It’s Gutekunst’s complete and total mismanagement of the offense that has the team in its current predicament.
It was Gutekunst who used a first-round pick on left tackle Jordan Morgan in 2024, only to stunt his growth by having him play other positions for two seasons. It was Gutekunst who gave the bank to left guard Aaron Banks in 2025 for no good reason . It was Gutekunst who released Elgton Jenkins after shifting him to center following the signing of Banks. It was Gutekunst who drafted Anthony Belton in the second round in 2025. It was Gutekunst, realizing the errors in his ways, who went to a rummage sale to find Laken Tomlinson, Kevin Zeitler and Mekhi Becton when his offensive line got crushed to start the season.
In 2019, which was LaFleur’s first season as coach, the offensive line consisted of left tackle David Bakhtiari, left guard Elgton Jenkins, center Corey Linsley, right guard Billy Turner and right tackle Bryan Bulaga. That team reached the NFC Championship Game.
On Sunday, the line was Morgan at left tackle, Tomlinson at left guard, John Williams at center, Travis Glover at right guard and Belton at right tackle. It was the team’s sixth starting combination this season. With mediocre blocking, musical chairs and a lack of continuity, Green Bay has one foot on thin ice and another foot on a banana peel in the playoff race.
The Packers should have five big-ticket investments driving the line with Morgan at left tackle, Banks at center, Sean Rhyan at center, Belton at right guard and Zach Bako-Bewele at right tackle. Banks, Rhyan and Bako-Bewele were given big contracts to sign/re-sign in free agency and Morgan and Belton are premium draft picks.
It’s not Gutekunst’s fault, obviously, that Bako-Bewele is out with a major knee injury for the second consecutive year, but there is practically no evidence that any of the four other starters he selected are good enough to be playing for a championship contender.
Which is perhaps why the Vikings for the second time this season showed the world that the Packers aren’t really championship contenders.
On Sunday, Banks essentially was a healthy scratch other than a few snaps on special teams. Imagine that – the ninth-highest-paid guard in the NFL isn’t good enough to start on a team with a porous offensive line.
The Packers like the 34-year-old Tomlinson so much that they moved Banks to right guard. It’s a position he didn’t play at Notre Dame and hasn’t played in the NFL.
“We were going to shuffle up the O-line a little bit,” LaFleur explained after the game. “I think Laken’s been doing a pretty good job and we put him back to his natural position, and we were going to let Banks compete at the right guard. He doesn’t have a ton of time on task at that position, so we went the way we did tonight.”
Banks should be a bedrock on the line, a reliable pass protector and power blocker. Instead, he couldn’t even unseat Travis Glover, who had missed the last four games with a knee injury, to be a starter at right guard on Sunday. At left guard, he is behind Tomlinson, a past-his-prime lineman grabbed off a practice squad.
During a feeding-frenzy game against the Vikings, Banks was a $77 million backup.
Offensive lines need to be powering teams into the playoffs. This offensive line is powering the team into a ditch.
At this point, LaFleur and his coaches seem to be in the chucking-crap-at-a-wall-and-seeing-what-sticks phase of the season.
That’s not what championship teams do.
Things should improve once Rhyan returns to the lineup, potentially against the Rams following the make-believe bye week. However, it’s not as if Rhyan as the ninth-highest-paid center in the league was playing like he was the ninth-best center at the time of his ankle injury at Detroit.
The personnel problems have been exacerbated by the clown show of learning before every game which five blockers will play the five positions. Continuity seems like a punch line to a joke rather than a plan on the offensive line.
And to top it all off, LaFleur and Love seemed to be expecting the blockers to perform like Fordham’s famous Seven Blocks of Granite line, which included Vince Lombardi, rather than the Five Blocks of Swiss. To summarize the first half: Love dropped back to pass, the receivers ran downfield routes and Love got sacked.
Love was sacked five times in the first half, which tied for the most for any full game in the LaFleur era. The sack total swelled to eight through two-and-a-half quarters, tied for the most allowed by any team this season.
It was almost as if the Packers didn’t watch the success the Bills had with a quick passing game during their convincing win on Monday night at Minnesota last week.
“It’s obviously a bad decision, because our quarterback was getting abused just like he did in the first game,” LaFleur said. “We had called some of that early on, and it really wasn’t successful until the second half.”
Finally, the Packers pivoted and they almost got back in the game, which led to this remarkable combination of stats, with Love throwing quick (either by design or by necessity) and still getting pressure at a staggering level.
The Vikings defense pressured Jordan Love on 21 of 35 dropbacks (60.0%) and sacked him 8 times. Love faced a career-high pressure rate despite averaging 2.33 seconds to throw, his second-quickest time in a game. @MINvsGB | #Skol
“I think we had some success in the second half jumping the ball, doing some things, but I think to your point, when you’re facing a defense that’s pressuring that way, you’ve got to be able to get the ball out quick and have those answers and find the holes in the defense,” Love said.
Love noted the complexity and challenges of dealing with the Vikings' defensive front but also said the Vikings didn’t do anything they hadn’t seen on film during the week of prep. So, in other words, the linemen were not prepared mentally and overmatched physically.
“It’s missed opportunities, that’s all it is,” Love said, “and the conversations are what can we do better? What plays can we do better to get the ball out? Obviously, whatever we were calling right there was not working.”
No, it was not. Which begs the question of now what?
The players are the players and the coaches are the coaches. Help is not on the way. Gutekunst picked the blockers. LaFleur picked Luke Butkus to coach them.
Ultimately, Gutekunst handed LaFleur a pile of chicken feathers. With seven games remaining, starting with Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald and the Rams next week, and a daunting road ahead just to squeak into the playoffs, it’ll be up to LaFleur and Love to turn them into something other than the chicken crap the Packers drowned in on Sunday.
From an ugly defeat, @JacobWestendorf has his weekly winners and losers for the Packers. ⬇️…

title: Texans' Key Matchups to Watch vs. Colts Include Nico Collins, Calen Bullock
full_text:
The Houston Texans have a pivotal game on the horizon on a short week against the Indianapolis Colts, as these two will be facing off for the second time this season on Thursday Night Football .
And this time, both teams have their backs against the wall with just three wins on the season and desperately need a victory on Thursday in order to keep any hopes of a late push to the postseason alive.
For the Texans to do just that, and also get revenge from their Week 3 loss against the Colts, they'll have to focus on a select few matchups that could dictate the result of this game, and take advantage of said battles.
Three matchups stick out more than the rest for this matchup, and deserve to be broken down a bit more to see just how the Texans can find their way to a fourth win on the season, and a bounce back performance from last weekend's loss to the Cleveland Browns .
With that in mind, let's take a look at three of the biggest matchups to watch for the Texans heading into their Week 11 matchup against their AFC South rival Colts:
When looking at the Colts' injury report, it's looking as if they could be without not just one, but both of their top corners on the boundary.
Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward have been listed as DNPs during the first two days of practice/walkthroughs, and seems to hint that Indianapolis might have to throw out a different look within their secondary against this Texans' passing attack.
Last week, it was slot specialist Justin Walley who took ahold of some of those snaps on the outside fo the Colts' secondary. And if that's the case again on Thursday against the Texans, there's a good chance that Nico Collins can go out and exploit that matchup in a big way.
Collins is coming off of one of his better performances of the season against the Cleveland Browns, where he saw a season-high 16 targets to convert that into nine catches, 94 yards, and a touchdown. Another game like that will make it a whole lot easier for Houston to consistently move the ball downfield, especially against a depleted Colts secondary.
The Colts' offense has struggled immensely when it comes to turnovers throughout the first half of the season, and a huge part of that blame can be placed on the shoulders of Daniel Jones. He's recorded a total of 17 turnovers over the course of Indianapolis' first 10 games of the season.
That creates a perfect opportunity for the Texans and their defense to take advantage of on Thursday night, and moreso within their secondary. Winning the turnover battle against this Colts offense is a must, considering how poor their ball security has been over the first half of the year.
And the name I'll be looking towards the most to try and generate those giveaways is Texans safety Calen Bullock, who currently leads Houston's defense in total interceptions on the year, combined with the fact that he just got his hands on an interception this past weekend against Deshaun Watson and the Browns.
Last time the Texans saw this Colts team and their offense, they won the turnover battle 3-0 and still came up short of a winning effort. This time, Houston will have to win that battle once again, but hope that it can result in chalking up a victory against this Indianapolis scoring attack that ranks 23rd in points scored and 29th in turnovers allowed.
The Texans' rushing defense has had its ups and downs over the course of this season.
Houston ranks just outside of the top 10 for total rushing yards allowed through the nine games they've played, but have had their fair share of lapses in games against the Jacksonville Jaguars, New York Giants, and LA Chargers, where they allowed over 100 total rushing yards on the day.
Ensuring that this week is not one of those games allowing 100 or more rushing yards will be extremely important to control the pace of the matchup. And knowing that the Texans have one of their toughest remaining matchups in terms of opposing running backs in Jonathan Taylor, it could be a task that's easier said than done.
The last time these two faced off , Taylor had a pretty quiet day for his standards. He had 23 carries for 68 yards, and had just one run that went off for 10 yards or more. A similar day on Taylor's behalf could be a huge lift to the Texans' chances of splitting their season series against this Colts team.

title: Where Texans' Playoff Odds Stand After Falling to 3-6
full_text:
The Houston Texans entered this season viewed as one of the NFL's safer bets to make the postseason.
After logging three straight playoff appearances and a Wild Card win in each , the writing felt like it was on the wall for the Texans to go and make another postseason run for 2026.
They had an elite defense on paper, an improved offense from the offseason, and a quarterback-head coach duo that has the necessary experience to seemingly make such a run possible for the fourth straight season.
But so far after 10 weeks, the Texans are far from in the driver's seat to make that fourth-consecutive postseason become a reality.
In fact, with their current record of 3-6 following this past weekend's loss to the Cleveland Browns , it projects to be a pretty steep uphill climb to make that playoff appearance actually happen.
No matter which way you look at it, the Texans currently project to be pretty comfortably on the outside looking in for the playoff picture in the AFC.
﻿ According to ESPN 's playoff odds via FPI , the Texans head into Week 11 with just a 31.2% chance of making the postseason.
To win the AFC South, those odds take a nosedive down to just 1.2%, considering the Jacksonville Jaguars sit four games ahead of Houston in the standings with just eight more weeks of action to go. The Texans have better odds to make the Super Bowl (1.6%) than they do to come out on top in the South.
Betting odds-wise, the outlook doesn't get much more appealing for the Texans. According to odds from FanDuel Sportsbook , Houston sits at +198 odds to make the postseason.
When stacked up against the rest of the conference, the Texans sit with the eighth-best odds to make the playoffs, sitting behind teams like the Cleveland Browns (-142) and the Pittsburgh Steelers (-300).
So is it impossible for the Texans to go on a run late in the season? Certainly not.
Actually, we saw Houston go on a similar run around this time last year when they rattled off nine straight wins after sitting at a 3-5 record after their Week 9 loss to the Denver Broncos ––and that also happened without their starting quarterback for three games.
Now, it certainly won't be easy for the Texans to repeat history here. Not only have they made things tougher on themselves by losing grip of some key head-to-head tiebreakers (against the Browns and the Bengals), but they'll also be dealing with a handful of impactful injuries over the coming weeks as well.
Azeez Al-Shaair was just placed on injured reserve to take him out for the next four weeks. Danielle Hunter is trending to miss his second straight game against the Indianapolis Colts. Even Houston's once-deep receiving core is slowly beginning to get more shallow without Jaylin Noel and Marvin Harrison Jr.
At the same time though, we know the talent that this Texans roster has around the building. Their defense has multiple Pro Bowlers, and the offense has been a step better than last year's product thanks to some C.J. Stroud heroics.
Pair that with a schedule that the Texans can take advantage of over the next few games against teams like the Colts, the Baltimore Ravens, and the Pittsburgh Steelers, and a nice three-game win streak could be exactly what Houston needs to breathe some life into their postseason hopes.
So while the Texans do have their work cut out for them in the weeks ahead if they want that postseason leap to come to fruition, they can't be totally counted out just yet.
If the next couple of games can swing in their favor, it could provide Houston the right amount of momentum that makes them a force that's too tough to stop in the second half of the season.
We've seen that be the case in 2025, and with a lot of the same pieces from that group still on the roster and the coaching staff, maybe history could be in line to repeat itself, despite many considering this Texans team to be dead in the water with a 3-6 record.
