title: Colts Week 10 Stock Report: 3 Risers and 3 Fallers From Win Over Dolphins
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts finally snapped their five-game losing streak with a 24-22 victory over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, lucking their way into a win. While it wasn't a clean performance by any stretch, several players made important contributions to help Indianapolis get back in the win column. However, there were also some concerning performances that left plenty to be desired.
Let's take a look at who's rising and who's falling in this week's stock report.
Seth McGowan continues to make a strong case for a larger role in the Colts' offense. The rookie rushed for 77 yards and a touchdown on 12 carries, averaging an impressive 6.4 yards per attempt against Miami. He consistently found ways to create positive yardage, using his physical running style to make life difficult for the Dolphins' defense. His touchdown also helped Indianapolis capitalize on one of its better offensive stretches of the afternoon.
McGowan has proven to be an excellent complement to Jonathan Taylor, giving the Colts another productive option in the backfield. He's shown an ability to handle meaningful opportunities when Taylor needs a breather and has made the most of the touches coming his way. With the Colts continuing to find ways to get both running backs involved, McGowan's role could become increasingly important down the stretch.
Justin Walley delivered one of his best performances of the season on Sunday.
Walley stripped Dolphins' quarterback Kyle McCord on the opening possession of the second half, setting up Adetomiwa Adebawore's fumble recovery in the end zone for a Colts touchdown. Walley also held his own in coverage, allowing just three receptions for 14 yards on six targets. It was an impressive all-around showing from a young defensive back who continues to earn opportunities.
Justin Walley and Adetomiwa Adebawore!!!! 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/6vRWIgioSk
Given the circumstances surrounding Indianapolis' secondary, Walley's play is extremely encouraging. With Charvarius Ward and Sauce Gardner both banged up, the Colts need their younger cornerbacks to step up and handle more responsibility. Walley is showing that he can contribute beyond simply filling a spot in the lineup, making plays on the ball and creating turnovers. If he can continue building on performances like this, he could become an important part of the secondary's long-term plans.
C.J. Allen continues to look increasingly comfortable as a starting linebacker in Indianapolis. The rookie recorded nine tackles, a tackle for loss, a pass breakup and a game-sealing sack against Miami, making an impact in multiple areas of the defense. He also appeared to come away with an interception in the fourth quarter, but the play was negated by a defensive holding penalty. Even without the interception counting, Allen put together one of his more complete performances of his rookie campaign.
CJ ALLEN INCOMING 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/7wGDIa7aCO
Beyond the individual statistics, Allen's growing responsibilities have been particularly encouraging. He's continued to take on a larger role in the middle of the Colts' defense, including responsibilities as the defensive play-caller.
Indianapolis has needed more consistency at the position, and Allen is giving the coaching staff plenty of reasons to feel optimistic about his development.
Though head coach Shane Steichen continues to vehemently defend his quarterback publicly, Daniel Jones has done absolutely nothing to warrant that level of defense.
Jones completed only half of his pass attempts (11-for-22) for 108 yards, a touchdown and two interceptions. His performance was bad enough to earn a 1.7 QBR, the worst by a starting quarterback in the NFL this season, according to ESPN Research.
Jones will remain the starter for now as the Colts go into a short week. Still, he’s running out of time to turn what has been a disastrous season around.
Tyler Warren had an unusually quiet afternoon against Miami, continuing his failry dissappointing season.
The second-year tight end finished with just two receptions for one yard on three targets. He also had one carry for three yards, giving him just four total yards of offense. The rookie tight end has been one of the Colts' most reliable offensive weapons this season, making his lack of involvement particularly confusing, especially in a game where the passing offense struggled to find much of anything. Indianapolis needed someone beyond its running game to provide a spark offensively, but Warren was unable to make much of an impact.
The Colts cannot afford to have one of their most important offensive weapons disappear from the game plan, particularly when the offense is struggling to generate production through the air. One quiet performance doesn't change much, but it's certainly an outing Warren would like to put behind him.
2026 has already been a tough season for Cam Bynum, and Sunday didn’t help him out.
The 28-year-old safety allowed a team-high 56 receiving yards and gave up a touchdown on a double-pass play by the Dolphins, failing to recognize the offense’s plan until it was already too late. As a result, Bynum finished with a 149.3 passer rating allowed.
Through 10 games in 2026, Bynum has struggled to replicate the success he had in his first season with the Colts, recording 34 tackles, only four passes defended and one interception. As a result, the defense has also taken a step back, making it pretty clear how impactful of a player Bynum can and needs to be for Indianapolis.

title: Colts Week 10 Position Grades: Young Stars Shine in Ugly Win
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts finally got back in the win column Sunday, defeating the Miami Dolphins 24-22 at Lucas Oil Stadium to snap a five-game losing streak.
But let's not pretend this was pretty.
Indianapolis improves to 3-7, and while there wasn't much to celebrate from an overall team perspective, a few young Colts are really starting to come into their own.
Seth McGowan, CJ Allen, and Justin Walley all made game-changing plays Sunday, and these three are giving Colts fans something to be excited about moving forward.
Here are my position grades from Week 10.
Another week, another brutal showing from Daniel Jones.
Jones completed just 11-of-22 passes for 108 yards, one touchdown, and two interceptions, finishing with an abysmal 41.5 passer rating.
Really, really bad. Again.
The calls for Anthony Richardson are getting louder and louder.
The lifeline of this football team.
Jonathan Taylor rushed for 83 yards, while rookie Seth McGowan added 77 yards and a touchdown on just 12 carries.
McGowan looks incredible, and with Taylor still getting back into his rhythm, Indianapolis might have a legitimate one-two punch developing in this backfield.
Not much to celebrate here.
No Colts receiver finished with more than 30 yards, but what can you really expect from a group of role players suddenly being asked to carry an NFL passing attack?
Laquon Treadwell's touchdown was a bright spot, but that's about it.
Tyler Warren has to be better.
The rookie finished with just four total yards of offense, and with Indianapolis losing nearly every proven pass catcher on this roster, Warren needs to become a reliable option.
Finally, some positive signs up front.
Despite losing Bernhard Raimann early, this group allowed just six pressures and helped Indianapolis rush for 172 yards.
Granted, it came against a struggling Miami defense, but I'll take it.
Indianapolis recorded three sacks and 12 total pressures, but much of that production came from blitzing defenders.
The front still struggled to consistently control the line of scrimmage, allowing Ollie Gordon II to rush for 76 yards.
CJ Allen absolutely balled out Sunday.
The rookie finished with nine tackles, two tackles for loss, and a sack that helped seal the victory.
This kid is starting to look like a legitimate building block for the future.
Considering Indianapolis played much of Sunday without Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward, things could've been worse.
Still, allowing Kyle McCord to throw for 209 yards in his first NFL start isn't exactly impressive.
Justin Walley, however, looked awesome. His strip-sack helped produce a defensive touchdown, and he's quickly becoming one of my favorite young defenders on this roster.
Not a great day in coverage, but the run defense showed improvement.
A.J. Haulcy's breakup on Miami's late two-point conversion attempt was absolutely massive.
The return game was excellent, averaging 27.6 yards per kickoff return.
Spencer Shrader drilled a 51-yard field goal, and the punting unit handled its business.
A win is a win, but this performance didn't exactly inspire confidence.
Still, watching McGowan, Allen, and Walley develop into legitimate contributors gives Indianapolis something it desperately needs right now: hope for the future.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Week 10 Snap Count Analysis: 3 Takeaways From Win Over Dolphins
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts came away with a narrow win over Miami, and Sunday's 24-22 victory also provided some interesting developments in how Indianapolis is distributing playing time across its roster. With several personnel changes and returning contributors, the snap counts offered a closer look at how certain players are fitting into their respective roles.
Let's take a look at the most notable takeaways from Indy's personnel usage on Sunday.
Few Snaps, Big Impact for Seth McGowan
Jonathan Taylor remains the centerpiece of Indianapolis' rushing attack, but the Colts have another running back increasingly making the most of his opportunities.
Seth McGowan continued his productive stretch against Miami, finishing with 77 rushing yards and a touchdown on 12 carries. Despite receiving considerably fewer opportunities than Taylor, the rookie once maximized every opportunity he got.
Taylor played 40 offensive snaps (68%) compared to McGowan's 17 (29%). McGowan's impressive efficiency (6.4 yards per carry) helped him and Taylor become the first duo of Colts running backs to rush for 75+ yards in the same game since Jordan Wilkins and Marlon Mack in 2019.
Taylor also had a productive afternoon, rushing for 83 yards on 16 carries while adding another 20 yards through the air. The two running backs combined for 160 rushing yards and a touchdown, providing one of the few consistent sources of offensive production for Indianapolis.
McGowan's development is particularly encouraging considering where he started the season. The rookie has gradually worked his way into the offensive rotation, and his recent performances have given the coaching staff another reason to trust him with meaningful opportunities.
If McGowan continues producing at this level, Indianapolis should have little reason to reduce his involvement in the offense.
Laquon Treadwell Leads the WRs
The Colts entered Sunday's matchup with a completely different receiving corps than a week ago after the trade deadline. That created opportunities for several players to take on larger roles, but one name stood out above the rest in the snap-count department.
Laquon Treadwell led all Indianapolis wide receivers with 52 offensive snaps, playing 88% of the team's offensive plays. Deion Burks was second with 34 snaps (58%), followed by Anthony Gould with 32 (54%). Ashton Dulin and Nick Westbrook-Ikhine played 13 and 11 snaps, respectively.
The early indications around Treadwell's workload show that he appears to have established himself as the Colts' primary receiver for the rest of the season. The veteran had already been a part of the offensive rotation, but the departures of Downs and Allen have seemingly opened the door for him to become a more prominent part of the passing game.
Treadwell made the most of one of his opportunities against Miami, catching a seven-yard touchdown pass, his first NFL score in over four years. However, his overall production was relatively modest, finishing with two receptions for 14 yards.
For now, Treadwell appears to be the biggest beneficiary of the changes to the receiving corps. His playing time suggests the coaching staff has considerable confidence in him, a logical line of thinking considering he's the most experienced player remaining. He'll have an opportunity to solidify that position as the Colts move forward.
Arden Key’s Return Takes Snaps Away From Caden Curry
The Colts received a significant addition to their defensive line against Miami, with Arden Key returning from injured reserve after missing five games with a hamstring injury.
Key immediately reentered the defensive rotation, playing 36 snaps (52%) in his first appearance since Week 4. His return also coincided with a reduced workload for rookie defensive end Caden Curry, who played just 13 defensive snaps (19%).
The difference in playing time is worth monitoring as Indianapolis gets another experienced pass rusher back into the lineup.
Before his injury, Key had been an important part of the defensive line rotation, starting each of the four games he appeared in. His absence created additional opportunities for the younger players behind him, including Curry, who had been working his way into a more consistent role after stringing together a couple impressive performances.
However, Key's return immediately changed that distribution.
That doesn't necessarily mean Curry has fallen out of favor with the coaching staff. Rather, the Colts now have another established option available along the defensive front, creating more competition for playing time at defensive end.
Key's experience and ability to generate pressure give Indianapolis another valuable contributor as it enters the second half of the season. His return also provides some additional depth to a defensive line that has dealt with injuries throughout the year.
For Curry, the challenge will be finding ways to earn back some of those opportunities. The rookie has shown flashes during his first NFL season, but the Colts' defensive line is becoming increasingly crowded as players return from injuries.
It will be interesting to see whether Sunday's distribution becomes the norm moving forward or if Curry can fight his way back into a larger defensive role.

title: Colts Keeping Jonathan Taylor Could Pay Major Dividends for Young Core
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have undergone significant changes over the past several weeks, with several established veterans departing as the organization begins looking toward its future. While those moves have created opportunities for younger players to step into larger roles, they've also left the locker room without some of the veteran voices that have carried the team through the last decade.
One player who remains, however, is Jonathan Taylor.
The Colts faced considerable uncertainty surrounding Taylor's future ahead of the NFL trade deadline , with the possibility of moving their star running back generating plenty of discussion. Ultimately, Indianapolis elected to keep him , providing some much-needed continuity for a roster that has experienced considerable turnover.
Taylor's value to the organization has never been difficult to recognize on the football field. He's one of the NFL's most productive running backs and remains a central part of what Indianapolis wants to accomplish offensively. But following the departures of players like Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, his importance to the organization extends well beyond his production.
Now one of, if not the most established, veterans remaining, Taylor has an opportunity to help guide a younger generation of Colts players.
And judging by the way some of those players already speak about him, his influence is being felt already.
Perhaps the best indication of Taylor's importance came following Indianapolis' 24-22 victory over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday.
Rookie linebacker CJ Allen, who has been working his way into a larger defensive role, was asked about Taylor's influence on the organization. His response offered an interesting glimpse into how much the veteran running back means to some of the younger players in Indianapolis.
"When I see JT play, he just inspires me because I know how hard he works," Allen said, then directing admiration towards Taylor for how much he appreciates the example that he sets.
"When I see JT play, he just inspires me because I know how hard he works" CJ Allen explains what Jonathan Taylor means to him and the Colts. 🎤: @AKinkhabwala pic.twitter.com/OutLrKVlS8
Allen explained that he pays attention to the running back's daily routine, including the way he approaches his preparation and gets his work done around the facility.
That distinction is important.
Taylor has already established himself as one of the league's premier players, earning All-Pro recognition and becoming one of the most productive running backs in franchise history. For a young player entering the NFL, having the opportunity to observe how someone at that level operates on a daily basis can provide a valuable example of what it takes to succeed professionally.
Allen is still early in his development, and the Colts are hoping he can eventually become a foundational piece of their defense. Having someone like Taylor around to demonstrate the importance of consistency, preparation and professionalism can only help that process.
The same sentiment was reflected by another Colts rookie, running back Seth McGowan.
McGowan, who has begun carving out a role behind Taylor in the Indianapolis backfield, made it clear just how much he appreciates having the veteran around, especially after all the trade speculation.
"I remember praying that he didn't leave just because I love playing with him so much," McGowan said. "He's become like a big brother to me."
"I remember praying that he didn't leave just because I love playing with him so much." #Colts running back Seth McGowan shared with Sports Director @ACwishtv how much he appreciates Jonathan Taylor's leadership: pic.twitter.com/DPlAV7ucyQ
For a rookie trying to establish himself in the NFL, having a player like Taylor in the same position room is an opportunity not many players get. McGowan has been able to learn alongside one of the best backs in football while beginning to establish his own identity within the offense.
The two have also developed a productive partnership on the field. Against Miami, Taylor and McGowan combined for 160 rushing yards, with Taylor leading the way with 83 yards and McGowan adding 77 yards and a touchdown.
Their relationship is another example of how Taylor's presence can benefit the organization beyond what he contributes individually.
Indianapolis is still evaluating what it has in McGowan and several other young players . Having an established veteran who can help them navigate the challenges of an NFL season provides a valuable resource as those players continue to develop.
Taylor's importance to the locker room has become even more apparent following the organization's recent roster restructuring.
The departures of Nelson, Buckner and other established players have changed the makeup of the Colts' locker room and leadership group considerably. While Indianapolis still has experienced players capable of providing that leadership, Taylor is perhaps the most important presence remaining.
Taylor acknowledged as much following the trade deadline, recognizing that those who remained needed to take greater responsibility for helping the younger players.
"We have to go out there and we've got to try to rally these guys," Taylor said, via ESPN's Stephen Holder. "But we also got to make sure that we're doing our things on and off the field the right way to show and set an example for the rest of the guys in the locker room."
Taylor has not necessarily been known as one of the most vocal leaders in Indianapolis, but leadership looks different for everyone.
Sometimes, the most effective way to lead is through example.
That's what makes Allen's comments particularly encouraging. Taylor doesn't need to be the loudest voice in the room. His actions are already providing an example for those around him.
Taylor's experience also gives younger players someone to turn to as they encounter the challenges that come with establishing themselves professionally. Whether it's navigating the demands of an NFL schedule, handling adversity or understanding the preparation required to compete at the highest level, Taylor has experienced just about everything the league can throw at him.
For a Colts team that is going to need significant contributions from its younger players moving forward, having that kind of presence around the building is important.
There is still plenty of uncertainty surrounding the direction of the Colts organization, particularly with the team undergoing significant changes and looking toward a different future.
Developing younger players will be one of the most important parts of that process. Indianapolis needs to determine which players can become long-term building blocks, and giving them opportunities to learn and grow will be essential.
Keeping Taylor provides the Colts with an established veteran who can help make that transition easier.
Allen and McGowan are two particularly encouraging examples. Both are beginning to find their footing in Indianapolis, and both have already expressed how much they value having Taylor around.
Those relationships could become increasingly important as the Colts continue evaluating their younger talent and determining what the next version of the roster will look like.
There is also something to be said for the continuity Taylor provides. With so many familiar faces no longer in the building, retaining someone who understands the organization and has spent his entire NFL career in Indianapolis gives the younger players another connection to the team's past.
Of course, Taylor's presence alone isn't going to guarantee that the Colts develop into a competitive team. Indianapolis still needs to make the right decisions with its roster, staff and overall direction.

title: Game Balls from the Colts' Historic Victory Over the Miami Dolphins
full_text:
Historic? Yes, that is a perfectly apt descriptor for the Indianapolis Colts ' victory over the now 1-8 Miami Dolphins.
Given the context provided by ESPN's Stephen Holder , that is one way to describe the Colts' 24-22 win over the hapless Dolphins .
According to ESPN Research: The Colts are the first team in the Super Bowl Era (since 1966) to win a game despite being outgained, losing the turnover battle and committing 10 more penalties than their opponent (13 to 3). This is a Dolphins statistic.
Despite the overall level of play at Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday, there were some players that stood out for their positive contributions in the winning effort.
Seth McGowan and Jonathan Taylor each have a case for the offensive game ball, but considering Taylor's fumble and McGowan's touchdown, I decided to bestow the hallowed honor upon the impressive rookie.
McGowan finished the game with 12 carries for 77 yards and a touchdown, good for 6.4 yards per carry.
Shane Steichen's post-game comments outlined how highly the Colts think of the seventh-round rookie, "Yeah, it's been great - he's seeing it really well, he's so explosive going through the line of scrimmage - when he sees it, he goes and gets it - but yeah, he just runs so hard and physical."
McGowan has seen his workload significantly increase since he received his first NFL carry in week 2 against Kansas City. On Sunday, McGowan's 12 carries were a career high, alongside a career-best 77 yards rushing.
The rookie's versatility and explosivity on kickoff also drew positive postgame comments from the head coach: "He's awesome, I mean, he's so physical, he cares so much, he puts in so much hard work, and so to have that versatility as a returner and a runner is awesome for our football team."
For years after the departure of Zack Moss,  Indianapolis has searched for a compatible backfield partner for Jonathan Taylor. As the Colts enter an uncertain future beyond the 2026 season, their backfield seems to have found a semblance of stability.
If all of CJ Allen's highlight plays had held up on Sunday, there would have been several voices in Colts' nation comparing the rookie's performance to another #53 who played linebacker in Indianapolis.
Despite having an interception erased by a Kenneth Harris' illegal contact penalty, Allen's presence left an indelible mark on Sunday's contest. The Georgia product finished the game with a team-leading 9 total tackles, 2 tackles for loss, a sack, and a pass defense.
It was the most impressive performance of the young rookie's career, which only spans three starts of significant playing time.
"Yeah, he's flying around - I mean, he's making a ton of plays, he's wearing the green dot [and] getting that experience in there is awesome for him - I'm really excited for his growth and his development right now," said Shane Steichen after Allen's stat sheet stuffing Sunday.
After an impressive first start filled with a few routine learning moments, the young linebacker continues to make strides every week.
His progress will be one to continuously monitor as the season dawdles along. Allen is beginning to show why he should be considered a foundational piece for the next regime to build the next winning Colts defense with.
Justin Walley also made a tremendous case to take home the game ball with his performance on Sunday. The young corner bounced back from a knee injury that had sidelined him for the last two weeks to put together a sterling performance for a secondary that desperately needed it. When healthy, Walley looks to have settled in as another bright spot on a struggling Colts' defense.
Spencer Shrader has been a revelation for a Colts team that is looking for small victories anywhere they can find them.
Against the Dolphins, Shrader finished the game 1-1 on his field goal attempt. His 51-yard boot amounted to the difference in the two-point win.
Each extra point, no longer the automatic conversion they used to be, ended up carrying its weight in the close win as well.
On the year, Shrader is 8-9 from 50+ yards, with a long of 59. After a close competition throughout training camp in which he was consistently pegged as the underdog, Shrader has given Indianapolis reason to consider a high-round RFA tender in the offseason.

title: Robert Hainsey's Absence Could Open a Door for Jaguars' Jonah Monheim Beyond 2026
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are set to turn to second-year center Jonah Monheim to start at the offensive line's anchor spot in Week 11, giving the former seventh-rounder a potential long-term open door.
The Jaguars will be missing starting center Robert Hainsey in a critical Week 11 bout against the New York Giants, head coach Liam Coen said Wednesday. ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported that Hainsey would be week-to-week with a knee sprain.
Jaguars starting center Robert Hainsey is considered week-to-week with a knee sprain, per sources. Very well could miss time but not season-ending. pic.twitter.com/8d6cqd5uxT
Now that Hainsey is set to miss at least one key game for the Jaguars during their playoff run, Jacksonville will get another extended look at Monheim. Good this look give them confidence in him as a potential starter in 2027?
Monheim, one of the Jaguars' last picks in the 2025 NFL Draft, has been able to carve out a role as a reliable depth piece for the offensive line since he was drafted. He started two games for the Jaguars in the place of an injured Hainsey last season, while also filling in for Hainsey during the second-half of the Jaguars' Week 5 Monday Night Football win over the Kansas City Chiefs.
Now, Monheim will have to do it again, and this time it will be on the road against an NFC divisional leader that has a defensive scheme that is meant to put pressure on the offensive line's communications and protection calls.
"We have a lot of confidence in Jonah," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said earlier this week.
"Jonah was playing really well during training camp, I don't know if you remember, and then we had the injury to Ezra [OL Ezra Cleveland], I believe, and we ended up playing Jonah at more guard. It kind of maybe put a curtain over how well he was playing at the time. We have a lot of confidence in him moving forward.”
Monheim was one of the few rookie centers to get playing time a year ago, giving the Jaguars an early look at a player who very well could develop into more than just solid depth. Monheim has impressed time and time again with the Jaguars, and there does not seem to be much concern over his ability to do so again this week.
"Jonah's only a second-year player, but he's very mature, takes things seriously, but doesn’t overcook it either, tries not to overdo it. Obviously played at a high level at USC and that's good football, so he's been in big games, he's been in big moments, he’s played big games," Coen said.
"And then I think just his preparation throughout the week, learning from Hainsey and that group and the communication. He gets a lot of reps during the week as well, whether it's stealing those reps in blitz protection walkthroughs, in run walkthroughs. In practice as well, he gets a lot of reps.
There are a few other Jaguars players whose futures look in doubt due to potential cap savings if they are released, and a strong stretch by Monheim could put Hainsey in a similar boat. According to OverTheCap, the Jaguars would save a little over $7 million in March if they release Hainsey with a post-June 1st designation. They would still have dead money for a few years due to void years on his deal, but it would make sense for the Jaguars to back out of Hainsey's deal a year early if Monheim plays well down the stretch.
Monheim's limited flashes over the last two seasons have looked at least on par with Hainsey, who was an important addition last March due to his connection with Coen after their time together in Tampa Bay. Hainsey has played solid football for the Jaguars, is a two-time captain, and is a big reason they are 7-2 with one of the NFL's best offenses.
But the NFL is still about drafting and developing. Teams around the NFL each year are seeing younger, cheaper players take prominent roles from more experienced veterans in the same situation. If Monheim plays well in Hainsey's place this week and potentially beyond, then the Jaguars will need to at least ask the tough question.

title: 3 Unsung Jaguars Who've Already Made Their Case to Stay in 2027
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars will have a lot of tough decisions to make after the 2026 season, decisions that got even tougher after the Jaguars' flurry of moves at the trade deadline a week ago.
But beyond those headline decisions, the Jaguars have smaller decisions to weigh just like they must each offseason. The decisions on which role players and underrated contributors to keep as the Jaguars continue to build and reinvent themselves each season.
So, which of those underrated players have played key roles in getting the Jaguars to 7-2 and deserve consideration to be brought back next offseason? We break it down below.
The Jaguars will be hoping the additions of Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates make an impact right off the bat in terms of boosting the defensive line and secondary. The one position group that wasn't touched by Jaguars general manager James Gladstone at the trade deadline was linebacker, where the Jaguars made a big bet this offseason on Ventrell Miller and Branson Combs to replace Devin Lloyd.
That bet has paid off, with Miller posing some of the best run-defense numbers of any linebacker in football. He is appreciated inside Jacksonville, but he is likely the best Jaguars player who gets no credit from outside analysts for the Jaguars' defensive success. It is hard to imagine the Jaguars would be as physical as they are without Miller in the middle, and the Jaguars should work to ensure that he sticks in the picture this offseason. He has plenty of value to the Jaguars' defense and is unlikely yto cost what Lloyd did last March.
The Jaguars' special teams unit had a few off games at the start of the season, but they have turned it around in a big way since then. They have been strong on kickoff and punt coverage more often than not, while the return teams have made some big plays in critical moments to give the Jaguars more bites at the apple. Jaguars backup linebacker Jahlani Tavai has been an underrated part of those efforts.
Jacksonville added Tavai during training camp when they were hit by a rask of injuries at the linebacker spot, and he has been consistent for them in his role since. He is a true core-four special teamer, and the Jaguars could bring him back next year the same way they brought back Quintin Morris and Matt Dickerson on small deals this past offseason. Tavai has been a helpful addition for the Jaguars special teams and deserves to stick around.
The Jaguars' running back room has played a big role in their success this season, with Bhayshul Tuten taking the massive second-year leap that has turned him into one of the NFL's most consistent producers at the position. Add in Chris Rodriguez's value as a short-yardage runner and then LeQuint Allen and Ameer Abdullah in specific roles, and the Jaguars would be wise to keep this room together next season as well.
The only member of the unit who is currently not under contract for 2027 is Abdullah, who has steppped in as the Jaguars' No. 3 running back this season after a stellar training camp. Abdullah has gotten chunk yards when utilized on offense, but his special teams value has been even clearer -- they do not beat the Eagles in Week 5 without his big return. Add in his leadership value to a young Jaguars' running back room and the Jaguars should do what it takes to bring Abdullah back as a key depth piece next season.

title: Giants Give Jaguars Their Toughest Post-Bye Week Test Yet, With Plenty of Answers at Stake
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are set to be tested in Week 11, which is a good thing.
The Jaguars have not played in many close games in 2026. Their loss to the Denver Broncos came down to one score in Week 2, and then they had three games in a row get decided in the late fourth quarter from Weeks 4 through 6. But ever since the bye week, things have gone smooth for Jacksonville. Too smooth, even.
Jacksonville is 3-0 since the bye week, outscoring their opponents 115-30 in the process. But for as dominant as the Jaguars looked during their Week 10 win over the Tennessee Titans, there are bigger challenges down the road. One of those challenges is set to come in Week 11 in the form of a road battle with the New York Giants.
The impressive thing about this Jaguars team is the fact that they have learned how to win games in so many different ways. Now that they are going on the road against a quality team with a young quarterback who has made a few plays, they will have to continue to find ways to adapt to win.
“Yeah, I think what's fun about this group is, you can win games but also keep coaching and keep learning and keep growing," Jaguars head coach Coen said on Monday.
"Sometimes, like we’ve said before, winning's a great deodorant. And sometimes things can get let go and maybe not harped on as much or you emphasize it, but the players are like, ‘Yeah, man, what do you mean, dude? We're winning. We don't really need to fix that.’ Does that occur still organically? I'm sure in some ways, but I think this team is very focused on improvement, on daily improvement, weekly improvement. They take it seriously."
The first three teams the Jaguars have played out of the bye week have been the Indianapolis Colts, a reeling Baltimore Ravens team, and a scrappy but losing Tennessee Titans team. That is far from a murderer's row of teams, while the Giants are 5-3-1 and look like a likely playoff team in the NFC. They are still early in the John Harbaugh era and JJ McCarthy is still far from a consistent quarterback, but they pose a greater threat to the Jaguars than any other team has since Jacksonville played the Houston Texans in London in Week 6.
But that is a good thing for the Jaguars. As impressive as their run has been, the Colts, Ravens and Giants are nothing like future tests the Jaguars face with the Chicago Bears and eventually a tough AFC playoff field. The Jaguars need to be tested, with Coen noting Monday that it was good to see the Jaguars have to put a game away in the fourth quarter after so many recent blowouts.
Those are the kinds of games the Jaguars will have to win down the road if they intend to do more than just win the AFC South. That is the kind of game the Giants could offer the Jaguars, giving them a test they have not seen nearly often enough over the last month or so. There are a few specific questions the Giants can help answer, too.
The Giants have a multiple front that throws blitzes, man coverage, and a barrage of pass-rushers at offense. The Giants rank No. 4 in the NFL in blitz rate, and these are the kinds of defenses that the Jaguars have been hit-or-miss against over the last 1.5 seasons. If the Jaguars can move the ball through the air against this unit, then there should be confidence in them doing so against several others.
As for the offensive side of the ball, the Giants have leaned on explosive plays downfield in McCarthy's limited time as their starter. It is a feast or famine play-style, and one that the Jaguars will likely see sometime again down the road in the AFC playoffs. For a defense that is set to add Jessie Bates III to the back end this week, the question of whether they can limit explosive passes is still very real.
The Jaguars are due for a test, and the Giants are uniquely set up to offer them the exact type of test they need to see on both sides of the ball. A win with some confidence behind it in Week 11, and we might have to start resetting the Jaguars' standard once again.

title: Good, Bad, and Ugly From Jaguars' Week 10: From New Faces to the AFC's Elite Tier
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are sitting alone at the top of the AFC South after Week 10, and there is plenty of good to go around.
After the Jaguars' 40-23 romping of the Tennessee Titans, the Jaguars are 7-2 or better through nine games for the first time since 1999, when they went on to finish 14-2 and reach the AFC Championship Game.
Jacksonville also has a +125 point differential this season, the best in the NFL and the 2nd-best through nine games in franchise history (+137 in 1999). This looks like one of the best Jaguars teams in franchise history through one half of the season, and this does not even account for the Jaguars' reinforcements via Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates III.
So, what exactly did Week 10 bring for the Jaguars? From the good, bad, and the ugly, we break it all down.
There was a lot of good to around for the Jaguars in Week 10. The Jaguars started the week off with a bang, adding two blue-chip defenders in Davis and Bates to positions where the Jaguars just got dealt season-ending injuries to their starters. The Jaguars value their defensive depth, but it would have been hard to match up with the Cincinnati Bengals and Buffalo Bills in January without making some kind of moves, and Week 10 showed us exactly why the Jaguars will need Bates and Davis to make a quick impact.
Jacksonville also scored 40 points against an AFC South foe for the second time this season, doing so earlier in Week 8 in a blowout of the Indianapolis Colts. In three AFC South games this year, the Jaguars have outscored their foes 113-64 ... and 34 of those points came against the Houston Texans. In the last two AFC South games, they have outscored the Colts and Titans 82-30. Jacksonville had the Texans open the door for a quick AFC South title run , and they certainly look capable of taking advantage of it.
Finally, there is the performance of rookie wide receiver Josh Cameron. He not only caught his third touchdown of the season on Sunday, but he also made a big impact as a run-blocker by springing Bhayshul Tuten on his fourth-quarter touchdown to give the Jaguars the 40-burger. He looks like an ascending piece of this offense in a big way.
The only real bad thing that happened to the Jaguars in Week 10 is the fact that the AFC's elite tier did nothing to help them when it comes to their big-picture goals. The Jaguars need to win the AFC South before they do anything, but once they do that they can turn to earning their first No. 1 seed of this century. But for that to happen, they need a few results to go their way over the next two months worth of games.
Those results did not happen in Week 10. The Buffalo Bills, Cincinnati Bengals, and Kansas City Chiefs went 3-0, while the Denver Broncos were on a bye week. It is a good thing that the AFC South race got boosted thanks to the Texans' big flop in Cleveland, but there were no other favors done for the Jaguars. For as good as the trade deadline and then game day went for the Jaguars this week, the rest of Sunday's results were not very friendly. It happens.

title: Jaguars Overreactions: Parker Washington Has Become a Bonafide WR1
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars continue to look like one of the best teams in football through 10 weeks, and they are answering more questions each week.
That, of course, does not mean each set of four-quarter battles do not give us new lessons and, in some cases, new overreactions based on the latest performances.
So, what overreactions do we have on hand after the 40-23 win over the Tennessee Titans? We break it down below.
The Jaguars may not have a No. 1 receiver by true definition, at least not in the same sense that so many other teams do. They do not have a singular high-volume target hog like some of the other top wide receivers in the NFL, so in some cases he might not be viewed from the same lens. The Jaguars spread the ball around (nine different players caught a pass Sunday), and it is often week-to-week on who will command the lion's share of the passing work in any given game.
Despite all of this, Washington is the Jaguars' alpha male in the receiver room. No matter what definition a No. 1 receiver has in the Jaguars' scheme, Washington fits it. He completely took over the game during a career-best first-half that saw him rack up nearly 150 receiving yards and a touchdown in two quarters alone. He also did it while serving as a momentary high-volume target, because that is what the Jaguars needed him to be at the time.
Washington ranks just No. 14 amongst qualifying wide receivers in target share, yet he has been able to produce with the NFL's best when the Jaguars do funnel their passing game through him. Washington is the Jaguars' go-to guy, and he is a legit No. 1 no matter what way you want to slice it, too.
Trevor Lawrence continued his recent heater , having another explosive game against the Titans and seemingly hitting big plays at will. I believe this is the best version of Lawrence we have ever seen, especially over the last four games. In that span, the Jaguars are 3-1, have averaged 36.5 points per game, and Lawrence has thrown 11 touchdowns, two interceptions and thrown for 1,110 yards. Even by the advanced metrics, this is the best four-game stretch Lawrence has ever played -- even counting the best four-game spans he had during his 2022 and 2025 hot streaks.
Lawrence has become a brand-new player for the Jaguars. He was already really, really good. Now, he is one of the best players in the entire NFL at the position, and he has the Jaguars capable of being a Super Bowl team in any given season if he stays at this level. Lawrence has played good quarterback throughout his career, but this is, by far, the best he has ever played as Jacksonville's franchise quarterback.
The Jaguars will be adding two important pieces to the defense in Week 11 in Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates III, and there is a fair question of which one the Jaguars might need more. Bates is a ballhawk who could provide the Jaguars with a reliable veteran playmaker to help replace Eric Murray in the defense's youngest position group, and he is also a legitimate All-Pro player. With that said, I think the Jaguars need Davis even more right now.
The entire basis of the Jaguars' defense starts with stopping the run, something the Jaguars have not done as well over the last two weeks without Davon Hamilton. The Jaguars play with a lot of light boxes on early downs, which means the defense needs to stop the run by its defensive line taking on double teams and re-setting the line of scrimmage, which has not happened often enough without Hamilton.
Against the Titans, the Jaguars allowed 105 rushing yards, 6.2 yards per run, four rushes of 10-yards or more, and their worst performance against the run this year in terms of rushing EPA/Play. The defense is missing a dominant nose tackle, and Davis will need to be that quickly.

title: 3 Areas Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates Must Help the Jaguars Right Away
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are set to see two big debuts in Week 11 against the New York Giants.
The Jaguars sat new defenders Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates in Week 10 against the Tennessee Titans, opting to give each veteran the bye week they never got before the trade deadline, which meant putting the debuts of two notable new faces on the backburner for at least a week. back burner
After a win against the Titans improved the Jaguars to 7-2 without their new additions, Week 11 will give us a chance to see what the new-look Jaguars actually, well, look like.
So with the Titans game in the rearview mirror as the Jaguars continue their push for an AFC South title, what are the areas the Jaguars will need to see Davis and Bates make an impact in right away? We break it down below.
The Jaguars' defensive line has played a massive role in the unit's strong play over the last two seasons, but especially in 2026. The Jaguars are entering Week 11 as the No. 4 defense in EPA/Play, No. 2 defense in points per game allowed, and No. 7 in success rate. There are things they could do better, just like any defense, but it is a very, very good unit, and the defensive line has been a critical piece to that.
But if there is one thing the Jaguars have perhaps not gotten from the defensive line at a high clip this year, it is splash plays. Jordan Davis may not be known much for his pass-rushing stats, but according to NextGenStats he has recorded 25 stops this year. A stop is defined as a play that results in negative EPA for the offense, and no Jaguars interior defensive lineman has more than 13 stops this year. The leader in stops among the defensive tackles is Davon Hamilton, who is out for the rest of the year.
Davis does not need to collect sacks at a high clip to create more splash plays for the defensive line. He is naturally suited to set things up for those around him with his ability to eat blocks as well as play behind the line of scrimmage. If he can help the Jaguars here, he can make the entire unit look different on early downs in terms of overall impact.
Missed tackles have not been a huge issue for the Jaguars throughout the season, but we have seen teams get explosive plays against them in recent weeks due to missed tackles. Liam Coen noted it was an area they could improve both after Week 9 and Week 10, and it directly led to one of the TItans' lone touchdowns after multiple missed tackles on Tony Pollard on one play. While it has not been a rampant issue, it can not afford to show up against better teams.
Bates is one of the best tacklers in football , especially in space. The veteran safety has proven time and time again that he can be a trusted last line of defense for a secondary, and that is exactly what the Jaguars have needed at times since the bye week ended. If Bates can come in and make reliable tackles from the jump, it will help the Jaguars instantly. Bates is good at a lot of things, but making tackles when needed to is what he might do best.
The Jaguars' issue with explosive plays, especially before the bye week, was not only a function of missed tackles at critical moments. The Jaguars simply had too many footballs go over their heads and too many communication breakdowns during the first-half of the season, which led to explosive plays allowed downfield in their only two losses of the season to the Denver Broncos and Houston Texans.
If Bates can take command in the backend of the secondary and help put an end to the explosive plays allowed by the defense through the air, it will pay dividends. The entire point of the Jaguars' scheme is to limit big plays and force offense to try to dink and dunk their way down the field to earn points. If the Jaguars can prevent big plays through the air with Bates in the middle of the field, it could take the defense from being better at just preventing points and red-zone scores. Take away the explosive plays, and there is not much more the unit would have to worry about.

title: 5 Most Improved Jaguars Since Bye Week, and Why They Could Tilt Scales in AFC
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are learning the value of winning in different ways.
The Jaguars have done it with air attacks, on the ground, shut-down days on defense, and everything in between. Sunday's 40-23 win over the Tennessee Titans felt like a game in which all three units had to chip in at the right times to lift them over the Titans and to 7-2.
"Was it perfect throughout the game? No. But situational football, these guys pay attention to because they know how many games come down to one scores in this league," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said Monday. "To not be ever losing in the game, I think was… We controlled the game. Was it perfect? Again, like I said, no, but they keep growing together as a team and learn to win different ways. That's what I think is cool about this group.”
The latest Jaguars win is the team's third in a row since the Jaguars' Week 7 bye week, and the Jaguars have seen the post-bye stakes and performances elevated just like they were a year ago. Also just like a year ago, that improvement has been based around several key performances.
So, which Jaguars have improved the most since the Jaguars' bye week, and why can each impact the Jaguars' eventual AFC run? We break it down below.
The Jaguars have gotten very strong play out of the cornerback room as a whole since the bye week, with three of their top four cornerbacks recording interceptions over the last few games: Montaric Brown and Jourdan Lewis against the Baltimore Ravens, and then Travis Hunter on Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. The Jaguars' cornerback group has been perhaps the most dominant and productive part of the defense during their three-game winning streak, and that can't all be accounted for by the weak group of quarterbacks they have played.
Brown and Jarrian Jones have been especially impressive since the bye week. Jones has made big plays from the slot and had a pivotal pass breakup against the Titans on Sunday, while Brown has seen his coverage numbers improve since he returned from his hamstring injury earlier in the season. Jones and Brown are both playing the best football of their seasons, and they are helping the Jaguars' secondary make a big leap.
This duo will be critical when the Jaguars face more productive passers down the road, such as Caleb Williams and CJ Stroud in December and then the AFC playoff quarterbacks down the road. But so far, the Jaguars' cornerback room has met every test since the bye week, and the Jaguars should have plenty of confidence in them moving forward.
The Jaguars have been using multiple-tight end sets at a high clip since the season began, but the ball is starting to go to their rookie tight ends a bit more. Neither is seeing a high volume of targets by any means, but the duo combined for six catches over the first six games of the season. Over the last three games, the rookie duo has combined for eight catches, a touchdown, and several first downs. It has been a slow burn for the rookie tight ends, but their impact has unquestionably increased since the
Liam Coen and the Jaguars' staff are trusting Koziol and Boerkircher to do more and more for them each week. That is good news for a team that likes to mix in different ways to produce explosive plays on the offensive side of the ball. With Koziol and Boerkircher improving and becoming bigger parts of the passing game and the offense as a whole, the Jaguars could be on track to have all types of tools at thbeir disposal once the playoffs come around in a few months. The rookies look better each week, and it could help continue to change the offense.
Trevor Lawrence was playing really good football for the Jaguars before the bye week, ranking top-10 in EPA/Play and success rate against quarterbacks. Since the bye week, Lawrence ranks No. 1 in adjusted EPA/Play and No. 3 in success rate. He was playing really well before the bye week. Since the bye week, he is in the same conversation as Brock Purdy and Joe Burrow as the most productive quarterbacks in football. Lawrence has a 7:1 touchdown/interception ratio since the bye week, and he is fresh off a 352-yard game against the Titans.
Lawrence had 32 touchdowns passes in 26 games from 2023-2024. He now has 50 in 26 games under Liam Coen, and a good chunk of those have come in the last few weeks. This is the best version of Lawrence we have ever seen, but he is still getting better weekly as well. That is bad news for the rest of the AFC, but great news for a Jaguars team that is trying to win back-to-back AFC South titles for the first time in franchise history.

title: How the Jaguars Can Secure an AFC South Title Before Texans Rematch
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are in a good spot in the AFC South. Such a good spot that there is a scenario where they can wrap things up before Christmas.
That is quite the statement considering the Jaguars were not even the most popular pick to win the AFC South entering the season. The Jaguars played second fiddle to the Houston Texans in most analysts' eyes throughout the offseason, despite the Jaguars winning the AFC South a year ago. Fast forward to Week 10, and things have changed after the Jaguars' 7-2 start.
The Jaguars have a firm grip on the AFC South with eight weeks left in the season, leading the 3-6 Texans by four games after the Texans' debacle of a loss against the Cleveland Browns in Week 10. Thanks to the Texans slipping against the Browns, and then the New York Giants earlier in the season, the Texans have gifted the Jaguars an opportunity to take them out of the AFC South battle.
In fact, the Jaguars can do it before these two teams meet again in Week 15 on Dec. 20, and here is how.
The Jaguars will eventually have bigger things on their plate than the AFC South, but the Jaguars can not afford to look too far ahead. Until the Jaguars have wrapped things up in the AFC South first, it does not make much sense for the Jaguars to worry about the top seed and things like the Buffalo Bills, Cincinnati Bengals, and the AFC West.
With that said, the next month can change things quite a bit for the Jaguars. Right now, the most important game on the Jaguars' schedule for the second-half of the season is their Week 15 battle with the Texans in Houston. With that said, that game's importance could shrink significantly depending on how the next four weeks go for both teams.
The magic number for the Jaguars is five. If the Jaguars can land some kind of combination of five combined Jaguars wins/Texans losses over the next four weeks, then they will win the AFC South before these two teams play again.
If the Jaguars go 3-1 over the next month, and the Texans go 2-2, then the Jaguars will have secured the AFC South. Same with them going 1-3 and the Texans going 0-4. Same with the Jaguars going 2-2 and the Texans going 1-3. Heck, same with the Texans going 3-1 and the Jaguars going 4-0. As long as the results land in some kind of combination of five Jaguars wins/Texans losses, then Jacksonville will secure a home playoff game.
At some point, the conversation around the AFC South will have to stop thinking about the Texans. They are at 3-6 and on life support for a reason. But it is the NFL, and the Jaguars certainly have players who remember not winning the AFC South after being 8-3 in 2023. The Jaguars still have to secure this division, but now it can be done quicker than anyone thought.
The AFC South is the Jaguars for the taking. Now, they need to take it faster than what was previously considered possible. If they do that, then they could turn their rematch with the Texans into just another Week 15 game.

title: 3 Things We Learned From the Jaguars' Beatdown of Titans: Bhayshul Tuten's Role is Clear
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars found another AFC South win in Week 10, this time putting up points in all kinds of different fashions on their way to a 40-23 victory over the Tennessee Titans.
The Jaguars' Week 10 road win was defined by explosive plays and great individual efforts on both sides of the ball, with the likes of Parker Washington, Trevor Lawrence, and Travis Hunter all making game-changing plays to lift the Jaguars to a win.
This is the last time we see this version of the Jaguars before their reinforcements join them for an AFC South title push in the form of Jessie Bates and Jordan Davis. So, what did we learn from the Jaguars this week? We break it down below.
This backfield has been Bhayshul Tuten's each week, and we certainly did not enter Week 10 with the impression that this would change against the Titans. But what we did learn on Sunday was that the Jaguars view the gap between the No. 1 and No. 2 spots in the backfield as one that is growing as the season goes on. This, of course, is because the usage of the Jaguars' top two backs demanded such an observation.
Even with Tuten at less than 100% , the second-year back played 70% of the snaps and had nearly 30 touches. Meanwhile, Chris Rodriguez had four carries and just 10 snaps played, giving him fewer snaps on the day than LeQuint Allen for the first time this season. Tuten has been the No. 1 running back all year long, but the last few weeks while he has been injured have really shown us how wide the gap is on the depth chart.
"Yeah, he played hard, man. He played tough. I think we were very close to breaking a few again," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game about Tuten. "Got to go look at it and see if there was some more opportunities there, but I was very proud of the way that he continues to challenge himself with very little practice preparation throughout the course of the week to come out and give us his best every Sunday these last two weeks of game day. He's not perfect. He's not 100 percent and he continues to play for this team, and I appreciate that."
The Jaguars' pass-rush is the most fascinating debate of the 2026 squad. The Jaguars recorded one sack of Titans quarterback Cam Ward, with Antonio Johnson getting home on a blitz in the second-half. A week earlier against the Baltimore Ravens, the Jaguars also recorded just one sack, this time from linebacker Foyesade Oluokun. Even half of the Jaguars' four sacks against the Colts in Week 8 were from non-defensive linemen, with Oluokun and Jalen Huskey each notching one.
That is to say the Jaguars are getting some results with their pass-rush, but it is not coming in the form of sacks from their top defensive linemen. The Jaguars are seeing pressures make an impact, such as on the Travis Hunter interception, but their defensive line has 9.5 sacks through nine games. Their non-defensive linemen have 6.5. The pass-rush has been unique this season, and nobody likely predicrted the Jaguars' big three on the defensive line would have 6.5 sacks by nearly Thanksgiving.
The Jaguars have made it work to this point. And perhaps the addition of Jordan Davis in some way impacts the rest of the pass rush's productivty. But a mix of scheme and game scripts have called for the Jaguars' pass-rush to have quite the confounding sack production through nine games.
Josh Cameron has been terrific for the Jaguars as a sixth-round rookie . It started with a red-zone touchdown against the Cleveland Browns in Week 1, and it has kept rolling since. Cameron now has three touchdown catches through nine games, which is quite the impressive mark considering his role in the Jaguars' offense. Cameron is not a high-volume route runner for the Jaguars who plays in a lot of three-receiver sets. His role has been more so in 12 and 13 personnel and in the red-zone, yet he has continued to find ways to make an impact as a rotational piece.
The Jaguars are still using Brian Thomas Jr. as a starting receiver , with Thomas seeing more targets Sunday than Cameron did (four to three). With the Jaguars opting not to trade Thomas at the deadline, they were making it clear that they like their receiver room as-is for the 2026 season. Thomas plays in three receiver sets when the Jaguars spread it out, Cameron makes an impact in heavier formations both as a receiver and as a run-blocker.
That is what they should continue to lean on, and next year is the actual appropriate time to start to look at a potential shift. Cameron can make an impact and get valuable experience now, and then the Jaguars can take another look at the makeup of the room after the season. It is very easy to see a scenario where Cameron gets a larger role in his second season after a strong rookie year, a lot like Bhayshul Tuten has done at running back.

title: Shipley's Dozen: Jaguars Continue to Roll in AFC South, Travis Hunter's Elite Level, and Much More
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are ... pretty dang good!
It felt like the Jaguars played at a C+, B- level against the Tennessee Titans in Week 10, but it still resulted in a 40-23 win on the road. The Jaguars are rolling, and the rest of the AFC is clearly on notice.
We break down the big Week 10 win and the bigger picture with this week's edition of the Shipley's Dozen column. Do not forget, you can read this column each morning after a Jaguars game.
This was the best version of Parker Washington we have ever seen, and not just because of the eye-popping numbers he put up during the first-half. Washington set career numbers in the first two quarters alone before finishing the game with seven catches for 152 yards and a touchdown. For my money, it was the best Washington has ever played for the Jaguars even beyond the numbers, simply because he showed the entire skill-set.
Putting the Titans' highest-paid defensive back in a spin cycle with his route-running? Check. Yards after the catch and toughness? Check. Ability to win in contested situations downfield? Check. Ability to win on the sideline with coordination and athletic ability? Check. Washington was elite on Sunday, and everyone on the field knew it.
How many cornerbacks in the AFC have played as well as Travis Hunter has this season? Hunter recorded his third interception of the season Sunday. He was targeted five times, giving up four catches for ... 13 yards. He has been a playmaker, he has tackled well, and there are simply not many cornerbacks doing the things he is doing every single week at the position. The case for him as an All-Pro are clear, and the only cornerbacks in the AFC who I think have played anywhere near his level are Denzel Ward and Nohl Williams. He has already become one of the best players at his entire position in the NFL, and the Hunter trade continues to pay off for Liam Coen and James Gladstone as a result.
"It was an unbelievable catch. Unbelievable play," Coen said after the game about Hunter's interception. "Critical because we had just turned it over, right? On the interception. Talk about having each other's back. That's what this group does. That's what this group is. Such a special play by obviously a special player.
It was a good week for the Jaguars. In fact, it was a great week. The Jaguars improved on paper more than any other team in the NFL at the very start of the week. Then the locker room responded in the right way in the middle of the week. Then the Jaguars finished it with another 40-point game and a road blowout of an AFC South foe, while seeing their positioning in the AFC South improve due to the Texans losing in Cleveland. The Jaguars sent a message all week , and it has been received loud and clear for all to hear.
"I think this was really just about our team, to be honest. Our team's got a lot of confidence. Our team was damn good without Jessie (Bates III) and Jordan (Davis) and Davon (Godchaux)," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game. "That's how these guys went into the week. Hey, we can beat people. We feel confident every time we walk out on the grass on Sundays and hopefully those guys can only come and add to an already talented, tough team as we get down a stretch that we're trying to go on a run here, you know?"
It should be clear why the Jaguars made the Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates III moves , at least in the short-term. The Jaguars were clearly the better team over the Titans so there was never any real chance of them having to pay for starting backups Matt Dickerson and Rayuan Lane at nose tackle and safety, but if they were playing the Chicago Bears or any other talented team, maybe the Jaguars would not have been as well off.
The Jaguars did not get much of an impact from their interior defensive line Sunday, both against the run and pass. Several times Cam Ward was pressued off the edge but stepped up in the pocket to scramble for yards, while there was not quite the elite run-stuffing effort we are used to seeing from Jacksonville. Add in a few missed tackles in space at the safety spot, and it is very clear where Bates and Davis can help the Jaguars right off the bat.
It is starting to get tougher and tougher to be surprised by rookie sixth-rounder Josh Cameron. Cameron has come up big for the Jaguars time and time again during his debut season, and Sunday may have been his best game. He caught three passes for 67 yards, including a 28-yard shot down the sideline on the opening drive and a 25-yard touchdown to give the Jaguars their first double-digit lead of the game with under 10 minutes left. Add in everything he did as a run-blocker and the Jaguars have quite the find with Cameron.
If there is one thing the Jaguars have gotten from backup center Jonah Monheim last season, it is the ability to step in on a whim and give them good snaps. Monheim has been the backup behind starting center Robert Hainsey since the Jaguars drafted him out of USC in the seventh-round of the 2025 NFL Draft, and they haven't really had to worry about their center depth ever since. This came up again Sunday, with Hainsey leaving in the first-half and Monheim playing well as he played 45% of the offensive snaps.
Monheim stepped in and played well for Hainsey on a few different occasions as a rookie, and the fact he has been so consistent at center should give the Jaguars confidence if Hainsey is out for an extended period of time. There is no update on Hainsey as of this writing, but the Jaguars will survive if they have to start Monheim.
I continue to be impressed by Jaguars safety Antonio Johnson, who looks like he will be a perfect fit next to the rangy Jessie Bates. Johnson is not collecting turnovers at a high clip like he was a year ago, but there is a good case to make that he is playing better now than he has at any other point in his career, and Sunday was another example of it. On a day with great individual performances across the board, Johnson's stood out to me as the most underrated.
Johnson's value to Anthony Campanle's pressure looks and blitz schemes have been clear all season, and he got home once again on a sack of Cam Ward on an important third-down in the second half. But for a defense that had some issues with tackling, Johnson also looked like the team's top player in that category, making several impressive stops in space after the catch. He has been one of their best defenders all season, and Sunday was another example.
I was surprised that we saw barely any Chris Rodriguez Jr. Bhayshul Tuten hasn't been healthy for two weeks now, and he is clearly not running with the same burst that he was even a few weeks ago. Despite that, we have seen Tuten lead the backfield in back-to-back weeks. He was the focal point against the Baltimore Ravens on a short week, while Rodriguez then barely sniffed the field on rushing downs against the Titans. Tuten is clearly hurt, but it is also still very clearly his backfield.
Trevor Lawrence having another stellar game. Lawrence threw three touchdowns, had several huge plays made with his legs, and simply looked like he was on another level tha anything the Titans were throwing at him. The scary thing is that this was all expected. Lawrence’s 352 passing yards were the fourth-most in a single game in his career, and his 120.2 passer rating marked his fourth game this season with a 120-plus rating (tied for the most in the NFL). He also has five games with three or more passing touchdowns, tied for the most in the NFL He is playing like an MVP right now.
James Gladstone. The Jaguars just put up 40 points for the second time in three weeks and this team should be even better moving forward after they added Jessie Bates III and Jordan Davis at the trade deadline. Gladstone has been as aggressive as any general manager in the entire NFL since he was hired, and the fact that the Jaguars can be an even better version of the team we just saw play is a scary thought.…

title: Grand Theft Contract: Which Chiefs Salary Cap Hits Are Holding KC Back in 2026?
full_text:
For those who may not be familiar with the cultural behemoth that is Grand Theft Auto VI , let's put it into context. The game, set to release on Thursday, is rumored to have cost more than $1 billion to develop . It has reportedly made more than $1.5 billion before being officially released .
For comparison, the NFL's salary cap in 2026 is set at just over $301 million per team.
So, with a new GTA just around the corner, let's take this tenuous link as an opportunity to review the Chiefs' 2026 salary cap and decide which players are underperforming on their substantial deals and which ones might be justifying their large cap hit.
While a $7 million cap hit isn't an outrageous number in a vaccuum, it is enough to make Harrison Butker the league's most expensive kicker in 2026. His $7.3 million cap hit narrowly outpaces Seattle's Jayson Myers ($7.2 million), but Butker and Myers have a $1.5 million lead on third place and beyond.
Of course, if you're reading Chiefs On SI , you don't need me to over-explain Butker's disastrous 2026 season so far. The team signed Justin Tucker to their practice squad and just worked out veteran kicker Matt Prater this week .
Still, the Chiefs are publicly holding out hope that Butker can stabilize this year. Could he return to something resembling his previous form by playoff time? It's possible! Will he have provided the kind of confidence and consistency that $7 million typically buys? Definitely not.
If there's any player who I expect an argument about, it's star defensive tackle Chris Jones. Through half the season, has he been worth nearly $45 million? No, that's an enormous number and makes him the priciest defender in the NFL this year.
The second-highest interior defensive lineman cap hit in the league belongs to Alim McNeill at $29 million, while the highest cap number for an edge rusher is T.J. Watt's $42 million . According to Spotrac , Jones has the third-highest cap hit in the entire NFL this season, behind only Matthew Stafford and Justin Herbert.
Has Jones been the best defender in football this season? No. So you'd assume his cap hit is borderline criminal, right? It's still not that simple for me.
If the 32-year-old Jones was having a better season and showing fewer signs of slowing down, I think the Chiefs would have restructured his contract by now. On his current deal , this '26 cap hit is his highest number, taking up nearly 15% of the Chiefs' cap. But any effort to restructure Jones' deal would move money into future seasons, making it harder to part with Jones in years to come. If the Chiefs wanted to cut Jones before the 2027 season, they'd free up $18.6 million in cap space but hold $19.5 in dead cap. If KC keeps Jones at his $38 million hit in '27, they could clear up $35 million in 2028 with "only" $9.75 in dead money.
Despite only having three sacks this season (with two coming against the New York Jets two weeks ago), I'm not sure that Jones' future has been decided. If he can regain his game-wrecking gear down the stretch while commanding attention from opposing offenses, he's still an extremely valuable player. Plus, I still just can't fault the Chiefs for being willing to overpay a franchise cornerstone in order to keep the defense's most important player under contract through the back end of his career while they continue to chase Super Bowls.
Is it a great contract for the Chiefs? No. Do I still understand why and how Kansas City agreed to a deal that would pay a 32-year-old $45 million this season? I do.
Jaylon Moore's time with the Chiefs has never really gone according to plan. He was expected to be the team's starting left tackle until they drafted Josh Simmons shortly after signing Moore in free agency, leaving Moore to move into a swing-tackle role behind Simmons and Jawaan Taylor in 2025. After starting six games in '25, Moore appeared to be in some level of competition with undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson for the right tackle position in training camp this summer. Moore looked to win the job before Simmons suffered a back injury, leaving Benson to take over on the left side.
This year, Moore has not performed particularly well on the right side while carrying the team's third-highest cap hit.
Free agent tackles are expensive because it's a tough position to confidently fill out and great players rarely hit the open market, but there's no real argument that Moore has met his contract numbers across his two-year, $30 million deal. I never cared which side of the line Moore played on, as long as he was a positive force. Unfortunately, it's hard to say that he's been much more than passable.
Kristian Fulton's two-year, $20 million contract looked like a borderline disaster last season, when Fulton never seemed to get fully into the mix at corner until he got more opportunity (and played well) at the very end of the year.
The Chiefs could have cut Fulton this offseason to free up $5 million with an $8 million cap hit, but through '26, Fulton has made an argument to justify his salary, even as the team's third corner.
Second-year third-round pick Nohl Williams has been the team's most consistent cornerback, playing 94% of the Chiefs' defensive snaps, while No. 6 overall pick Mansoor Delane (54%) has been excellent when he hasn't been sidelined due to a recurring shoulder injury. Meanwhile, Fulton (47%) has been very good in his part-time role. Is $13 million an expensive No. 3 corner? Sure, but with Delane's injury and so much youth in the room, Fulton's cap hit is large, not egregious.

title: Chiefs Reportedly Adding Tackle Depth: What Does It Mean for Battered O-Line?
full_text:
It's been a trying season for the Kansas City Chiefs' offensive line, as a combination of fluctuating performance and lackluster durability has created some obstacles despite a 7-2 start for the team.
Week 10's win over the Atlanta Falcons may have summed that up to perfection, as Kansas City dominated the opponent but also showed plenty of cracks in the foundation along the way. Ahead of Sunday's contest against the Arizona Cardinals, general manager Brett Veach is doing something to potentially improve the situation.
Per a Wednesday morning report from Ian Rapoport of NFL Network and ESPN , the Chiefs are signing former Philadelphia Eagles offensive tackle Fred Johnson to the practice squad.
The #Chiefs are signing former #Eagles OT Fred Johnson to their practice squad and he’ll likely be elevated to the 53-man roster. pic.twitter.com/zV3ITTxp48
Johnson, who entered the league as an undrafted free agent in 2019, has spent time with the Pittsburgh Steelers, Cincinnati Bengals, Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Jacksonville Jaguars as well. He's appeared in 86 regular-season games to date, making 22 starts and logging just under 1,900 offensive snaps in total.
Rapoport adds that Johnson is "likely" to be activated to the 53-man roster at some point, whether it be via standard elevation (he's allotted three during the regular season) for game day or a straight-up signing down the road.
Johnson brings a defined set of skills to the table, yet it's ironic that one of his core traits is versatility. According to Pro Football Focus , the 29-year-old has played most of his snaps at either right tackle (893) or left tackle (833), with a decent chunk still residing at the right guard spot (158).
He split time between tackle alignments during his fill-in duties with Philly in 2024 and 2025. His most extensive experience came during that window — he combined for 626 pass blocking opportunities and surrendered 57 total pressures.
The eighth-year man boasts intriguing physical tools, too. Per MockDraftable , Johnson is in the 94th percentile in height (6-foot-7), the 91st percentile in wingspan (84.5 inches) and the 88th percentile in hand size (10 5/8 inches). It's easy to see why the Chiefs were interested in him, especially given the state of affairs with the offensive line.
Neither tackle position is in a good place. On the left side, Kahlil Benson turned in one of his worst games as a professional down in Atlanta and looks like less of a true answer with each passing week. Projected starter Josh Simmons remains on the injured reserve list and, via head coach Andy Reid, wasn't expected to return to practice this week.
On the opposite side, veteran Jaylon Moore is dealing with a lingering ankle injury and hasn't fared particularly well when available. The jury is still out on backups Joshua Ezeudu and Diego Pounds , both trade acquisitions from August. The former is coming off a solid outing that saw him get credited with a pair of pressures ceded but appear much more competent in the lineup.
There are multiple paths the Johnson add can take. At the extreme end, he could be signed to an active roster contract and finish out the season in place of someone like Pounds if the club felt its depth needed to be improved. Thinking more conservatively, it's also possible that Kansas City simply desires someone with the ability to pinch hit at multiple spots.
Being able to count on another battle-tested chess piece is nice this time of year. That's without even factoring in right guard Trey Smith also getting banged up in Week 10. A player like Johnson entering the fold makes plenty of sense.
It's as low-risk as it gets for a franchise that's battered and bruised along the offensive line.
