title: The Next Step for Raiders' Offense Has Come Into Focus
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' Week 10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks was more productive than the game's results may show.
After leading the league in sacks allowed last season, Las Vegas' offensive line entered Week 10 allowing the third-fewest sacks in the league. The Raiders' line allowed only 11 sacks through the season's first nine games. However, this was partially because of Kirk Cousins.
The veteran's experience factored in on several plays where he got rid of the ball in time to prevent a sack. Mendoza's inexperience factored in as the opposite happened on Sunday. As Kubiak noted, some of those six sacks were on Mendoza. Some were on position groups other than the line.
“I think overall, as an offensive line, there’s a solid first half of run game production followed by a very poor half of protection, and that’s not all on them. That’s on getting open, that’s on getting rid of the ball, that’s on play calls. It’s a team thing. So, we win together and we lose together.”
With Mendoza now leading the way, the season's final seven games will be about setting up him and the Raiders' offense for the future. Those seven games will provide valuable experience as they continue working their way through one of the league's toughest schedules.
More importantly, the next seven games will solidify where on the offense the Raiders' front office must make wholesale changes this offseason. After 10 games, every position on Las Vegas' offensive line could use additional help or a complete overhaul this offseason.
Kolton Miller's performance does not match what the Raiders are set to pay him next season. Both of their offensive guard positions are underwhelming. After 11 games, Las Vegas still does not have answers at either guard position. Collectively, the position group is derailing the offense.
DJ Glaze has shown impressive durability, starting nearly every game at right tackle for the Raiders since being drafted a few seasons ago. He could use more development, but his durability and potential, performance-wise, make him a valuable asset to Las Vegas.
The Raiders will enter the upcoming offseason in desperate need of multiple offensive linemen. They could potentially be in need of several starting-caliber ones, which is far from ideal, but it is the reality of the situation. The six sacks allowed on Sunday weren't all on the Raiders' offensive line.
The sacks that could be attributed to Mendoza directly correlated with his inexperience, which he can only get by playing on Sundays. Such sacks and negative plays are a normal part of what comes with a rebuild being led by a rookie quarterback and first-time head coach.
There are certain things Mendoza will have to learn the hard way, to the tune of sacks, turnovers, and missed opportunities, but that is the only way for a player to learn. That is the NFL. That is life. The rookie shared some of his thoughts on playing in the NFL after his first career start .
“It’s a lot different. The NFL is a whole different level, and you need to understand your hot routes, which I need to do better, and we need to understand and essentially be a master at the protection scheme, because it’s one thing when we’re in the meeting room saying, ‘Okay, I would do this, this’ rather than in the heat of the battle," Mendoza said after the game.
"So those are things I need to improve on and will improve on and aspire to improve on to best help my team.”
Teams that select first overall in the draft usually do so because their roster was bad enough to lose enough games to earn the pick. That is how bad the roster Las Vegas had at the beginning of this offseason. The moves Las Vegas' front office made were enough for them to take a step forward.
However, the fact that all four of their wins have come against teams with losing records and all six of their losses have come against teams with winning records confirms the Raiders are somewhere in between those two opposing ends.
The next step they take will require them to add to both their offensive line and their group of wide receivers. Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer can only do so much. Sunday made it fair to believe that with a better supporting cast , Mendoza could lead this team to the playoffs as soon as next season.
Depending on how the cookie crumbles, he could potentially do so this season. It will depend more on the talent around him than him, though.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders Have Begun Process of Adding New Element to Offense
full_text:
Since the start of the 2023 season, the Las Vegas Raiders have gone through nearly 10 different quarterbacks. Until Week 10 against the Seattle Seahawks, the most mobile quarterback the Raiders started was Geno Smith, or possibly, Desmond Ridder. Think about that.
In a league where the best quarterbacks are a legitimate threat to run the ball, Smith and Ridder were the Raiders' most mobile signal callers in years. Sunday, the Raiders turned the page on years of failed quarterback acquisitions.
Las Vegas' second No. 1 overall pick in franchise history landed them Fernando Mendoza. Although he showed that he was a rookie quarterback in his first career start, he much more often showed a blend of skills that has largely been alluded to in seven quarterbacks the Raiders have started since 2023.
Sunday, Mendoza displayed many of the reasons why he was the top pick.
In Week 10, the Raiders rolled Mendoza out of the pocket on the first two plays of their opening drive. This continued through the first half and was effective. Mendoza's mobility kept Seattle's defense honest early in the game, as he extended plays that would have resulted in a sack in previous weeks.
Still, Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak wants Mendoza to prioritize throwing the ball first when escaping the pocket.
“Well, remain a passer. Number one, keep your eyes downfield. Remain a passer like he did to Jack Bech on that left sideline, like he did to Ian [Thomas] early in the game, getting through his progression. Remain a passer, and then obviously protect yourself when you start to run down the field," Kubiak said on Monday.
Entering Week 10, Las Vegas often struggled to sustain drives until they were down by double digits and multiple possessions in the second half. Mendoza's ability to move the pocket and run when necessary directly correlated with the Raiders extending drives in a way rarely seen this season.
Those extended drives for the Raiders' offense kept their defense off the field. This kept the Raiders' defense more rested than in recent weeks. In turn, the Raiders' defense played the best it has in weeks, and the team was the most competitive it had been for four quarters in months.
The coaching staff and players can fix more than a few things moving forward this season. Some of these things cannot be fixed until the offseason. However, Sunday's loss was arguably the best the Raiders have played on both sides of the ball in a full game this season.
The Raiders must not hesitate to let Mendoza use his legs, even if it is only for a couple of yards. The threat of Mendoza running can help open things up for Las Vegas' pass-catchers. Maybe more importantly, Mendoza's ability to extend plays and drives will help the Raiders' defense immensely.
As much as Mendoza's mobility adds to the Raiders' offense, there is a fine line for him to walk. Mobility is a nice quality to have, but it must be used wisely to be effective. Along with better blocking, live action on Sundays will help him figure out how to navigate.
“I need to stand in there more. I was a little sped up today. There were some times that if you can extend the play and it gives a good chance to get out clean, not take a sack, and extend the play because the defense did a really good job covering, then that’s acceptable,” Mendoza said after the game.
“But there are some times that I should have stayed in there, stepped up with one hitch, and then delivered a strike, rather than already looking to scramble. And it’s credit to Seattle’s defense. However, I need to be better, be more composed in the pocket.”
A quarterback starting his first career game against the defending Super Bowl champions and one of the best defenses in the league is a tall task. In his first full football game since January 19, as a collegiate athlete, it is fair to say Mendoza played a solid game.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: From Criticism to Applause: Raiders Brass Earns Unexpected Praise
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders are sitting at 4-6 on the year, but to those who are informed, they are in the midst of an extraordinary metamorphosis.
For over two decades, the storied Silver and Black franchise has languished in mediocrity. As soon as the fan base went ballistic, wholesale changes occurred that, whether they made sense or not, happened, abandoning the previous work and, while never publicly acknowledged, sending the Raiders back to the drawing board to fix the problem.
At no time was it clearer than when Mark Davis and his advisors hired Tom Telesco, who had just been fired by his fellow AFC West rival, the Los Angeles Chargers. He had spent the previous 11 seasons as the Chargers' general manager, from 2013 to 2023.
The firing of Telesco by the Bolts was shocking around the NFL, but not for the reasons those judging superficially would think. With the Chargers, Telesco's NFL Draft class success in hitting on blue-chip first-round talent like Justin Herbert, Joey Bosa, Derwin James, and Rashawn Slater was unquestioned. His low was an abysmal 84–95 overall record across three different head coaches, including his last, which was an epic failure.
I have a very close friend who worked in LA with Telesco, and vehemently defended him for several poor decisions, which my friend laid squarely at the feet of an ownership group that left “Less than desired football IQ.”
As a testament to his integrity, despite my private and public criticism (including in private, offering specifics that I was aware of through my friend), Telesco refused to blame ownership for anything. He could have defended ownership in public and in our private conversations, but he didn't. It happens all the time in this league. He never did.
That is why, to this day, I consider it an honor to call him a friend.
Telesco was hired as the Silver and Black general manager, a role that lasted only one season, from January 2024 until he was fired in January 2025. ​With the Raiders, his biggest high was nailing the 2024 draft class by landing All-Pro tight end Brock Bowers at 13th overall and starting right tackle Delmar “DJ” Glaze, The Mule, in the third round, LB Tommy “Freaking” Eichenberg in the fifth round, and burgeoning special teams star Dylan Laube in the sixth.
He inherited a first-year coach in Antonio Pierce, whom ownership hired before his selection, and a WR that I would best classify, in my opinion, as me-first diva, in Davante Adams.
Additionally, he signed free-agent splash Christian Wilkins, who suffered a season-ending foot injury, and oversaw a 4–13 season in which, other than the Wilkins injury, which he had no control over, virtually nothing he did failed, but several things he didn’t do.
It is ridiculous to me that, given the quality of so many NFL GMs, Telesco is not in one of the coveted 32 NFL chairs.
Additionally, the regime change that ousted him lasted only one year with Pete Carroll and a total collapse in 2025.
The Raiders have moved on, and despite Tom Brady remaining the dominant voice, things have changed since they trusted GM John Spytek with a louder voice last year.
The Raiders' rebuild is in full swing, and good things are happening as they finally show a true commitment to excellence, not just a mantra echoed to stir the faithful.
Speaking on AM 570 in Los Angeles, Telesco said of the trade of Kirk Cousins and the development of Fernando Mendoza, “I think they played this quarterback transition period perfectly. And they had a plan going in; they talked about the plan right after they drafted Fernando Mendoza, as far as how they were going to approach this season. And they stuck to the plan.”
Telesco then dropped a truth bomb on the organization’s past, but also offered high praise for what is happening now. He continued, “Believe me, from someone who has worked there, that hasn’t always been the case. So right now they had a plan, they totally stuck to it, and it's worked out perfectly.”
Telesco said out loud what multiple people have said quietly over the years, and I have reported it loudly.
Ownership deserves the blame for the past, but that doesn’t mean they don’t deserve praise for the present discipline and success.
Telesco has the right to be bitter; his integrity doesn’t allow that. But he's a voice of reason, and yet another NFL executive singing the praises of the unified front of Mark Davis, Brady, Spytek, and Kubiak.
Telesco's stamp of approval says a lot when you see it through the lens of what he endured here. It should encourage Raiders fans.
A few simple words should be Viagra to the soul of Raider Nation. A few words that haven’t been said around here in decades: “They stuck to the plan.” You may not have expected to hear that kind of praise from a fired employee, but the fact that you are should tell you a lot. After years of being kicked in the butt, the Raiders are finally earning pats on the back.
Davis, Brady, and Spytek all got a slap on the back. After years of this franchise getting kicked in the butt, it should tell the amazing fans, who see their fandom as a way of life, that good things are happening in year one of the Kubiak regime.
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: 3 Key Raiders’ Narratives Emerging From Week 10 Defeat
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders fell to the Seattle Seahawks, 21-13, falling to 4-6 on the season.
Despite the loss, it wasn't all negative for the Silver and Black. Here are a few narratives surrounding the Raiders based on what transpired at Allegiant Stadium on Sunday.
Fernando Mendoza made his first career start on Sunday against one of the league's best defenses, and looked the part. The Indiana product showed why he was the unanimous top quarterback prospect in this past draft class. The Raiders went through it last season, leading to them inheriting the No. 1 overall pick, but fans will look back at 2025 and live with the result, as they have their future franchise quarterback .
The final stat line doesn't depict how impressive Mendoza was in his debut. The 6-foot-5, 225-pound signal caller completed his first six passes against Seattle. The Raiders' opening drive was flawless, as Klint Kubiak leaned on the run game to facilitate the offense. Mendoza capped off the drive with a 10-yard touchdown run. His mobility opens up an element of the offense that wasn't available with Kirk Cousins.
Mendoza was tricked several times by disguised blitzes, but that pre-snap diagnosis will improve with time. You can't be too harsh on the rookie quarterback for those lapses, as Mike Macdonald has made established quarterbacks look lost pre-snap. Overall, I was very impressed with Mendoza, and assuming Las Vegas' front office adds more talent on the offensive line and on the outside this upcoming offseason, Mendoza should have ample success starting in 2027.
As noted, Mendoza and the offense looked incredibly effective and sufficient in the first half, taking a 10-7 lead into halftime. That's when everyone was available. Bowers suffered an ankle injury early in the game, missing a handful of snaps in the first half.
The 23-year-old tight end would play sporadically in the opening two quarters and didn't appear to be completely hampered by the injury. However, Bowers was ruled out for the rest of the game after halftime. In the first half, the Raiders had 136 total yards, 10 first downs, and went 7-for-10 on third down.
Without Bowers in the second half, the Raiders' offense fell off a cliff, scoring three points, totaling 27 yards, and going 0-for-7 on third downs, producing only two first downs in the final 30 minutes of the game. Without his top pass-catching option, Mendoza completed 6-of-16 passes. When Bowers is off the field, Las Vegas' lack of a bona fide WR1 is glaringly apparent. That second half showed how far the Raiders are from competing in the AFC.
Again, I don't think it's fair to be overly critical of the Raiders in this game, considering Mendoza was making his starting debut against the reigning Super Bowl champions. Not to mention, nobody gave Las Vegas a shot at beating the Seahawks.
That said, results around the league allowed the Raiders to solidify their position in the race for the final wildcard spot. The New England Patriots fell to the Detroit Lions earlier in the day and potentially lost Drake Maye for the rest of the season. Their season looks over at this point. Meanwhile, the Houston Texans slipped to 3-6 with a loss to the Cleveland Browns.
Las Vegas is now two games out of the playoff picture, with an upcoming matchup against the Denver Broncos. With another loss next week, I think you could say the Raiders' playoff hopes might be over.
Logan Lazarczyk is a graduate of the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in Communication Studies with an emphasis in Journalism. Logan joined our team with extensive experience, having previously written and worked for media entities such as USA Today and Union Broadcasting.

title: What Rob Leonard, Raiders' Defense Proved in Week 10 Loss
full_text:
Sure, according to the Seattle Seahawks' depth chart, Drew Lock is the backup quarterback. However, Lock has over 30 career starts. That is significantly more starts than nearly half of the Las Vegas Raiders' defense. Still, Las Vegas' defense showed up on Sunday.
In his first start, rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza was one touchdown away from helping the Raiders tie their season-high first-half point total.
In Week 9, the Raiders lost the time-of-possession battle by 17 minutes! In Week 7, they lost it by over eight minutes. In Week 4, they lost it by over 10 minutes. Yes, the defense can do a better job of getting off the field on third down and tightening up against the run early.
However, teams do not lose the time of possession that badly just because of their defense. Entering Week 10, the Raiders' offense has struggled to sustain drives, much less score points. There have been more than a few five- and six-play drives for the Raiders this season.
Entering Week 10, even when Las Vegas' struggling defense forced turnovers, the offense has routinely turned the ball over shortly thereafter or punted just a few plays later. The unit has failed to sustain drives throughout the season. Michael Mayer alluded to as much on Sunday.
“One thing I noticed for us as an offense, is getting the first, first down is pretty important for us. So we got to get that first first down to get rolling, to get going, to get Klint [Kubiak] in his bag with the play calling, those type of things,” Mayer said following Sunday’s loss.
Mayer didn't bring that up for no reason. He's emphasizing the importance of the "first" first down because the Raiders' offense has struggled to get that first down often this season. That first down is what gets drives going. It is literally impossible to sustain a drive without that first down.
Not scoring points can be mitigated by sustained drives. A couple of first downs and a punt are understandable throughout a game. Although they struggled to do so again in the second half against the Seahawks after losing Brock Bowers, the unit did well overall.
Not scoring points and punting the ball back after a handful of plays, and wondering why the defense everyone knew had roster issues is struggling, is interesting, to say the least. Yes, the defense needs to improve, but their teammates on offense have to help, too.
The Raiders started 3-0 because, albeit against bad teams, the offense took advantage of the defense's hard work. In each of those three wins, the Raiders' defense made significant plays that gave Las Vegas' offense short fields. Once the defense could not do that, Las Vegas' offense faltered.
An offense's job is to score. A defense's job is to stop the other team from scoring. In their 3-0 start, the Raiders' defense wasn't just stopping teams from scoring: the unit forced turnovers that actually set the offense up with advantageous field position; they were doing their job, and then some.
Even against the New York Jets, Joe DeCamillis' unit scored 14 of the Raiders' 38 points. That included Dylan Laube's historic kickoff return for a touchdown, which was half of the Raiders' 14 first-half points. In their wins, Las Vegas' offense has been aided by defense or special teams.
In all of their losses, Leonard's defense has been left out to dry by an offense that goes extended periods of time without sustaining drives or scoring points.
In the first half of Week 10 , Mendoza and the Raiders' offense produced two drives that took over six minutes. They produced another drive that they did not score on, but took over four minutes off the clock.
It was the best first half the defense had played in weeks.
The Raiders had the ball right before halftime and right after halftime. They scored zero points, while Rob Leonard's defense held the defending Super Bowl champions to seven points in the first half. Leonard's unit held Jaxon Smith-Njigba to 11 reception yards in the first half.
In the second half, Las Vegas took the field without Bowers, and the Seahawks turned up the heat. Five of the Raiders' six second-half possessions lasted three plays before they punted.
Each took about a minute and a half or less off the clock. Las Vegas' offense scored six points in the final three quarters. It was yet another dry spell for a Raiders offense that has had plenty this season.
It was a microcosm of the season, but inflated quarterback stats in multiple blowout losses and close wins against four of the league's worst defenses blinded many.
Leonard's unit can't be responsible for scoring points, too. Everybody has to do their job, not just the defense.
After forcing two more turnovers on Sunday, Las Vegas' defense ranks fifth in the league in forced turnovers, and the unit ranked higher than that for much of this season. In the first half of Week 10, Leonard's defense proved that it can compete well when the offense sustains drives.
Even when the Raiders' offense didn't sustain drives in the second half, the defense kept the team within realistic reach of mounting a comeback, more so than in any of their previous losses. It may not be pretty, but defense doesn't need to be pretty. It needs to be effective at the right moments.
Las Vegas' defense can do that, but with all that Las Vegas' front office invested in its offense this season, the unit must at least sustain drives. If they can, Leonard and his defense will be just fine.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: How Raiders Priorities Becoming Clearer As Season Progresses
full_text:
In just one offseason, the Las Vegas Raiders made solid improvements to their roster. While those improvements deserve the praise they have received, they've also made it even more glaring where more work is needed.
The Raiders have had an up-and-down season, which is progress from the past two seasons, which were both down seasons. The Raiders lost 10 straight games in both seasons. Las Vegas' progress is undeniable, but they need so much more to follow up this past offseason's step forward with another.
Las Vegas' defensive backs have had forgettable performances. Lately, and unexpectedly, that has been veteran cornerback Eric Stokes. Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak explained why Stokes was benched for several plays in Week 10.
“When you have a big play and you’re not finishing the down, then yes. However, number five [Eric Stokes] has been one of our key players this year. He covers the best receivers every week. He gives great effort. There were a couple plays there that he did not, but that doesn’t mean that he’s not a player that we’re going to count on moving forward,” Kubiak said.
“So, we’ve got to learn from those moments and see how big of moments they are. And it wasn’t just him. We’ve got to continue to attack the quarterback and not let him get the pass off either. So, one guy gets highlighted on a play, but the fact is, it’s a whole defensive effort of making sure that we don’t give up those explosive plays.”
It is easy to pile on Stokes, as he is the team's top corner and has had several subpar games. This is in addition to the new contract Las Vegas handed him during the offseason after a solid 2025 campaign. However, the entire defensive backfield has struggled this season.
Heading into the season, this was expected. Still, the unit's struggles extend well beyond Stokes, and the issues have been so significant that they have negated the positive gains the defense has made as a whole. Stokes is far from the only defensive back who has struggled this season.
Stokes just happens to be the leader of the unit in experience and pay. That rightfully comes with heightened expectations in the NFL, as it would in any other profession. Yet the Raiders filled out their defensive backfield largely with rookies and second-year players.
This is a roster issue. They have no real safety net at corner after Stokes. If Stokes has a bad game, the entire unit likely will. That is a lot of pressure on a player, and he is the only player on the defense for whom that is the case.
The issues run so far beyond Stokes that defensive coordinator Rob Leonard is still being forced to rotate Darien Porter and Hezekiah Masses with Week 11 just days away. In Week 10, the defensive backfield's issues left Leonard between a rock and a hard place while covering Jaxon Smith-Njigba.
Few corners in the league can cover Smith-Njigba man-to-man, but he had success against zone coverage, too. Especially in the second half. That is because the defensive backfield isn't dependable as a whole.
It took years of misguided signings and draft picks to deplete the Raiders' defensive backfield to where it is now. The position group will undoubtedly be a primary focus for the Raiders' front office this summer.
Multiple general managers, head coaches, and defensive backs have come and gone over the past few seasons, and the defensive backfield is still problematic. The issue is bigger than the players and isn't necessarily anyone's fault. The defensive backfield's struggles were inevitable.
It certainly isn't Leonard's fault that none of the three different general managers Las Vegas has had in his four seasons with the team have adequately addressed the position group. Leonard can only do so much until more talent is added to the defense's back end.
The Raiders must thoroughly address the position group this offseason with at least a few quality veteran additions. Las Vegas is early in its rebuild, but it will only become more of a passing league over time.
The 2026 season will go down as a quality developmental year for Las Vegas' young defensive backfield. However, the Raiders need proven talent at the position and multiple players with it.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Why Raiders' 2026 Season Was Always Bigger Than Wins, Losses
full_text:
Rebuilds are far from easy, and quality rebuilds take time. This offseason, the Las Vegas Raiders' front office made sweeping changes to its coaching staff and roster to kickstart its rebuild. Las Vegas' 3-0 start confirmed that those changes were a major step in the right direction.
Las Vegas' undefeated start made it easy for some to forget where they are in their rebuild. However, the Raiders have one of the league's toughest schedules. The undefeated start was a nice change from recent seasons, but the weeks since have confirmed that Las Vegas' rebuild is just beginning.
Their four wins in 10 games are more than they won all of last season. The Raiders have won seven games combined in the past two seasons. Their four wins this season and their six losses accurately depict where they are in their rebuild.
They are slightly better than the league's worst teams, such as the Los Angeles Chargers and Miami Dolphins. However, the gap between them and the league's elite has been on full display over the past two months. Yet this season was always about more than wins and losses.
Rebuilds take time, especially when rebuilding the roster that secured the No. 1 pick in this year's draft. John Spytek and the Raiders are not just rebuilding; they are rebuilding arguably the league's worst roster over the past three seasons. That will take more time than typical rebuilds.
Las Vegas is 4-6 this season, but the 2026 season was always bigger than wins and losses for a Raiders team that has lost nearly 30 games over the past two seasons. This season was about laying the foundation for the future while developing their young talent in critical positions.
That has required more patience with Klint Kubiak and his staff than with prior coaching staffs. Success in his first year, while working with a revamped version of the league's worst rosters in 2025, was always going to be hard to come by, making things other than wins the metric for success.
Among other things, Las Vegas' inconsistent play has led to more wins, but also more than a few blowout losses that confirmed which position groups the Raiders must fix the most this offseason. It has also given the Raiders' new coaching staff their first true taste of adversity together.
Less than half a season after selecting No. 1 overall, and before the No. 1 overall pick ever played more than a series, unreasonable questions surrounding defensive coordinator Rob Leonard were being raised entering Week 10.
Instead of throwing his defensive coordinator under the bus as Las Vegas' young defense struggled, Kubiak publicly supported Leonard and the defense last week. On Sunday, Leonard's defense kept the Raiders in the game, while the offense struggled at times.
The Raiders' defense played some of its best football in weeks. On Monday, Kubiak explained his confidence in Leonard and Las Vegas' defense.
“Well, like I said, we’re supporting our coaches, we’re supporting our players, and we’re focused on growth and we're focused on getting better at the fundamentals and the little details,” Kubiak said Monday afternoon.
“I think the positives of yesterday are that you see the fruits of having your guys’ back, standing behind them. Instead of bailing on them, you fix the problems, you keep getting better, and you give guys opportunities. You give new guys chances if someone’s not getting it done. So, we just keep trying to improve as a team, as a coaching staff.”
Losing is not fun, but it's undoubtedly a part of the early stages in a rebuild, and the trust that comes from receiving support and, in turn, proving those who supported you right is bigger than winning a Week 10 matchup that likely won't matter much to the Raiders' fate this season.
It was not pretty, and the Raiders lost. However, Las Vegas' focus should be primarily on continuing to fix the culture within the locker room and developing as many of their young players as possible.
The 2026 season is only the beginning, as the Raiders will continue to add talent. When the Raiders' future success happens, they will point back to this season as part of the reason why.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders Sign Notable QB After Cousins Trade: What It Means
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (4-6) are headed to the Mile High City to take on the Denver Broncos (7-2) this weekend, but before they do, they had some housekeeping to do.
GM John Spytek dealt 15-year veteran QB Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings this past week in what was nothing short of a brilliant move that essentially got them tremendous tutelage for their rookie QB Fernando Mendoza and their young backup Aidan O’Connell, for nothing, while garnering the Vikings a third-round pick.
That left a major hole in the Raiders' roster. They needed a third QB, and ideally one with experience, a great teammate, and, in a perfect world, one who could contribute to the development of the two young signal callers.
Since moving on from Pete Carroll and last year’s collapse, Spytek somehow continued to navigate the Silver and Black in that perfect world, because his latest move did just that.
GM John Spytek quickly signed an NFL journeyman quarterback, but not just anyone: Brett Rypien is best known for his record-setting college career as a Boise State Bronco and is even more famous for his athletic family. He now sits on the Raiders' practice squad.
​Rypien’s famous last name is instantly recognizable to any NFL fan, thanks to his uncle, Mark Rypien. Mark was an iconic two-time Pro Bowl quarterback for Washington. He won two Super Bowls and was named MVP of Super Bowl Twenty-Six. A stunning performance that still reverberates in sports bars everywhere.
But Mark and Brett are far from the family's sole sports legacy, which extends even further. Brett's father, Tim, played minor league baseball. His late cousin, Rick Rypien, and another cousin, Shane Churla, both played in the NHL. Obviously hockey, but that reflects the toughness Brett and Mark are known for. Additionally, Brett had another uncle, Wes, who was a Canadian boxing champion—continuing the toughness narrative.
​A native of Spokane, Washington, Brett obliterated state high school passing records before attending Boise State, where he became the Mountain West Conference's all-time leader in passing yards. He entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent with the Denver Broncos in 2019, starting a handful of games over four seasons.
Since leaving Denver, Brett has been a reliable veteran backup and practice squad quarterback for several franchises, including the Rams, Seahawks, Jets, Bears, Vikings, Bengals, Colts, and Texans.
The Raiders needed a third QB for insurance, but true to Spytek’s and Kubiak’s leadership, playing chess. In contrast, others play checkers; they added yet another veteran, a well-recognized good teammate and someone who can continue to help their two primary QBs mature in their development.
It is imperative to understand what his role will be, as before Cousins' trade, the Raiders had three QBs on the 53-man roster. That is not the case with this signing.
NFL teams are not allowed to designate a practice squad quarterback as their emergency third quarterback on game day. But that doesn’t mean they can’t; it will just take some clever maneuvering.
To use the emergency third quarterback rule, the player must be on the team's 53-man roster. While teams can use one of their standard practice squad elevations to dress a third quarterback on the regular active game-day list, they cannot use the emergency inactive designation for a practice squad player.
This was a great move by the Silver and Black. If Rypien plays, it will be in a worst-case scenario, but they'll address it in the best way possible. The Raiders also announced, “In a corresponding move we have released DE Bralen Trice from the practice squad.”
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. He serves as the Senior Writer for NFL and College sports, and is the beat writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders. Additionally, he is the editor and publisher for several sites On SI. Carpenter is a member of the Pro Football Writers Association (PFWA), the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA), and the United States Basketball Writers Association (USBWA).

title: Breaking Down the Latest Dolphins Roster Moves, with Another Win for the 2026 Draft Class
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins have made their decision on rookie edge defender Max Llewellyn, and for the moment at least want to keep him around.
That's the takeaway from the latest Dolphins roster moves, as they signed Llewellyn from the practice squad to the active roster, clearing the way for him to be able to play against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on Sunday.
In an accompanying move, the Dolphins signed punter Jack Browning to the practice squad to fill that slot. Browning has appeared in five NFL games, all with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2024 when he averaged 42.5 yards on 10 punts, with a net of 34.6 yards.
Browning has been out of the NFL since December 2024 except for a one-week stint with the Arizona Cardinals in training camp this summer.
The Dolphins, of course, have veteran Bradley Pinion to handling the punting duties and there's nothing about Browning that suggests he could be a long-term answer, so perhaps Pinion is dealing with some sort of physical issue.
Llewellyn, the seventh-round pick out of Iowa, had been on the practice squad since he was waived the day after the cuts to the 53-player limit to accommodate the eight newcomers the team brought in from the outside.
Llewelly played the maximum three games allowed as a practice squad elevation when he suited up against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 2, the New York Jets in Week 7 and the New England Patriots in Week 8.
In those three games, he got only six total snaps on defense and eight more on special teams, but clearly the Dolphins liked his potential enough to want to see him in action again.
He becomes the sixth edge defender on the 53-man roster after Eric Watts also was signed from the practice squad Tuesday.
The Dolphins are very light at the defensive tackle position with only three players — Kenneth Grant, Keith Cooper Jr., Jordan Jefferson — after placing Zeek Biggers and Jordan Phillips on IR, but Watts (6-5, 277) might be able to slide inside for a certain number of snaps and veteran Matthew Butler figures to get elevated from the practice squad for the Buffalo game.
Llewellyn was the last of the Dolphins' league-high 13 draft picks this year and all of them are with the team — 11 on the active roster, linebacker Trey Moore on injured reserve, and guard DJ Campbell on the practice squad.

title: Why This Dolphins Season So Far Has Been a Success ... Even Beyond Getting a High 2027 Draft Pick
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins are tied for the worst record in the NFL after starting 1-8 in Jeff Hafley's first year as head coach, and it would surprise no one if they ended up at the very bottom of the league standings by the end of the season.
But the truth is they're still having a productive season, and not just because they'll end up with one of the very first picks in the 2027 NFL draft.
See, this season never was about wins and losses, something Hafley said time and time again to make sure his message didn't get lost or expectations would start surpassing reality.
The 2026 season, once the Dolphins overhauled their roster to clear up their cap situation for a fresh financial start, became about establishing a foundation, player development and player evaluation.
With regards to those objectives, the Dolphins are winning.
NFL writer Jourdan Rodrigue put it perfectly with a comment that accompanied placing the Dolphins in Tier 1 of teams in terms of problem-solving when it comes to roster management.
"If you don’t think the 1-8 Dolphins belong in this tier in this specific exercise , you simply don’t appreciate the elegance of the line they currently walk," Rodrigue wrote. "(I will add, it has to be really tough on the players and coaches.) From a team-building perspective, they have struck a perfect balance between showcasing young talent — rookie receiver Caleb Douglas is electric, second-year running back Ollie Gordon is a blossoming star and rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez will have a long career — while not sacrificing draft positioning. Even with recent injuries to starting quarterback Malik Willis and defensive lineman Zach Sieler, getting the present group valuable experience while keeping focus on a bright future is what is important here. They have also proven to be a scrappy out, including for the talented Detroit Lions."
Because we don't like the term, we're not going to use "culture" here even though many would, but regardless of the term the one identity the Dolphins have established in terms of play style is that they will play hard.
Just check out the weekly press conferences with opposing coaches and invariably they will mention how hard the Dolphins compete. Of course, maybe they'd be saying the same thing even if it weren't true because buttering up the opponent before a game is part of the game, but it's true in this case and it's actually pretty obvious to anyone who watches the Miami games.
While there's a lack of high-end veteran talent on the team, there's absolutely nothing lacking in terms of want-to.
This is a highly engaged group, and the postgame celebration after that one win against the New York Jets, while criticized in some circles for being over the top given the team's record, showed you a group of players who really want to win for their coach.
Now, contrast that to the shot of Justin Herbert in the L.A. Chargers locker room when they were celebrating their first win after an 0-8 start Monday night, and see if you can spot the difference.
That's a team in the middle of a storm with nothing but dark clouds ahead.
The Dolphins, on the flip side, also may be in the middle of a storm but there are clear skies on the horizon.
Beyond the early positive impression Hafley has made as head coach, including the fact he has an undermanned defense ranked 10th in the NFL in total yards allowed, are the contributions of the 2026 draft class.
One of the biggest goals for this season was having the largest draft class in the NFL produce a handful of players who would become key contributors on the road back to contention, and this looks like mission accomplished nine games into their rookie year.
It obviously starts at the top of the rookie class with Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez and Caleb Douglas, with GM Jon-Eric Sullivan looking very much like he nailed his top four draft picks in his new job.
Beyond those four, safety Michael Taaffe is starting as a rookie fifth-round pick, leads the team with three interceptions, tight end Will Kacmarek should have a long NFL future as a blocking specialist, and Kyle Louis is getting more and more work as a nickel linebacker.
And that's not even mentioning Chris Bell and Trey Moore, who also could become contributors at some point.
Another goal for this season was getting a good sense of whether Malik Willis could become a long-term answer at quarterback, and that remains unsolved for a variety of factors, including how much he's limited by his supporting cast and durability concerns with him currently on IR.
Regardless, the Dolphins always were going to need to beef up the roster around the quarterback, Willis or somebody else, before they really can think about competing.
This season was about taking the first steps in the right direction, and it says here the Dolphins absolutely have done that.
It does stink that the Dolphins have such a poor record, but anybody thinking playoffs with all the personnel losses and dead cap space they were carrying was fooling himself.
The goals for 2026 simply were different. And in that respect, the Dolphins are having a perfectly fine season.

title: Poup's Perspective: Honest Assessment of Kyle McCord's Dolphins Debut
full_text:
Kyle McCord's NFL debut for the Miami Dolphins on Sunday was fine.
Nothing more, nothing less.
It was the kind of debut that told us we need to see more before forming any sort of big-picture evaluation in terms of McCord's ceiling and whether his ceiling is potential future starter, dependable backup or not even that much.
The final numbers were pedestrian, with McCord completing 17 of 32 passes for 209 yards with no touchdowns and no interceptions and a passer rating of 73.6.
More than anything, McCord showed the moment wasn't too big for him, which actually is a solid accomplishment because there have been previous quarterbacks — and we could name a couple of Dolphins examples — who clearly were overwhelmed by the moment.
Something else that was positive is the Dolphins had a chance to win the game and we could go as far as suggest they should have won the game but didn't because kicker Zane Gonzalez missed three kicks that cost the team seven points in a two-point loss.
The question, of course, is how much would McCord have had to do with the victory considering the Dolphins got a pick-six from rookie cornerback Chris Johnson and their first touchdown was a pass thrown by wide receiver Malik Washington.
To be sure, McCord was working at a disadvantage in a way because the offensive line was missing its best player, Aaron Brewer, and it might not be coincidence that the three passes batted down at the line of scrimmage came when his replacement Andrew Meyer gave ground to a defensive lineman.
That, of course, included the failed fourth-and-17 attempt for Kevin Coleman Jr. on the Dolphins' final drive.
The flip side, though, is that McCord had the benefit of going up against a bad Indianapolis defense.
This was a Colts defense a week removed from giving up 508 total yards against the Dallas Cowboys, that was missing two starting linebackers, that lost its two starting cornerbacks — and two best defensive players — to injury in the first half when Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward were injured.
So, Brewer or no Brewer, this was about as good an opportunity for a quarterback making his first start as there was.
And again, McCord was fine.
But, no, he wasn't better than Malik Willis.
The eye test should have been enough to see that, but for those who want numbers, we can try these:
-- McCord completed 53.1 percent of his passes; Willis topped that number in six of his eight starts and is at 58.2 on the season.
-- McCord's passer rating didn't match Willis' season number of 76.1, which includes figures of 130.7 and 92.1 against the Jets and Patriots before that number dropped to 50.1 against the Lions when he was visibly compromised by the groin injury that landed him on injured reserve.
-- In terms of yardage, McCord's number was higher than Willis' season average of 176.1, but Willis has four games between 208 and 220 yards.
In terms of certain analytics, there were some favoring McCord and some favoring Willis.
But one thing that was clear is the Dolphins designed a game plan to make things simpler for McCord, highlighted by a couple of screen passes that proved very effective.
In fact, McCord's first NFL completion was a short throw to fullback DJ Herman after he leaked out of the backfield that converted a third-and-7.
McCord had a couple of really nice throws, the sideline shot to Caleb Douglas, the deep middle crosser to Douglas, but he was victimized by a couple of drops and a couple of throws where his receiver simply didn't get open.
In other words, McCord was dealing with the same issues that have hampered Willis all season.
The one difference is that McCord was healthy, whereas Willis has barely spent a week without being on the injury report with one issue or another.
McCord will get at least three more shots at starting for the Dolphins before Willis is eligible to return from injured reserve, and it does look like he'll do his part and at the very least be able to manage the game.
That's the baseline that he seemed to establish with that start against the Colts, and there's no to dismiss the idea there could be more to his game because this, after all, was his first NFL appearance.
And for a first go, again, it was just fine.

title: More Bad News Amid Flurry of Dolphins Roster Moves
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins indeed went the familiar route when it came time to replenish the defensive tackle position, which took another hit Tuesday.
The team announced a series of roster moves that included Jordan Phillips joining Zeek Biggers in going on injured reserve.
The Dolphins also signed three players from their practice squad to the active roster — defensive tackle Jordan Jefferson, quarterback Brady Cook and edge Eric Watts.
Lastly, the Dolphins signed four players to the practice squad, including kicker Daniel Carlson. The others are WR Brady Boyd, DL Matthew Butler and DL Chris Smith.
The biggest shockwave of all the moves obviously involves the D-tackle position, where Phillips has joined Biggers in sustaining a season-ending injury, with ESPN's Marcel Louis-Jacques reporting Phillips will have surgery to repair a biceps tendon.
Phillips was spotted leaving Lucas Oil Stadium with his arm in a sling Sunday and was scheduled to undergo an MRI on Monday, so it always was fair to be concerned his injury also could be season-ending.
As we suggested in a story earlier Tuesday, the Dolphins replaced Phillips and Biggers with players with whom they're familiar because Butler was with the team in 2025, playing 12 games with one start, and was in training camp this summer before being released.
Because Jefferson is the only new defensive tackle on the 53-man roster, the Dolphins still have only three at that position with Kenneth Grant and Keith Cooper Jr. as the other two, so Butler seems like a logical candidate to get elevated for the game at Buffalo on Sunday considering his familiarity and experience.
Smith, the other new defensive tackle, hasn't played in an NFL game since 2024 when he made his five career appearances with the Detroit Lions after coming out of Notre Dame.
Grant now becomes the only defensive tackle of the Dolphins' projected group with Biggers and Phillips having joined Zach Sieler on injured reserve.
Thanks to those four, the Dolphins have moved up to 10th in the NFL in total defense and 10th in rushing yards allowed per carry, and those rankings figure to take a pretty big hit with the three players gone.
Watts' signing puts the Dolphins back at five edge defenders, as he joins Chop Robinson, Josh Uche, Malik Herring and Rodney McGraw.
Cook being signed to the 53 figures to be just a matter of time because he's going to be serving as the backup quarterback for at least four games while Malik Willis is on injured reserve.
Carlson, who tried out for the Dolphins a couple of weeks ago, seemed like the logical candidate after Zane Gonzalez was waived following his three misses in the 24-22 loss against the Indianapolis Colts.
The Dolphins didn't sign Gonzalez to the active roster until he exhaused his three practice squad elevations, so maybe they will use the same approach with Carlson — certainly hoping for better results.
As we indicated Tuesday, the Dolphins' field goal kicking has been a problem all season, with Miami next-to-last in the NFL in field goal percentage.

title: Examining Potential Dolphins DT Replacements
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins already were down two defensive tackles as of late Tuesday morning as we continued to await word on the status of yet another injured player at the position.
And regardless of what prognosis is delivered for Jordan Phillips, it's clear the Dolphins are going to need reinforcements at the position — and sooner rather than later.
In fact, we'd expect a flurry of roster moves by late Tuesday afternoon with the practice week kicking off Wednesday and we'd expect one and maybe two defensive linemen being added to the 53-man roster and/or practice squad.
The big question, of course, becomes who that one or two players will be.
One place to start would be on the Dolphins' own practice squad, where they simply could promote Jordan Jefferson to the 53-man roster. A 2024 fourth-round pick of the Jacksonville Jaguars with 10 career regular season appearances, Jefferson fits the mold of the players they've brought in this year as a 25-year-old unproven player looking to jump-start his career.
If they prefer a more veteran presence but someone they're also familiar with, then another logical choice would be Matthew Butler, who played 12 games with the team last season and performed well in training camp before he was released in favor of summer surprise Keith Cooper Jr., who was waived and then re-signed off the Carolina Panthers practice squad and now stands with 2025 first-round pick Kenneth Grant as the only healthy D-tackles on the 53.
And there's also Fatorma Mulbah, who showed flashes in training camp and has some NFL experience from his time with the New York Jets.
Yet another, even more familiar name is Christian Wilkins, who hasn't played a game since October 2024 and seems like a forgotten man in league circles. That idea doesn't appear to have any legs.
There are other defensive tackle without a team at the moment, and another place the Dolphins can look is on the practice squads around the NFL.
If the Dophins want to go the veteran route, options could include Phidarian Mathis with the Buffalo Bills, Isaiah Loudermilk with the New York Jets, Austin Johnson with the Jacksonville Jaguars and Byron Cowart of the Washington Commanders, a player who spent time in Miami a couple of years ago.
That, however, would go against the pattern the Dolphins have established, which is looking for those young players with upside who just haven't delivered yet.
Looking at the physical make-up of the three DTs the Dolphins have lost — Zach Sieler, Biggers and Phillips — we also should expect any addition to have some size, meaning undersized DTs need not apply.
Two names to watch here include Jordan Miller of the Denver Broncos because he was on the Dolphins practice squad at some point and the Seattle Seahawks' Cole Brevard, who the Dolphins tried out a few weeks back.
Former Dallas Cowboys first-round pick Mazi Smith is on the Packers practice squad, but the Dolphins already had him on their practice squad and moved on from him, so logic says Miami isn't going down that road, but who knows?
In any event, we'll find out soon enough.
In the meantime, here's a pretty comprehensive list of D-tackles around NFL practice squads who could interest the Dolphins: Amari McNeil (Jets), Eric Gregory (Patriots), David Olajiga (Ravens), Howard Cross III (Bengals), Zion Logue (Bengals), Junior Tafuna (Texans), Brandon Cleveland (Raiders), Zion Wilson (Eagles), Gabe Hall (Eagles), P.J. Mustipher (Giants), Jeffrey M'ba (Lions), Zacch Pickens (Falcons), Jalen Hunt (Rams).

title: Updated Dolphins Draft Picture With Critical Next Two Weeks Coming Up
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins are trying to win games this season while the main objective remains player development and evaluation, and it's also only natural to look ahead to the 2027 draft and how high a pick they could wind up having.
To that end, Week 10 of the 2026 season was a very good one for them, most notably their closs loss against the Indianapolis Colts and the Monday night game that saw the Los Angeles Chargers get their first victory of the season.
The Dolphins, Chargers and Tennessee Titans now are tied for the worst record in the league at 1-8, though the Dolphins' tougher strength of schedule currently has them with the third pick behind the Titans at number 1 and then the Chargers.
The rest of the current top five has the New York Jets (2-8) and the Philadelphia Eagles (2-7).
There are now eight weeks left in the regular season, so plenty of time for the exact order to change. And there could be some movement pretty soon actually because the Jets and Chargers face each other at SoFi Stadium on Sunday, and then the Jets come to Hard Rock Stadium to face the Dolphins in Week 12.
We could debate what's actually the worst team in the NFL right now among the Titans, Chargers, Dolphins and even Jets, but injuries likely will become a factor and Miami has gotten hit pretty hard over the past two games with Malik Willis, Zach Sieler, Zeek Biggers and potentially Jordan Phillips.
After the games of Week 10, the Dolphins are considered front-runners to land that top overall pick.
The Dolphins' current projected win total over/under betting line is at 2.5, according to DraftKings Sportsbook. That's the lowest in the league, with the Chargers and Titans at 3.5, the Jets and Eagles at 4.5, and the Colts at 5.5.
Of the Dolphins' remaining eight games, they have two that should be considered very winnable — the home games against the Jets and the Chargers in Week 16 — and the season finale against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium now looks different with the injury to quarterback Drake Maye, especially if the Pats are out of playoff contention by then.
Miami will be heavy underdogs in the other five games — at Buffalo, at Denver, home against Chicago, at Green Bay, and home against Buffalo.
Since the NFL went to a 17-game schedule in 2021, the worst record ever compiled was the 2-15 by the Carolina Panthers in 2023.
Finishing 3-14 has meant a top 3 pick every time except this year for the Titans, who picked fourth. And ending up 4-13 has meant a top 5 pick every time except for the Las Vegas Raiders having the sixth overall selection in 2025.
So based on their projected win total, the Dolphins are expected to have no worse that the fourth overall pick.
There will be plenty of time after the end of the season to really start diving and digging into the top prospects, but the early popular names include WR Jeremiah Smith, QB Drew Mestemaker, CB Leonard Moore, DE Colin Simmons and DE Dylan Stewart, and a case could be made for the Dolphins drafting any of them.
One thing to consider, too, is that the higher the pick the better chance of getting offers to move up from a team that's really zeroed in on a particular prospect, a move that could provide the Dolphins with more draft capital, which would help as they continue replenishing the roster.

title: Zeek Biggers News Is Another Big Setback for Dolphins D-Line, But It Could Get Worse
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins are going to be running out of bodies at the rate they're going — big bodies, that is.
In their first game with Zach Sieler on injured reserve, the Dolphins watched both Zeek Biggers and Jordan Phillips leave their 24-22 loss against the Indianapolis Colts with injuries, and the verdict has come on the severity of one of them — and it's not good news.
Biggers is done for the season after sustaining a meniscus injury in his right knee, according to NFL insider Ian Rapoport, citing sources.
#Dolphins DT Zeek Biggers, a former 7th round pick who has earned a starting role, will have knee surgery to repair his lateral meniscus, sources say, a procedure that ends his season. Biggers will make a full recovery in time for 2027. pic.twitter.com/nK6i2JzrPM
The question now is whether Phillips' injury wil be as severe after he left Lucas Oil Stadium with an arm in a sling and was scheduled for an MRI on Monday.
Head coach Jeff Hafley said Monday afternoon that both players needed more tests to determine the severity of the injury, but now the best the Dolphins will be able to do is salvage a second of the four defensive tackles from last year.
If Phillips is sidelined for a while, the Dolphins will be down to 2025 first-round pick Kenneth Grant and Keith Cooper Jr. on the 35-man roster, with Jordan Jefferson the lone defensive tckle on the practice squad.
The bad luck, of course, began when Sieler sustained a season-ending biceps injury in the Week 9 loss against the Detroit Lions.
Biggers' injury means the Dolphins will need to add at least one defensive tackle to the 53-man roster, and that number will go to two if Phillips also winds up having to go on injured reserve.
Two names to watch would be Fatorma Mulbah and Matthew Butler, who both were with the Dolphins in training camp before being among the final cuts to the 53-player limit.
Former Dolphins first-round pick Christian Wilkins certainly is an interesting name, but there's been no indication that any team has reached out to him this year and he hasn't played in a bit more than two years after sustaining a serious foot injury while with the Las Vegas Raiders in 2024.
Now that any time would be good for these kind of injuries, the timing really isn't good because the Dolphins are about to face one of the best rushing teams when they travel to Buffalo on Sunday.
Biggers was injured during Seth McGowan's touchdown run in the first quarter that gave the Colts a 7-0 lead.
He played in all nine games this season and made two starts, contributing at both defensive tackle and defensive end.
He was a seventh-round pick in 2025 after the Dolphins had selected Grant in the first round and Phillips in the fifth round.

title: How Jarrett Kingston Is Emerging as the Best Waiver Wire Pick-Up for the Dolphins As Another One Bites the Dust
full_text:
Hours after the much-publicized move to waive kicker Zane Gonzalez, the Miami Dolphins made another transaction Monday, that one involving edge defender Jamree Kromah.
And, like Gonzalez, Kromah was waived, ending his brief time in Miami that began after he was claimed off waivers from the Chicago Bears.
Kromah was let go after appearing in two games for Miami, including the 24-22 loss against the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday when his playing time occurred strictly on special teams.
The move left the Dolphins with three openings on their 53-man roster because they were at 52 players when they faced the Colts and haven't yet replaced either Gonzalez or Kromah.
More significantly, the move with Kromah provided more evidence that picking up players on waivers is a sound practice for rebuilding teams looking for hidden gems wherever they can find them, but it also rarely provides great answers.
This isn't to suggest the Dolphins should stop looking at the waiver wire in the hope of finding a good player on whom another team gave up too quickly, but at the same time understanding that the pieces to what the organization ultimately hopes is a contender likely will come through other methods, such as the draft or free agency.
Kromah was the 16th and most recent waiver wire acquisition by the Dolphins so far in 2026, a total that's just four shy of what they did in 2019 when they were undergoing another rebuilding project.
Of those 16 players picked up through waivers this year, exactly half already have come and gone. Of the other eight, only safety Julius Wood and guard Jarrett Kingston have started a game, and it's been one start each.
At this time, none of the waiver wire pick-ups has a significant role, though Wood is a core special teams player and Kingston just became the team's sixth offensive lineman for the game against Indianapolis on Sunday.
But the chances of any of the waiver wire pick-ups becoming key contributors on the team's road back to contention are pretty slim, and that's just the reality of making those moves.
And the Dolphins likely aren't done with moves like that because, who knows, maybe one of them could turn into Zach Sieler.
That's what happened in 2019 when the Dolphins claimed the defensive lineman from the Baltimore Ravens. Nearly seven years later, Sieler is well established as a core player for the Dolphins, a team captain and a major loss now that he's on IR.
To a much lesser degree, the Dolphins also hit in 2019 with Mack Hollins, but the success stories are extremely rare when it comes to waiver wire pick-ups.
It's why we always caution against expecting too much whenever a newcomer arrives, whether it's Kromah or even former Seattle Seahawks third-round pick Christian Haynes, who was claimed just a few days before Kromah.
The rationale is pretty simple: There's a reason the player's former team let them go.
Yes, there will be an exception to the rule at some point, which is why there's no harm in "turning over stones," as the saying goes. That's what the Dolphins did with Kromah.
And even though it didn't pan out, it still was worth the gamble.

title: What the Week 10 Film Told Us About the Miami Dolphins
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins nearly completed a 14-point comeback, but ultimately fell 24-22 to the Indianapolis Colts in Week 10. Struggles in the trenches litter the all-22 tape of a game that Miami failed to win in key moments, so let’s take a look at some of the biggest lessons from the film review.
Without Aaron Brewer and Malik Willis, communication and protection issues were to be expected, and this game certainly had its fair share of them. Late rushes and rotations led to unblocked defenders in the run and pass game. What’s more worrisome, though, is the seemingly downward trend of individual performances that continued against Indianapolis.
pic.twitter.com/8GAzhCBXjk
The right side tandem of Jonah Savaiinaea and Austin Jackson remains ineffective when stressed, both in one-on-one protection and as the point-of-attack blockers on rushing plays. Miami attempted to prop them up with pullers and misdirection, but it led to a few whiffs by Kadyn Proctor, Patrick Paul, and Will Kacmarek, and players left unaccounted for by the aforementioned late rotations.
In the absence of Chris Bell, Miami also used Kevin Coleman and Malik Washington as key blockers from the slot on runs to their side, and considering both of them are listed under 200 pounds, it went about as well as you’d expect.
pic.twitter.com/cpSmtaHevF
In this game, Miami was without its best offensive lineman, and the duo of Patrick Paul and Kadyn Proctor, who have a combined 38 starts between them, were asked to be the steady-handed adults in the room. Both are capable of high-level reps (and even had some in this game) but lack the refinement to consistently prop up the others around them with such little margin for error. They were put under a microscope and often asked to overcompensate, and thus bear the least of the blame among the starting five.
Miami’s defensive line was a mirror image of their offensive counterpart: without their best player, and unable to make up for it, with young players failing to provide consistent performance.
Kenneth Grant and Jordan Phillips were knocked off the ball consistently. While both have done a solid job standing their ground against double-teams in recent weeks, this was an abysmal showing. The Colts’ 1.75 yards before contact per attempt ranks eighth in the league in Week 10, pending Monday Night Football.
pic.twitter.com/EmtBJdTanv
Much like the offense, Miami tried to make up for their one-on-one deficiency, this time by slanting their edge defenders inside. Indianapolis was able to exploit it, however, and used Miami’s aggressiveness against them to find creases along the outside.
With the primary goal of this season being player development, it’s important to look at Miami’s rookie class, whose performances were a mixed bag in Week 10.
Caleb Douglas once again flashed, making a couple highly contested catches, including one on a dagger concept where the safety triggered down late. Douglas showcased his strong hands and body control by maintaining possession of the ball through the contact. For the second straight week, though, he dropped a pass on his body that he had to lower his hands for, so he definitely has something to work on.
pic.twitter.com/kXBmeGOonl
Kevin Coleman Jr. struggled in his increased role due to the absence of Chris Bell. His size profiles him more as a slot receiver, but with the Dolphins' lack of depth, they've attempted to use him on the outside. His lack of physicality showed on an early curl route that was broken up by Charvarius Ward, and he was unable to get going.
Outside of their interceptions, Chris Johnson and Michael Taaffe struggled. Miami threw out plenty of unorthodox looks, as they continued their trend of putting more and more on the secondary’s plate, and there were several instances of receivers running open in between the second and third levels. Furthermore, Taaffe took some poor pursuit angles, and was dominated by blockers on a screen pass to Jonathan Taylor. Jacob Rodriguez also wasn’t very impactful, as the struggles of Miami’s interior defensive line allowed blockers to move up to the second level with relative ease.
Undrafted rookie DJ Herman was inconsistent, but made a few high-level blocks that really created displacement and afforded Ollie Gordon room to run. The linebacker-convert has continued to get better in recent weeks. Kadyn Proctor and Will Kacmarek were similar, moving bodies, but also having a few standout misses that killed opportunities for the run game to create explosives.
Tyler DeSena is currently a journalism student at the University of Central Florida. Prior to joining Dolphins On SI in 2026, DeSena worked with dolphinstalk.com, and created independent social media content on X, YouTube and TikTok.

title: Miami Dolphins 2026 Week 10 Snap Counts Stories: Tolbert Time, First-Round Picks Pick It Up
full_text:
What stood out regarding play counts in the Miami Dolphins' 24-22 loss against the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday:
We'll start with the list of inactives, which was highlighted by injured players Aaron Brewer, Chris Bell and Jared Wayne.
The only Dolphins players who were active but did not play were backup quarterback Brady Cook (after he was elevated from the practice squad) and guard Christian Haynes.
Since we've been keeping track every game, the starting lineup was back to seven rookies with fourth-round pick Kyle Louis again starting as a nickel back. The other six starters were Kadyn Proctor at left guard, DJ Herman at fullback wide receiver Caleb Douglas, linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe.
-- The Dolphins offense was on the field for 69 snaps, and what stands out here is the heavy work load for wide receivers Malik Washington (59 snaps) and Caleb Douglas (58).
-- Active again because of the absences of Bell and Wayne, Jalen Tolbert played only 11 snaps on offense and had the first touchdown of the game for the Dolphins and one can't help but wonder why he didn't get more work.
-- At tight end, one has to think that Will Kacmarek continuing to show up on the injury report every week is playing a role in his limited snap count. He got 20 offensive snaps against Indy, with Greg Dulcich leading the way at tight end with 42. Regardless, the Dolphins aren't getting enough production out of their tight ends.
-- Jarrett Kingston took over for Caedan Wallace as the extra offensive lineman for this game and played eight snaps when the Dolphins had six linemen on the field and another two when center Andrew Meyer left the game with an apparent hand injury.
-- Jaylen Wright played only 12 snaps at running back to give Ollie Gordon II a spell and again wasn't productive. Kaytron Allen played only two snaps on offense.
-- Five players were on the field for all the team's 59 defensive snaps, the exact same number as the Detroit game in Week 9 — LB Jordyn Brooks, LB Jacob Rodriguez, S Michael Taaffe, CB Chris Johnson and S Dante Trader.
-- Chop Robinson, who is playing the best football of his career, tied his season high with 50 snaps, but in this game it represented an eye-opening 84.7 percent of the team's defensive snaps. This easily was the highest percentage of his career, topping the 71.2 percent against Kansas City in the home opener this season.
-- Kyle Louis not only got a start for a second consecutive game, but he also doubled his snap count on defense to 25 against the Colts after playing 11 against Detroit.
-- With Zach Sieler on IR, and Zeek Biggers and Jordan Phillips both getting injured in the game, Kenneth Grant saw his work load increase dramatically. He played 41 snaps against the Colts, a big jump from the 21 he played against Detroit. The 41 snaps tied for the second-highest total of his career behind only the 44 snaps against the Colts in the 2025 season opener, Grant's NFL debut.
-- On the edge, it was pretty much all about Robinson and Josh Uche (44 snaps), with Malik Herring next in the snap count with a modest 18.
-- Jason Marshall Jr. again didn't start at cornerback, but he did get a good amount of work along with Johnson and JuJu Brents, with a little more than 50 percent participation (31 of 59 snaps).
-- There were six non-specialists who saw action only on special teams: LB Shaka Heyward, S Julius Wood, LB Jackson Woodard, CB Jaylin Simpson, EDGE Jamree Kromah and T Chukwuebuka Godrick.
-- Rookie tight end Seydou Traore and Woodard again tied for the team lead in special teams snaps, this time with 23. They were followed with 19 for Louis, Zayne Anderson, Wood and Heyward.

title: Vikings' Snap Count vs. Packers: Biggest Winners, Losers & Role Changes in Week 10
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings surprised many fans watching the team's Week 10 game against the Green Bay Packers. The 30-10 victory was controlled from the start by the Purple and Gold, who finally put together a complete game.
The attack plan from head coach Kevin O'Connell and defensive coordinator Brian Flores worked extremely well at Lambeau Field, giving hope that the team can remain a contender for the remainder of the season.
How O'Connell and Flores managed their personnel was important too. Several contributors missed time due to injury . Knowing which players to use to fill particular roles paid off handsomely for the Vikings. Here are some winners and losers from Sunday's snap counts.
T.J. Hockenson was ruled out of this game with a wrist/chest injury, so the next man up to start was second-year tight end Gavin Bartholomew. He played the ninth-most snaps on offense for Minnesota against Green Bay, getting in on 53 offensive plays.
Bartholomew caught three of four passes thrown his way by quarterback Kirk Cousins, gaining 36 yards and scoring his first touchdown as a pro. On that 20-yard touchdown catch in the fourth quarter, he stiff-armed a Packers defender to give himself a path to the end zone.
James Pierre is having a great first season in Minnesota, earning a 72.7 Pro Football Focus grade this year, but he saw his workload on defense cut from 50 defensive snaps against the Bills to 27 against the Packers.
Pierre still ended the day with a pass breakup and a tackle, but the drastic decrease in usage on defense is alarming. He was still the third-most-used cornerback behind Byron Murphy Jr. and Isaiah Rodgers, so hopefully this isn't a sign that he's in the doghouse.
When Caleb Banks was a healthy scratch last week against the Bills, plenty of rumors were floating around about what was going on with the rookie defensive lineman. However, he played 17 defensive snaps against the Packers and looked great.
Earning a 90.6 PFF initial grade, Banks had two tackles (one solo) against Green Bay. This was an important statement game for the 23-year-old, and he put forth his best showing as a pro to date.
While Banks saw significant playing time against the Packers, fellow rookie defensive lineman Domonique Orange went from playing 22 defensive snaps in Week 9 to seven in Week 10 against the Packers.
Finishing the game with two tackles (one solo), the Vikings got amazing play out of Banks, Levi Drake Rodriguez, Jalen Redmond, and Elijah Williams, all of whom earned a PFF grade of over 70 in the big divisional matchup.
It was a big day for Minnesota's rookies last Sunday, and second-round pick Jake Golday participated in the action. With starting linebacker Blake Cashman out, Golday and Ivan Pace Jr. did their best to hold down the defense, and the results were mixed.
He struggled as a pass rusher, as evidenced by his 54.2 PFF grade (last on the team). He was much better as a tackler against the Packers, bringing down five ball carriers, including three solo efforts.
