title: Breaking Down Titans’ Injuries in Week 11: Xavier Restrepo In, Wan’Dale Robinson Out vs. Cowboys
full_text:
After falling to the Jacksonville Jaguars at home in Week 10, the Tennessee Titans will pack their bags and hit the road for AT&T Stadium to square off against the Dallas Cowboys in Week 11.
Tennessee enters Sunday's contest against Dallas with a 1-8 record, while the Cowboys are 4-6. Both teams have had disappointing seasons so far, and both will be looking to bounce back from losses. Dallas lost a close 46-40 shootout to the San Francisco 49ers this past weekend.
The Titans will return to the practice field on Wednesday to prepare for Dallas, but before then, the team made a few roster moves, including placing one of its prized free-agent additions from the spring on injured reserve.
On Tuesday, the Titans announced that wide receiver Wan'Dale Robinson is being placed on injured reserve . Robinson left Sunday's loss to the Jaguars in the third quarter with an ankle injury.
As a result, Tennessee promoted second-year receiver Xavier Restrepo to the active roster and added Jamari Thrash to the practice squad.
Robinson, who signed a lucrative four-year deal with the Titans in March, will now miss at least the next four games. However, the slot receiver's role in Brian Daboll's offense was already diminishing before he exited the game on Sunday .
Tennessee opted to give Chimere Dike more of the work at receiver than Robinson. Elic Ayomanor also out-snapped Robinson. Dike finished Week 10 with two catches for 16 yards, while Ayomanor posted five receptions for 79 yards.
Robinson has been incredibly underwhelming this year, tallying just 38 catches for 272 yards and three touchdowns. The 25-year-old hasn't been the consistent slot threat he was with the New York Giants, and we may not see him again until late December.
Restrepo played just 16 passing snaps against Jacksonville, but made the most of his opportunity by hauling in three passes for 31 yards. The Miami product is now on the active roster and should receive even more opportunities.
Depending on whether Carnell Tate returns from his shoulder injury this week, Restrepo could find himself in a starting role in Dallas this weekend. Even if he doesn't, the former undrafted free agent receiver should be an active part of the offense with Robinson out, and given his chemistry with quarterback Cam Ward, he should be able to make an impact.
These next few weeks will be critical for Restrepo and his future in Nashville. We'll see if he rises to the occasion.

title: How Cam Ward, Titans' Offense are Making an Undeniable Case for Tennessee to Draft WR Jeremiah Smith
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans opened this season with demanding questions about the offense. Cam Ward looked unsteady, and Carnell Tate had a rough rookie preseason that threw his trajectory as the Titans' WR1 into doubt. Those worries lasted all the way up until Tennessee got a win in Week 6.
Then, things began to change. The Titans are 1-3 from Week 6 on, but the team's averages have changed drastically. In fact, it's Robert Saleh's defense taking the majority of the public heat, while Brian Daboll's offense has fallen somewhat into the background.
In Weeks 1-5, the Titans averaged an abysmal 11.6 points per contest. Since that turnaround against the Indianapolis Colts, in Weeks 6-10, the average has leapt to 25.5.
Tennessee's offense has been on the rise the last few weeks 📈 (via: @Ihartitz ) pic.twitter.com/oZS4mMfvaT
That's more than double, and the sample size is consistent. Ward has gotten better, and as a result, the body of the snake has too. It's a working system that, sooner rather than later, is likely to win the Titans a few games.
But if it doesn't? Well, the offense's rapid uptick is making the perfect argument for Tennessee to use their currently-held first overall pick on a generational WR talent. Jeremiah Smith is on the board, and the Titans look more ready than ever to make good on drafting him.
Ward's 4:1 touchdown-to-INT ratio in the last two contests, combined with two of his three 200+ yard games on the season, tell the story of a rising franchise QB in Nashville. Smith, a former teammate of Carnell Tate (who has turned out just fine, by the way) at Ohio State, is as promising a prospect as they come.
At 6'4", 222 lbs, Smith has the physicality you'd expect from a superstar playmaker. His 80 receptions (15 touchdowns) speak for themselves. He also holds the B1G record for receiving yards and touchdowns. Any team could make a case for drafting Smith.
No team could pair Smith with Tate, however, and with Ward developing at this rate, the signal caller also appears to be an ideal fit as someone who could grow alongside Smith. It's a blessing and a curse for Tennessee's offense to be clicking at this juncture in the season.
Robert Saleh is vying for more wins; a late-season playoff push is off the table, but the Titans can absolutely top their three-win total from the previous two seasons. Without a doubt, that would disallow drafting Smith.
We'll see what happens, but if the Titans' defense is the reason Tennessee ends up with the top pick, Smith ending up in the baby blue and white is starting to look all too convincing.

title: Titans' Snap Count Analysis vs. Jaguars: 2 Playmakers Pulled Away, While 1 WR Keeps Slipping
full_text:
A battle between the top-seeded team of the AFC South and the bottom seed ended in a 40-23 blowout, with the Jacksonville Jaguars proving supreme. Unfortunately, Titans' fans haven't seen a home win in almost an entire year. Tennessee's lone victory this season came against the Indianapolis Colts on Week 6 at Lucas Oil Stadium.
The Titans' last home win came against the Patrick-Mahomes-less Chiefs on Dec. 21, 2025, last season. With three home games left on the schedule, the original Nissan Stadium is yet to see a win in its final season.
It's time we dive into the snap-count winners and losers for the Titans in Week 10.
After missing Week 1 with a concussion, many fans assumed LB Cedric Gray would return to action as one of the primary linebackers for the Titans this season. However, Gray has been regulated to around 30 snaps per game, behind the likes of LB Cody Barton and rookie standout LB Anthony Hill Jr.
However, against Jacksonville, Gray was one of the only bright spots on the Tennessee defense.
He capitalized on his season-high 68 snaps. A big uptick from Week 8 against Cincinnati, where he only recorded 33, according to PFF . On Sunday, Gray recorded his first career interception while leading the Titans with nine tackles, one tackle for loss, and two pass deflections. Making him the first Titan to accomplish those stats since former First-Team All-Pro S Kevin Byard in 2020 .
Last season, Gray racked up the fourth most tackles in the NFL with 164, which was the most of any Titan. The 24-year-old linebacker is still a difference maker on a young Titans defense.
On Sunday, WR Elic Ayomanor had his best game of the season. For the second consecutive week, blooming star and rookie WR Carnell Tate was out with a shoulder injury, which has placed a greater responsibility on the remaining wide receiver core.
Ayomanor was the answer for second-year pro QB Cam Ward, serving as his top target throughout the game. He recorded a career-high 79 receiving yards from five receptions, including a 50-yard from a perfectly run post route by Ayomanor, resulting in a career-high pass and catch for Ward and Ayomanor.
Against Jacksonville, the 6-foot-2 wideout recorded 54 snaps, which is up from 50 snaps previously played against the Bengals. Although the number difference appears insignificant, Ayomanor's role was the difference.
Ayomanor was targeted 10 times against the Jaguars, which is a season-high, and double the targets he received from the previous game in Cincinnati. His targets and snaps saw an uptick, and so did his production.
In Cincinnati, Ayomanor had three catches for only 34 yards. However, his performance against the Jaguars was a positive for the future of Tennessee's offense.
This offseason, WR Wan'Dale Robinson was the big ticket acquisition for the Titans. The former New York Giant signed a massive four-year contract worth up to $70 million, making him the highest-paid Tennessee signee this past offseason, according to Spotrac .
Against the Jaguars, Robinson's snap count was down to 20 with an early exit due to an ankle injury. It could be assumed that his low snap count was because of his injury. However, Robinson's injury wouldn't tell the whole story because it didn't occur until late in the third quarter.
Robinson's production has been far from elite this season. In Cincinnati, Robinson recorded 72 of 77 offensive snaps but was still out-gained by TE Gunnar Helm and WR Chimere Dike, who aren't considered to be focal point offensive players.
Part of Robinson's decline in snaps has to do with drops and a recent trend of being outplayed by other receivers like Tate, Ayomanor and Dike.
Against Jacksonville, he only recorded three catches for 10 yards. His fourth game with three or fewer receptions this season, which is an obvious concern for a receiver one year removed from a career year where he had 1,000-plus yards with the Giants.
Robinson hasn't been the player Tennessee expected, especially for how much they paid him. In times like these when Tate is out due to injury, Robinson should be stepping up and playing like a true top receiver.

title: Chargers' Win Just Delivered Titans the Top Pick in 2027 Draft — But How Long Will it Last?
full_text:
Last night under the bright lights of primetime, the Los Angeles Chargers toppled the Baltimore Ravens for their first win of the season. Justin Herbert and the squad are now 1-8, but they weren't the only ones celebrating the victory. The Titans scored big on Monday.
As a result of Los Angeles pulling even with Tennessee's record, the Titans now hold the first overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. If the event were to kick off today, Mike Borgonzi and Robert Saleh would have their pick at any player in one of the best classes in recent memory.
This is massive news for any rebuild, but the kicker is obvious; we've still got eight games of football ahead of us. The Titans' overhaul demands a refresh of young talent, with that need being exasperated by Jeffery Simmons and Amani Hooker both being traded.
But if the last two weeks of competition have taught us anything about this Titans team, it's that they're both getting better and getting closer to beating good teams. Tennessee almost took down the Cincinnati Bengals on the road in Week 8.
This past Sunday, the now 7-2 Jacksonville Jaguars were in a tight race with the Titans through three quarters. A failed fourth-down conversion turned the tide negatively in what has previously been a close contest.
Either way, this is a Titans team ticking up, led by Cam Ward's steady development. This puts the franchise between a rock and a top pick. With a player like Jeremiah Smith on the line, the difference between a few spots is no laughing matter.
The superstar Ohio State pass-catcher is the B1G's all-time leader in receiving yards (3,875) and receiving touchdowns (42). A former teammate of Titans' stud Carnell Tate, reuniting the two would give Ward perhaps the best young playmaking duo in the NFL.
That would only be one of two first-round selections for Tennessee, no less. The vision is there for a historic draft class led by Smith that could turn a near-solid Titans team into a winner overnight. But win a few games now, slip a few picks, and Smith is out of the picture.
You see the conundrum. As Tennessee enters what I believe is a favorable matchup with the Dallas Cowboys in Week 11, Titans fans shouldn't grow too attached to this projection. The Titans haven't finished with less than three wins since 2014, when they went 2-14.
1-8 won't last forever, and the sweepstakes for the first-overall pick have really just begun.

title: Grading Every Titans Position Group After Week 10: Defensive Ups and Downs Define Defeat vs. Jaguars
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans put up a valiant effort despite being severely undermanned, losing to the Jacksonville Jaguars 40-23 in this past Sunday's matchup.
This game was far more competitive than the score would indicate. The Titans are improving on a week-to-week basis, but the much more talented team pulled away... as things currently stand in the AFC South.
Nevertheless, there were a handful of discussion-worthy spot on either side of the ball as we ease out of the bye week and back into weekly football. So, let’s not waste any more time and get right into this week’s positional grades breakdown.
QB Cam Ward produced another strong performance against the Jags on Sunday. The second-year signal caller completed over 71 percent of his passes, totaling 231 passing yards, 39 rushing yards, two touchdowns, and one interception.
These aren’t numbers to write home about by any means, but there’s no denying how much he’s improved from Week 1 to now. Ward undoubtedly still has plenty of room to grow, but he’s quietly strung together a couple of games that should have Titans fans feeling optimistic about his potential going forward.
Over his last two games, Ward has completed 68% of his passes for 535 yards through the air, 80 yards on the ground, along with four touchdowns to just one interception.
And what’s most impressive is the fact that he’s done this without his best receiver and top two guards. At this rate, you can’t help but wonder what he could look like a year from now once Tennessee has turned its picks into actual players who could help the team.
It’ll be interesting to see how Ward closes out the season, especially once rookie WR Carnell Tate returns. But if this is the type of production the Titans get moving forward, then they should feel confident that they have their guy under center for the foreseeable future.
The Titans’ ground game was unable to find any kind of rhythm throughout the contest. RBs Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears combined for just 61 yards on 13 carries.
It’s hard for any running back to get going when you’re not even hitting 10 carries for the game. Unfortunately, the Jaguars’ high-powered offense essentially forced the Titans to throw more than they probably wanted. That unbalanced attack put the Titans in a position where they simply didn’t have the offensive firepower to match the team across from them.
The majority of Pollard’s production came in the passing game, catching a team-high eight catches for 66 yards and one touchdown. So, for that, I’ll give this group a slightly above-average grade. But make no mistake, for this offense to reach its full potential, they need the ground game to be more of a factor than it was on Sunday.
Given the context that this group was once again without their best player, it was a very solid performance overall. Sadly, it wasn’t nearly good enough to compete with an elite team like the Jaguars.
WR Elic Ayomanor led the way with 79 yards on five catches, while WR Xavier Restrepo sneakily added 31 yards of his own.
No other receiver on the team eclipsed the 20-yard mark, as WRs Wan’Dale Robinson and Calvin Ridley were once again non-factors throughout the contest. A looming divorce with both veterans feels inevitable at this point, so limiting their snaps as much as possible would be ideal going forward.
Look for Tate to have an even bigger role once he returns from his shoulder injury, especially if Ward continues the progress at the rate he is.
TE Gunnar Helm was unable to follow up his big game in Cincinnati with another strong performance. The Texas product reeled in just four balls for 23 yards, while TE Daniel Bellinger added a touchdown and six yards off his two grabs.
The two also played a part in the ground game’s shortcomings with their inconsistent blocking, so I believe a C- is more than fair for this mediocre-at-best performance.
According to PFF , the Titans’ offensive line allowed a total of 19 pressures and one sack on Sunday. RT JC Latham and LG Chandler Zavala led the way, each giving up three pressures on their 43 pass-blocking snaps.
Certainly not ideal, but a solid performance overall, considering they were down two starters along the interior.
Nonetheless, their lack of a run game starts with this group upfront, and with LG Peter Skoronski on injured reserve, this could be a budding issue that could become more of a problem as the season plays out.
The Titans’ defensive line combined for just six pressures and one sack between the entire unit. DL John Franklin-Myers led the way with three pressures, while DE Jacob Martin added two of his own along with the lone sack of the game.
But it’s clear that without DT Jeffery Simmons, this is a group that appears to be punching above its weight class more often than not.
Martin has had his moments, and to be fair, he’s surpassed everyone’s expectations to this point. But the reality is, he’d be much better suited playing opposite another dominant edge as opposed to trying to be the lead dog himself.
Not having a reliable pass rusher who can wreak havoc on a down-by-down basis is why QB Trevor Lawrence ultimately lit them up the way they did.
The Titans were down both starting linebackers in this one, subsequently forcing LB Cedric Gray into a full-time starting role for the first time this season, and he made the most of it, totaling nine tackles, five run stops, and one interception.
The  top tackler was among the best at his position in Week 10:
#Titans ' Cedric Gray posted a 90.5 overall defensive grade, per @PFF , highest of any LB with at least 10 snaps so far in Wk. 10.
Dorian Mausi also played the first defensive snaps of his career on Sunday, and he performed admirably, all things considered. Mausi finished with seven tackles and two run stops. Nothing truly notable at the end of the day, but they were hardly the defense’s biggest problem on a day where they got gashed for 459 yards of total offense.
Not every DB was bad on Sunday. S Tony Adams continues to be one of the most underrated players on the team, earning a team-high grade of 84.1 for his performance against the Jags.
But that’s pretty much where the positivity ends for this secondary. The Jaguars had their way with the Titans’ pass defense. WR Parker Washington, in particular, looked like prime Megatron out there with how unguardable he was throughout the contest.
Washington finished the game with seven catches, 152 yards, and one touchdown en route to a comfortable 17-point win. As for Lawrence, he completed over 71 percent of his passes for a whopping 352 yards, three touchdowns, and one interception.
The Titans’ trio of corners Cor’Dale Flott, Joshua Williams, and Alontae Taylor allowed a staggering 284 yards between the three of them, per PFF . As if those numbers aren’t jarring enough, the three of them were targeted a combined total of 20 times on Sunday, 17 of which were completed.
Those are unsustainable numbers by NFL standards. You can’t consistently win at this level when your starting corners are giving up nearly 300 yards on 85 percent of their targets, especially when facing elite quarterbacks.
The Titans don’t have the talent to overcome that type of offensive output, and until this gets cleaned up, the Titans will need to score a lot of points just to have a chance on Sunday’s.
This group as a whole had a solid outing, but K Joey Slye is what gets this grade to an A.
On top of nailing all three of his kicks from beyond-50, Slye went viral for a monstrous hit on Jaguars KR Josh Cameron that separated him from the ball. It was the type of hit we haven’t seen from many Titans defenders this year.
That type of effort, along with his perfect performance in the kicking game warrants the only A grade for the game. I don't make the rules (I do). Slye's all-time slam deserves a special nod on this 1-8 Titans team.
Shaun is a longtime Titans fan who has years of experience in the field. He missed being on the team beat, and is here to change that.…

title: 2 Major Reasons Why Titans' Performance in Loss to Jaguars Hints at a Breakout Coming in Week 11
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans have never made losing feel so tolerable as they have in the last two weeks. It's worth saying again that there are no moral victories; this football team is 1-8. That won't cut it in any circumstance.
Although, the Titans are improving. Slowly, steadily, but unavoidably. The Tennessee team from the past two weeks looks lightyears removed from the one that took the field in Week 1 vs. the New York Jets.
Robert Saleh has this group moving in the right direction, and their performance against the Jacksonville Jaguars yesterday suggests a breakout could finally be on the horizon. Here are three reasons to expect it when the Titans face the Dallas Cowboys on the road next Sunday.
Cam Ward, who we'll get to, started settling in right when his favorite target was sidelined with a shoulder injury. Leading rookie receiver Carnell Tate, along with starting LBs Anthony Hill Jr. and Cody Barton, were forced to miss in Week 10.
Today, Coach Saleh said the Titans are hoping to get all three back against the Dallas Cowboys next week. It was the defense that needed help yesterday, even with LB Cedric Gray making his case as a starter without his two teammates on the field.
If all three of Tate, Hill, and Barton return, it'd be at the perfect time on either side of the ball. Ward can only benefit from returning Tate, while the defense will get one of their top tacklers and foremost veterans back. That's a win-win, that could lead to an actual win.
Circling back to Ward, the Titans' QB is starting to look the part of a franchise guy. Ward has doubled his season-long touchdown count in the past two games compared to the previous six. He's settling into an up-tempo offense that, finally, looks crafted for him.
A showing from Ward akin to Weeks 8 and 10 against a non-playoff team, like the Cowboys, could finally yield the winning result Tennessee fans have been waiting on. Every game from here on out is about Ward's development, but at this pace, he appears capable of winning at least a few of them.
The sophomore passer has already cleaned up many of his consistent early-season mistakes. With two straight two-touchdown outings under his belt, it's about crossing the finish line for Ward from here. Week 11 is shaping up to be a promising opportunity to do so.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Titans' Worst Position Group is Also Among Their Most Expensive - Why 2027 Draft is the Only Fix
full_text:
For the second consecutive week, the Tennessee Titans have given up 40 or more points for the first time since 2014. On Sunday, the AFC South rival Jacksonville Jaguars handled the Titans 40-23 in Nashville. The week prior, the Cincinnati Bengals out-dueled Tennessee 43-36 in an overtime shootout on the road.
Against Cincinnati, the Titans allowed QB Joe Burrow to score six total touchdowns and 462 yards passing while completing 79% of his passes. He threw three interceptions in that game too, all intercepted by veteran S Amani Hooker, who was recently dealt to the Buffalo Bills.
Without Hooker, Jaguars QB Trevor Lawrence diced up the Titans secondary. By halftime, Lawrence reached a milestone by throwing for 234 yards, the most of his career in the first half.
Lawrence finished the game with a season-high 352 pass yards and three touchdowns while completing 71% of his passes. Tennessee LB Cedric Gray caught Lawrence's lone interception from a batted pass at the line of scrimmage tipped by DL Solomon Thomas.
According to PFF , CB Alontae Taylor was picked apart by Lawrence as he gave up seven receptions on seven targets for a whopping 143 yards. This is another disappointing performance from Taylor, who was recently signed to a three-year deal worth up to $60 million this past offseason.
Alongside Taylor, Joshua Williams allowed 86 yards from six receptions on seven targets, including a 25-yard touchdown to Jagaurs' WR Josh Cameron. It was clear busted coverage, allowing Cameron to be wide open at the goal line, which left S Terrell Burgess on an island to attempt to make up for Williams' error.
Williams was another signee from the 2026 offseason; he inked a two-year deal worth up to $8 million. Prior to joining the Titans, Williams won back-to-back Super Bowls as a member of the Kansas City Chiefs defense.
On Sunday, he allowed a near perfect passer rating of 157.4. That brings us to our third CB, Cor'Dale Flott. He signed a three-year deal worth up to $45 million to become a Tennessee Titan.
Against the Jags, Flott allowed 55 yards on four of six targets, including an uncontested back-of-the-end-zone touchdown to WR Parker Washington. Lawrence recorded a 135.4 passer rating when targeting Flott.
Washington was Lawrence's favorite target, recording a career-high 152 yards receiving with seven catches and a touchdown against the Titans. All in all, Taylor, Williams and Flott combined  to allow 284 of Lawrence's 352 passing yards and two touchdowns. From a combined worth of $113 million in contracts for the trio.
Those numbers are not an encouraging sign for the Titans' secondary, or the front office that assembled it. But improvement may not be far.
As of Week 10, the Titans hold the projected rights to the second pick of the upcoming 2027 NFL Draft with a bottom-dwelling 1-8 record. Additionally, Tennessee has ownership of Chicago Bears' first round pick from the Jeffery Simmons trade earlier this season.
The Bears stand at 7-2 and are contending for an NFC North title with fellow 7-2 rivals the Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings, while the Green Bay Packers loom with a 6-4 record. If the season ended today, the Bears-turned-Titans pick would be the 28th pick of the first round, per the aptly-named Tankathon.
There are three CBs on ESPN's 2027 draft big board projected to go in the first round.
Notre Dame's Leonard Moore is second on the entire board, only behind standout Ohio State WR Jeremiah Smith. The next CB on the list is Clemson's Ashton Hamption, who is projected to go ninth. Lastly, projected at 29th is Mississippi State's Kelley Jones.
These forecasts are obviously set to change until the draft is underway in late April of 2027. Nonetheless, if the Titans are looking to address an underperforming position group, having the Bears pick gives Tennessee flexibility to draft high with a talent like Moore and Hamption or wait for Jones later in the round. There are highly-touted options here.
Over the last couple of weeks, Tennessee's secondary has revealed itself to be the underbelly of a worsening defense. Expect the Titans' front office to try and fix their blunders at CB in the offseason.
Isaiah is an award-winning journalist and photojournalist. A graduate from the University of Kentucky, he has previously been published by BloodHorse, KY Insider, and the Kentucky Kernel for multimedia sports coverage. Isaiah is a Tennessee Volunteer at heart bringing his local expertise to Titans coverage.

title: Calvin Ridley’s Week 10 Snap Count Makes Titans Not Trading Him Even More Confusing
full_text:
Week 10 yielded a handful of promising results for the Tennessee Titans after their trade deadline decisions. The multiple draft picks speak for themselves, but keeping Tony Pollard around clearly paid off - Cam Ward threw him a touchdown. DE Jacob Martin, who was held, nabbed another sack on his way to a potentially record-setting year.
One outlier remains, however, in Calvin Ridley. The Titans' oldest WR came into this season as a veteran presence that could potentially help anchor the team's pass-catching core. It took very little time for that dream to die.
Ridley apparently wasn't moved at the deadline for the same general reason as Pollard: Ward needs as much help as he can get. But if that's the case for Ridley specifically, why did he have only four snaps yesterday against Jacksonville?
That's 7% of the total share with Carnell Tate sidelined. Ridley had no targets. Practice squad regular Xavier Restrepo had three receptions in his first extended appearance of the season. I hate to keep pressing the point, but Restrepo's three receptions in Week 10 halved Ridley's year-long total of six.
On those six receptions, Ridley has brought in just 91 yards. He has two drops on the year and, in one less game through the entirety of last season, Ridley had 17 catches. This is arguably the Titans' worst regression this year; Ridley's value has completely dissipated.
We can talk numbers all day, but they all point to the same conclusion: The Titans should've traded Calvin Ridley. Robert Saleh said today that he wants to do a better job of getting Ridley on the field, but at this rate, what's the point?
There was enough noise around Ridley in the trade market that this move should've been a no-brainer. With at least a baseline interest in Ridley being paired with Tennessee's relatively low asking price, we could've seen the Titans add more draft capital and lose basically nothing on offense as a result.
This is not to say that Ridley has exhausted his usage entirely, but the WR has long lost connection with the Titans' rebuild. Holdovers from previous coaching regimes generally don't fare well as is, but Tennessee drafting over the 31-year old receiver was the final toll of the bell for his role in Nashville.
With a contract that runs through the 2027 campaign, the Ridley question will now run through the offseason and into the following year, assuming the Titans don't make a move to cut off the water before then.
This isn't a debilitating mistake, but if the Titans were willing to trade two of their best players for draft picks, it makes you wonder why they'd hold on to Ridley and reject the same prize.

title: Commanders Daily: Bengals Allow Five Yards Per Carry. Pittsburgh’s Loss Is a Warning for Washington
full_text:
The Cincinnati Bengals have won five straight games; despite being on a roll, they do have weaknesses. The Bengals have allowed 1,115 yards rushing on 224 carries (5.0 yards per carry), including 11 runs of at least 20 yards. On the flip side, the Washington Commanders have rushed for 1,051 yards on 243 carries (4.3 yards per carry), a number that has slipped recently. Against the Giants, they ran it 33 times for 105 yards (3.2 yards per carry); the Commanders have produced seven runs of at least 20 yards this season and have struggled with consistency. Steelers running back Jaylen Warren ran for 127 yards in Pittsburgh's first game against Cincinnati. In Sunday’s rematch, the Bengals held him to 15 yards on seven carries in a 38–18 win. Pittsburgh still rushed for 102 total yards on 23 attempts, but the Steelers trailed 24-3 at halftime, limiting how often they could turn to Warren. After the game, Bengals safety Jordan Battle said, "The run is on the unit. We take pride in that. We got a lot of run stops and that was big." Against New York, Rachaad White had 47 yards on 11 carries, including a nice 18-yard run, and Austin Ekeler ran nine times for 26. Together, that was 73 yards on 20 carries. Jayden Daniels added 28 yards on 11 attempts. Washington will be attempting to move the ball against a front that includes two former NFC East defensive tackles: Jonathan Allen and Dexter Lawrence II. If they're being honest, the Commanders were glad to see Lawrence leave the conference after seeing what he was capable of two games a season while in New York. With Cincinnati scoring at least 31 points in five straight games, Washington won't be able to rely on a high number of carries alone to keep pace ; they'll need the run game to set the table for shorter third downs and help drives end in seven points. What they desperately need is for the rushing game to turn what looks like an opening with Cincy into meaningful gains without depending on Daniels to be Superman rushing the ball from the quarterback position. title: Can the Commanders Keep Pace With Joe Burrow Without Terry McLaurin?
full_text:
A month after tying the Giants, the Washington Commanders beat them 24–21 Thursday night and kept their season alive. Monday brings a familiar quarterback in Joe Burrow. Jayden Daniels beat him and the Bengals 38–33 in 2024. Now Washington faces the prospect of keeping pace with Burrow without Terry McLaurin.
Daniels, in just his third career game, began his iconic rookie-year scoring reel in Cincinnati, at a time when the Bengals were still respected as one of the NFL's feared contenders. His 27-yard pass to lead wideout Terry McLaurin was one of the most electrifying instances of the stars' immediate chemistry, as well as one of the first indicators of the potentially special underdog roster that Washington's executives had compiled.
The last time Commanders played the Bengals this happened pic.twitter.com/2vE16Ed63v
McLaurin caught four passes for 100 yards against Cincinnati in 2024. He’s out for the season after tearing his patellar tendon. Stefon Diggs caught the winning 32-yard touchdown against the Giants last week, and Antonio Williams scored from 31 yards out. If Monday requires the same kind of scoring from Daniels, those are plays Washington needs from its current receivers. Cincinnati’s defensive front looks different from the one Daniels faced in 2024. After Trey Hendrickson’s departure, Boye Mafe became a primary edge rusher, while Dexter Lawrence and former Commander Jonathan Allen added strength inside. Cincinnati’s defense gave up 36 points to Tennessee on November 1, so Daniels should have chances. The Bengals have since beaten Atlanta and Pittsburgh, holding the Steelers to 18 points Sunday while Burrow threw for 409 yards and four touchdowns . Cincinnati is 7–2 and has won five straight. Washington may need far more than it scored against the Giants to keep up Monday.
Beating the 7–2 Bengals would give Washington its biggest win since it upset the Seahawks in Week 3. At 3–5–1, the Commanders could claim a third victory in four games and remain in the NFC East race. Cincinnati has scored at least 30 points in five straight games. Washington has reached 30 only once this season, in its Week 3 win over Seattle. Diggs and Williams both scored against New York, but the Commanders will need more than a few big plays if Burrow turns Monday into another scoring race. Stopping Chase Brown on the ground is one thing; the Commanders have proven they can prevent the run. It's the Bengals' pass-catchers that Washington will have to worry about; beyond Brown, who's happy to rack up yards off of short check-downs and screens, the defensive backs will have their hands full with Ja'Marr Chase, fresh off 11 catches for 231 yards on 14 targets against the Pittsburgh Steelers, and overqualified WR2 Tee Higgins stretching the defense.
JOE BURROW MOOOOON BALL TO JAMARR CHASE pic.twitter.com/KRH1ULHSDX
The explosively acrobatic Chase is as threatening as any target the Commanders have had to try and neutralize this season, and that's including the masterclass that Puka Nacua put on at their expense just earlier this month. They took their time before getting their own ducks in a row out deep, but seem to have narrowed the playable cornerbacks down to Amik Robertson, Trey Amos, and Rasul Douglas, with Nick Cross and Jeremy Reaves expected to make the plays between the gaps at safety. Burrow, too, remains a challenge individually. He's posting league highs in completion percentage (74.7) and passing touchdowns (27) while keeping his usually high sack rate at a career-low 4.49%. On the other side of the quarterback battle, Daniels has impressed by completing 68% or more of his passes over four of his five performances since returning from the dislocated elbow, and he hadn't thrown an interception this season until the Giants picked him off twice Thursday. If the line holds up and the receivers keep producing without McLaurin, Daniels has a chance to keep pace with Burrow and move Washington closer in the NFC East. title: Commanders Open Door for Jacory Croskey-Merritt to Play Against Bengals
full_text:
The Washington Commanders opened running back Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt's 21-day practice window Tuesday ahead of Monday Night Football against Cincinnati. Bill will be eligible to practice while he technically remains on injured reserve, meaning the team will still have to activate him before he can be used. Croskey-Merritt originally went on injured reserve on October 19 with a groin injury and has missed the last four games.
Every Bill Croskey-Merritt rush from Week 5 #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/19ZT7Esq24
Before the injury, Bill had 239 yards and two touchdowns on 67 carries in five games. This included the first Giants game, his last game, in which he had 11 carries for 82 yards and a touchdown . If activated, Bill will rejoin a room that, in the past two games, has seen Rachaad White get 18 carries for 75 yards, and Austin Ekeler get 17 for 42, with both finishing with 52 yards from scrimmage against New York . White gained 47 on the ground. Ekeler ran for 26 and caught four passes for another 26. White played 37 offensive snaps to Bill’s 22 the last time they played together . If Bill is ready to go, Washington could give him a few of the carries White and Ekeler have been splitting. Ekeler can still get touches as a receiver if some of his work on the ground goes to Bill. Washington’s first practice for Cincinnati is Thursday. How much Bill does that day should give us a better idea of where he stands for Monday night. title: Commanders Daily: Joe Burrow Beat Pittsburgh’s Blitz. Why That’s Only Half of Washington’s Problem
full_text:
Monday night, the Washington Commanders will play host to a Cincinnati Bengals team that took the Pittsburgh Steelers behind the woodshed with a 38-18 divisional win in Week 10. On Monday, Bengals offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher laid down the gauntlet for opponents sending extra rushers: "Every time they blitz us, it is a big play opportunity for us," Pitcher said. "That's how we have to look at it." The quote was meant overall, but given the Commanders' blitzing percentage (35.7% according to Pro Football Reference ), defensive coordinator Daronte Jones should feel called out. According to Next Gen Stats, Joe Burrow completed all 12 attempts for 186 yards against Pittsburgh's blitz. The Steelers sacked him once but hit him three times. Next Gen Stats measured pressure on only 17.4% of his dropbacks, even though his average time to throw was 2.96 seconds. Running back Chase Brown put in the extra work and picked up early blitzes, an important part of why sending another defender did not necessarily produce a free rusher. Burrow acknowledged that Brown was a major factor in the process: "Chase's ability to do that has really opened up some things for us on third down." Burrow threw four touchdown passes against the Steelers; all of them came against four or fewer rushers. Three touchdowns came on plays when Burrow held the ball for at least four seconds, including two over six seconds. Cincinnati scored touchdowns on five of its six red-zone trips. That’s the other half of Washington’s problem. Sending extra rushers can give Burrow room to throw, but Pittsburgh’s smaller rush gave him time to wait for someone to get open. Washington has found pressure both ways. Against the Eagles, it recorded four sacks while rushing four or fewer. The extra rushers still did work: Washington generated 10 pressures on 12 blitzes against Philadelphia, although only one of those plays ended in a sack. Against the Giants, Nick Cross blitzed eight times and generated five pressures. Those games show Jones has options, but neither tells him what will work against Burrow and Cincinnati’s protection. Quinn said Monday that defending Burrow requires precise leverage and positioning . Can Washington reach Burrow quickly enough when it sends extra rushers, and make him move or throw sooner when it doesn’t?

title: Commanders News: Who Could Return for Bengals? Quinn Updates Four Injured Players | Burgundy Roundup
full_text:
With Washington getting a mini-bye this week after playing Thursday night and not having another game until the following Monday, this is the team's last chance to rest up before the stretch run to end the season. Washington can open running back Jacory ‘Bill’ Croskey-Merritt’s 21-day practice window this week. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn said Monday: "We haven’t decided yet, but he’s certainly trending in the right area ." Center Lucas Patrick remains in concussion protocol, leaving his availability for Monday uncertain. On the positive side, Quinn liked Nick Allegretti's strength and pass protection against the Giants. If Patrick isn't cleared by Monday, Allegretti remains the likely starter . Quinn had a Laremy Tunsil update, saying his latest doctor visit went well and that he is beginning the strength phase of his triceps rehab, with no timetable for playing. Also, linebacker Leo Chenal is back at the facility, which Quinn said has brought “a significant lift” to the team, but said it is too early to know what the future holds for Chenal. The finish against New York gave Quinn something he wants to see again. Washington got a defensive stop, Daniels led the winning touchdown drive, and the defense got another stop to finish it. After so many close games went the other way, Quinn said the feeling on the sideline was "not like here we go again, but like here we effing go." He believes a finish like that can carry forward during a season. The Commanders still have to make it happen again.
that time it was his 👋 @RasulEra | #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/WWr7bwtCIv
Washington trailed 21–17 with 5:31 left and had reached the Giants’ 24 when Jayden Daniels took a first-down shot to Chig Okonkwo. Jevon Holland intercepted it at the 2. Quinn liked the decision anyway. "We’ve got some guys that can take shots down the field," he said. Quinn wants Washington to keep testing defenses vertically; he said those throws can create more space elsewhere. Quinn called Ben Sinnott’s game against New York "the best game he’s played as a Commander." He singled out Sinnott’s downfield blocking along with what he did as a receiver. Kain Medrano could get more work on defense, too. Sonny Styles and Frankie Luvu have taken nearly all the linebacker snaps, but Quinn said he would favor finding Medrano some plays. Washington used him in a four-lineman package against Seattle, and Quinn pointed to his man coverage as a strength. Whether those snaps come against Cincinnati is still open. Deatrich Wise played less against the Giants because of how New York deployed its offense, Quinn said. Washington uses him inside on some running downs, and his experience matters with Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw on injured reserve. Jer’Zhan Newton is back, while Shy Tuttle and Tim Settle remain part of the group trying to replace what Washington lost inside. Dallas lost Sunday, but Washington remains third in the NFC East . The Cowboys and Commanders are now both two games behind New York. Cincinnati is coming off a 38–18 win over Pittsburgh , its fifth straight game with at least 30 points. Joe Burrow threw for 409 yards and four touchdowns, and Ja’Marr Chase caught 11 passes for 231 yards. Burrow and Chase are up next for a Washington defense still working through its coverage problems . One of the linemen protecting Burrow left Sunday’s game. Right guard Dalton Risner played 32 offensive snaps before a knee injury forced him out; Jalen Rivers handled the final 34. Zac Taylor said Monday that both of Risner’s knees were bothering him, but did not rule him out against Washington. Left guard Dylan Fairchild was limited last week by a pectoral injury and also left Sunday’s game in the fourth quarter. Receiver Andrei Iosivas, cornerback Jalen Davis and guard Brian Parker II practiced last week while working back from injured reserve, but none played against Pittsburgh. Cincinnati’s first injury report for the Commanders game should give a clearer picture.
Vernon Davis spent much of his NFL career away from Washington, but that's where his football story began. He grew up in the city, played at Dunbar High School and Maryland, and eventually returned home to finish his career in a Redskins uniform. Between those stops came the sixth overall pick in the 2006 NFL Draft, two Super Bowl appearances, and a championship with Denver. title: Commanders Still Have a Coverage Problem Joe Burrow Could Exploit
full_text:
The Washington Commanders beat the Giants last Thursday , but Isaiah Likely’s 66-yard touchdown didn’t disappear with the final score. He caught nine passes for 127 yards, and Dan Quinn said Monday that some of Washington’s coverages won't carry into the Bengals game. Quinn was asked about the room Likely found over the middle and what happens when the Bengals put Mike Gesicki in that area. During the break between games, Washington’s staff reviewed what to stop, start, and continue. One concern is what the defense gives up when it sends a blitz and plays zone behind it. “You just don’t want to be that vulnerable inside,” Quinn said. He did not identify the coverages he would take out or say what would replace them. Likely had already given Washington reason to examine that space . He caught 11 passes for 94 yards and two touchdowns in the teams’ first meeting . Add Thursday’s performance, and he finished the season series with 20 catches, 221 yards, and three touchdowns. Washington got the stops to win the rematch. It did not solve Likely.
Isaiah Likely was creating problems for Washington's defense all night. 9 REC, 127 YDS, 1 TD, 11 TGT vs Commanders. His connection with J.J. McCarthy was one of the biggest positives for New York. pic.twitter.com/FV1spG72fC
Quinn gave a separate explanation for the 66-yard score . On third-and-seven in the fourth quarter, Washington brought pressure. Quinn compared it with an earlier blitz that ended in Odafe Oweh’s sack, but said he thought Nick Cross hesitated when he had a chance to get to J.J. McCarthy this time. The coverage behind the rush was a fire zone with three defenders underneath and three deep. Quinn’s point on that play was that a blitzer cannot pause when he has a shot at the quarterback. His later concern about open space inside the zone went beyond that one snap.
What was Nick Cross doing here? pic.twitter.com/oXJYiFKu8L
Cincinnati can punish a blitz that stalls or a zone that opens over the middle. Joe Burrow threw for 409 yards and four touchdowns against Pittsburgh , with Ja’Marr Chase catching 11 passes for 231 yards. Tee Higgins gives him another outside option, and Gesicki has six touchdown catches this season. Quinn said Washington will need the right leverage and positioning because Burrow can throw to the space a defender leaves open. Protecting the middle matters, but the Commanders cannot lose track of what Cincinnati has outside. Quinn likes the defense’s improved communication and tackling. He also called explosive passes its last hurdle. The Giants win showed Washington can make late stops; Likely’s touchdown turned Washington’s three-point lead into a four-point deficit. Monday night will show which coverages Quinn and Daronte Jones trust against Burrow. title: Hughes’ View: Nick Allegretti’s Giants Start Should Change the Commanders’ Center Plan
full_text:
When Lucas Patrick went down with a concussion, rookie Matt Gulbin took over while the Washington Commanders ' original plan at center, Nick Allegretti, stayed on the sideline, a move I thought was odd . Against the Giants, with Patrick still out, the team turned back to Allegretti, who looked good in the process. All five starters on the offensive line played 69 snaps Thursday and surrendered only one sack (four pressures) to the Giants, after giving up five sacks in the first meeting , which ended in a tie.
"I gotta give a lot of love to the Commanders' offensive line." @willcolon66 gives credit to the @Commanders ' big men for their impact on the team's win against the @Giants 🙌 pic.twitter.com/0KWwxUWvzC
After the Rams game, Commanders head coach Dan Quinn said Gulbin entered because he had taken the most reps at center. Allegretti had been spending more time at guard. With Patrick in concussion protocol, Washington named Allegretti the starter before Thursday’s game . The bigger question is why Allegretti wasn't getting more reps at center during the week leading up to the Rams game. The Giants blitzed on 62% of Daniels’ dropbacks in the first meeting, according to Next Gen Stats . Following Thursday’s game, New York head coach John Harbaugh credited the Commanders for staying out of long third downs : "They got in the third-and-short too often. And they weren’t in the third-and-long enough. So, credit them for that." Those shorter situations also gave the Giants fewer obvious passing downs to attack Daniels . The better protection Thursday belongs to the whole line. Allegretti was still at center for every snap. At the very least, Allegretti earned the right to be considered at the position moving forward. Even when Lucas Patrick returns, if he gets the starting job back, Allegretti should still take center reps each week. title: Vernon Davis Q&A: Jayden Daniels, Redskins Homecoming and Life After Football
full_text:
Vernon Davis spent much of his NFL career away from Washington, but that's where his football story began. He grew up in the city, played at Dunbar High School and Maryland, and eventually returned home to finish his career in a Redskins uniform. Between those stops came the sixth overall pick in the 2006 NFL Draft, two Super Bowl appearances, and a championship with Denver. There is plenty of football to talk about, including how much the tight end position has changed, what Davis sees in Jayden Daniels, and what he learned during his years in Washington. But retirement hasn't exactly slowed him down. These days, Davis is acting, producing films, and pursuing an entirely different kind of career. In a Q&A interview with Commanders On SI, Davis answered questions about his NFL career, the modern game, his retirement, and his work in Hollywood. Here is the full exchange, organized by topic.
Philip Hughes : You came into the NFL as the sixth overall pick at a time when taking a tight end that high was unusual. When you watch the position in today's NFL, what has changed the most from the position you entered in 2006? Vernon Davis : When I came into the league in 2006, the tight end position was still viewed primarily as a guy who could block and make plays in the passing game when his number was called. I was fortunate to come in with the mindset that I could do both, but I also knew I was part of a changing position. The biggest difference today is how much the tight end has become a featured weapon in an offense. Teams are moving tight ends around the formation, lining them up in the slot, out wide, in the backfield—basically treating them like oversized receivers who can also block. The athleticism at the position has really taken off. When I watch today’s game, I see tight ends being asked to do things that weren’t as common when I entered the league. They’re creating mismatches against linebackers and safeties, stretching the field vertically and becoming major parts of the passing game. The position has evolved tremendously. That’s something I’m proud to have been a part of. When I was drafted sixth overall, there was a lot of discussion about whether a tight end should go that high. Today, I think people have a much better understanding of the impact an elite, versatile tight end can have on an offense. Philip Hughes : Your combination of size and speed was considered unusual when you entered the league. If a 22-year-old Vernon Davis entered the NFL today, how do you think an offensive coordinator would use him differently? Vernon Davis : I’d be a matchup problem every single week . They’d move me all over the formation and force defenses to decide how they wanted to cover me. If you put a linebacker on me, I’d take advantage of the speed. Put a safety on me, I’d use my size. The goal would be simple: create mismatches and get the ball in my hands. Philip Hughes : We hear so much now about tight ends being "matchup weapons," but the position still requires players to block defensive ends and linebackers. In your mind, what separates a great receiving tight end from a truly complete tight end? Vernon Davis : To me, a great tight end is somebody who can catch the ball and make big plays. But a complete tight end is somebody who can do it all. You’ve got to be willing to put your face in there and block a defensive end, block a linebacker, do the dirty work—even when you know you’re not getting the ball. That’s what separates you. You have to be a football player first. If you can block, catch, run and create mismatches, you’re a complete tight end. Philip Hughes : Which tight ends playing today do you enjoy watching most, and what specifically do you see in their games that you appreciate as someone who played the position? Vernon Davis : I love watching George Kittle. That guy plays with an attitude. He’s physical, he’ll block, he’ll catch the ball, and when he gets it in his hands, he’s looking to make something happen. I see a lot of the things I loved about playing the position in him. I also like Trey McBride. He’s got that toughness and versatility you want in a tight end. He’s not just out there trying to catch passes—he’s willing to do the dirty work, too. As a former tight end, that’s what I appreciate. I like watching guys who play the position like football players, not just big receivers. Philip Hughes : Defenses have become faster and more versatile since you played. Has that made life harder for tight ends, or has the way offenses create mismatches actually made the position more valuable? Vernon Davis : I think it’s made the tight end more valuable. Defenses are faster and more versatile, but that just creates more opportunities for a tight end who can do it all. If you can run, catch, and block, you’re a problem. Every time you line up, the defense has to make a decision—and that’s where you create the mismatch. Philip Hughes : From a tight end's perspective, what can the position provide a quarterback that a wide receiver or running back simply can't? Vernon Davis : I think it’s the versatility. As a tight end, you can help your quarterback in a lot of different ways. You can stay in and block, you can protect him, or you can release and go make a play down the field. And because you’re bigger than a receiver but can still run, you can create some real problems for a defense. When your quarterback knows you can do whatever the play needs, that’s a big advantage.
Philip Hughes : Washington currently has different types of tight ends in Chig Okonkwo, John Bates, Ben Sinnott and Colson Yankoff. How valuable is it for an offense to have tight ends with complementary skill sets instead of asking one player to do everything? Vernon Davis : I think it’s huge. You don’t have to have one guy trying to do everything. You can have a guy who’s really good at blocking, another guy who can go make plays in the passing game, and guys who can do a little bit of both. That gives your offense a lot of flexibility and makes it harder for the defense to know what’s coming. When you have a tight end room like that, everybody has a role, and you can play to each guy’s strengths. Philip Hughes : Okonkwo is an explosive athlete whose ability after the catch is one of the strengths Washington wants to utilize. When you have a tight end with that kind of speed, what are the best ways to create favorable matchups for him? Vernon Davis : You’ve just got to find ways to get him in space . Move him around, put him in the slot, motion him, line him up outside—make the defense figure out who’s going to cover him. Once he catches the ball, just let him do what he does. Get it in his hands and let him make a play. Philip Hughes : Ben Sinnott is now in his third NFL season. Tight end has traditionally been considered one of the more difficult positions to learn. Why can development take longer there, and what tells you that a young tight end is beginning to put everything together? Vernon Davis : It takes time because you’re really learning two positions at once. You’ve got to learn how to block, how to read defenses, how to run routes, and understand the timing with your quarterback. It’s a lot. For me, you know a young tight end is putting it together when the game starts slowing down for him. He’s not thinking about every little thing anymore—he’s just playing. He knows his assignment, he’s confident, and he starts making plays without having to think so much. That’s when you know he’s starting to get it. Philip Hughes : What does playing with two tight ends do to a defense before the snap? From a player's perspective, why can 12 personnel create problems even when neither tight end actually gets the football? Vernon Davis : When you put two tight ends out there, the defense has to think a little more. They’ve got to figure out what you’re doing—are you blocking, are you releasing, are you going in motion? You’re making them make a decision before the ball is…

title: Commanders and Cowboys Are Both Two Games Back. Why Is Dallas Still Second?
full_text:
Dallas scored 40 points Sunday and lost. San Francisco beat the Cowboys 46–40 , dropping them to 4–6. Washington had already done its part with a 24–21 win over the Giants on Thursday. The Commanders got help while they were off, but they’re still third in the NFC East. The difference is winning percentage. The NFL counts a tie as half a win and half a loss , giving Washington the equivalent of 3.5 wins in nine games. That’s a .389 winning percentage. Dallas has four wins in 10 games, or .400. There’s no head-to-head tiebreaker to apply; the Cowboys are still ahead.
Dallas began Sunday a half-game closer to first-place New York than Washington. Now both teams are two games back. That’s the ground the Commanders gained without playing. Dallas hosts Tennessee next Sunday, November 22, at 1 p.m. ET. Washington won’t face Cincinnati until Monday night. If the Cowboys lose, they’ll fall to 4–7 (.364), and the Commanders will move into second place before taking the field. They would still have to keep it. A loss to the Bengals in that scenario would drop Washington to 3–6–1 (.350) and put Dallas back ahead. And if both teams win next week, the Cowboys would remain second by an even thinner margin: .455 to .450. title: Commanders Midseason Report Card: Washington Is Wasting a Plus-Seven Turnover Margin
full_text:
This past Thursday's 24-21 win over the New York Giants gave the Washington Commanders their third victory in an up-and-down year in which they’re plus-seven in turnover margin but haven't been able to string together consecutive wins. In most seasons, we'd already be talking about the draft, but since the NFC East is still up for grabs, the eight games remaining on Washington's schedule still matter. The following grades are from the first nine games. Quarterbacks: B Jayden Daniels has thrown for 1,499 yards with 10 touchdowns, two interceptions, and a 97.1 passer rating in seven games, and has 280 rushing yards and two TDs in 42 rushing attempts. Both picks came against New York, which is precisely why his winning drive mattered: the offense had needed him to make up for possessions he had just given away. The elbow injury cost him two full games. Marcus Mariota threw four touchdown passes without an interception and looked good in relief before he reinjured his knee. Rookie Athan Kaliakmanis played in that game and went 15-of-33 for 186 yards, a touchdown, and an interception in London.
Jayden Daniels had an up and down night but came through late against the Giants. 23/33, 249 passing yards, 3 TD, 2 INT, 28 rushing yards. His late touchdown to Stefon Diggs completed the comeback for Washington. pic.twitter.com/NQZgUbb2Vr
Running backs: C− Washington has 1,051 rushing yards. Daniels has 280 of them. Rachaad White leads the actual running backs with 275 yards on 65 carries. Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt had 239 on 67 before his current trip to injured reserve, and Austin Ekeler has 109 on 33 since returning. White and Ekeler have helped as receivers, but the rushing attack hasn't provided a dependable answer when the offense needs a few extra yards. Blocking and play calls share in that result; the group grade reflects the overall production, not a claim that every short run is the back's fault. Wide receivers: B− Stefon Diggs has six of Washington's 15 passing touchdowns. His 36 catches for 386 yards lead the receivers, and the 32-yard winner against the Giants was his biggest play yet in the Burgundy and Gold. Rookie Antonio Williams has 28 catches for 326 yards and two touchdowns. He played 59 of 69 offensive snaps Thursday, more than any other Washington receiver, and has made a case for a starting role beyond this season . Treylon Burks has made 14 catches for 260 yards. Those contributions became more important when Terry McLaurin tore his patellar tendon and was lost for the season. The group has found answers, though it has not made the passing game consistently dangerous. Tight ends: C Chig Okonkwo has 27 catches for 263 yards but no touchdowns. John Bates contributes in the blocking game, where his five receptions don't tell much of the story. Ben Sinnott had one catch this season before Thursday . He caught four passes for 42 yards and a touchdown against the Giants, giving Daniels another option when the offense needed one. It was the tight ends' most encouraging recent development. One game does not rewrite what the group did over the previous eight. Offensive line: C− The center situation has supplied the clearest snapshot of the season. Lucas Patrick left the Rams game with a concussion. Rookie Matt Gulbin finished it, and Nick Allegretti started against the Giants after playing just two offensive snaps since Week 3. Washington allowed four sacks against Los Angeles. Allegretti played all 69 offensive snaps Thursday. The line gave Daniels much better protection in the rematch, allowing one sack and four pressures, although Brandon Coleman added another false start. Washington has allowed 21 sacks over nine games, with three players taking snaps at center. Sam Cosmi has played above the group’s C− grade. He has allowed just five pressures on 297 pass-blocking snaps. At Washington’s nine-game mark, PFF ranked him fifth among guards in pass-blocking grade—All-Pro-caliber work in that part of the game. The Giants' performance is the standard to build on, but it's not enough by itself to erase the earlier questions about the center plan. Defensive front: B− Odafe Oweh has five sacks, and K'Lavon Chaisson has 3½. Chaisson has also forced three fumbles. The team has 18 sacks and has allowed 934 rushing yards, roughly 104 per game. The run defense gives this grade some weight. Washington held Dallas to 66 rushing yards in Week 2 and Seattle to 44 the following week. Oweh had a sack, forced fumble, and recovery against Indianapolis. Daron Payne added a sack and forced fumble in the first meeting with the Giants. Chaisson has made that kind of play in three different games. The front has given the Commanders more than its sack total alone shows. The interior has changed since those early games. Payne and Javon Kinlaw went on injured reserve after Week 8, putting more on Shy Tuttle and Tim Settle as Jer’Zhan Newton returned from a torn pectoral muscle. Tuttle has two sacks, including one in the five-sack win over Philadelphia. Dorance Armstrong forced a fumble in that game that Charles Omenihu recovered. Five of Washington’s 18 sacks came against the Eagles; the other eight games produced 13 combined. The work against the run and the turnover plays earn the B−. The uneven sack production keeps it from going higher. Linebackers: B Sonny Styles leads Washington with 80 tackles. Frankie Luvu has 55 and two sacks. Styles’ 13 tackles against the Giants included a crucial third-down stop after Daniels’ second interception. He recognized the play before the snap , dropped McCarthy for a two-yard loss and forced a punt. Without it, there might not have been a final winning drive. Leo Chenal's season-ending neck injury removed an expected piece of the rotation. When Chenal went down against Seattle, Kain Medrano returned an interception 50 yards for a touchdown in a 33-31 win, on a play Styles called out at the line. Styles and Luvu have carried substantial work since. They have been among Washington's best answers on defense.
Sonny Styles’ INSANE play recognition led to his game-saving tackle against the Giants. The Commanders rookie LB is one of the SMARTEST apex predators in the NFL 😳🧠 pic.twitter.com/JCqOTPBNTc
Secondary: D Opponents have thrown for 2,341 yards in nine games. Isaiah Likely caught 11 passes for 94 yards and two touchdowns in the first Giants meeting. Puka Nacua caught 14 passes for 150 yards against Washington . Four days later, Likely went for nine catches and 127 yards, with 66 coming on a third-and-seven touchdown. Nick Cross has played better than the group grade suggests. Defensive coordinator Daronte Jones has moved him between deep safety, the box, and nickel , and Dan Quinn praised his nickel work after the Eagles win. Cross played all 75 defensive snaps against the Rams, finishing with eight tackles, three passes defensed, an interception, and a fumble recovery. He added six tackles and a quarterback hit while playing all 65 defensive snaps against the Giants. Rasul Douglas has three interceptions, and Trey Amos has returned to a significant role. Coverage, rush, and calls all affect a passing total. The repeated large games by opposing targets still make this the lowest grade among Washington’s position groups. Special teams: C+ Drew Stevens has been successful on 17 of 20 field goals and connected from 57 yards. He is 15-for-18 on extra points, with one of the failed attempts recorded as blocked. Those PATs have to be part of the grade, with the operation on each miss considered before assigning individual blame. Tress Way is averaging 48.7 yards on 40 punts. Luke McCaffrey has given the return game some life, including a 44-yard kickoff return against Philadelphia. The unit has produced field position. Its placekicking has been less even than the field-goal number alone suggests. Coaching: D+ The numbers Dan Quinn and David Blough can't talk around are the 40 conversions in 120 third-down attempts. Washington also ran…
